Before any model: the setup, the loss, the fit, and the honest measurement. 01foundation

Supervised, Unsupervised & Self-Supervised

Not which algorithm. Where the right answers come from, and when they arrive.

Every one of these differs in a single thing: where the right answers come from. Sometimes a person has already written them down for you. This email was spam. This loan defaulted. Sometimes nobody has, and all you can do is look for structure that was already sitting in the data. And sometimes you can manufacture the answers out of the data itself. Hide a word in a sentence and make the model guess it. Cut a patch out of a photograph and make it fill the hole. Nobody labelled anything by hand, but the training that follows is the completely ordinary kind, because you always knew what you had hidden. That third option is the one people describe wrongly, and it is the one that changed the field.

Like revising from a past paper. With the mark scheme attached you can check every answer, so you learn quickly. With a pile of unmarked essays you can only sort them into rough piles and hope the piles mean something. Or you cover the final line of a worked solution, guess it, then uncover it — you built your own mark scheme out of a book that never had one.

The taxonomy is about the label source, not the algorithm. Supervised learning has an externally supplied target, and the cost is annotation money and annotation latency. Unsupervised has no target at all, so you optimise a proxy — reconstruction error, within-cluster variance, density — and evaluation is the genuinely hard part. Self-supervised builds the target out of the input’s own structure: masked-token prediction, next-token prediction, contrastive pairs from two augmentations of one image. It then runs an ordinary supervised loss against labels nobody wrote. BERT and SimCLR are both supervised training on a manufactured target. Reinforcement learning is a different object: no per-example target, only a scalar reward from an environment you act on, plus credit assignment across a sequence of actions. If a supervised framing exists, take it.

Two neighbours worth naming. Semi-supervised sits between the first two — a small labelled core plus a large unlabelled pool, which is what pseudo-labelling and consistency training exploit. Weak supervision replaces the annotator with noisy programmatic rules, which is exactly what Snorkel’s labelling functions are. Underneath all of it sits label latency: a click label lands in seconds, a chargeback in weeks, a loan default in months. That number sets your retraining cadence, and it is usually what the question is really probing.

You reach for it when

  • Scoping a problem before anyone has picked a model
  • A stakeholder wants a model and no labels exist yet
  • Deciding whether to pay for annotation or pretrain on raw data
  • Someone proposes reinforcement learning for a ranking problem

The trap

Calling self-supervised learning a kind of unsupervised learning. Unsupervised has no target; self-supervised manufactures one out of the input — a masked token, the next token, two crops of one image — and then runs an ordinary supervised loss against it. The second trap is reaching for reinforcement learning because the problem sounds sequential. If you can log an outcome per example, you have a supervised problem and you should take it.

The math the only difference

supervised: minθ​E[ℓ(fθ​(x),y)]  ·  self-supervised: the same, with y:=g(x)The loss is the same object in both lines. In the second, the target is a deterministic function of the input — mask a span, hold out the next token, take another crop — so labels cost nothing and the training loop is unchanged. Reinforcement learning does not fit this template at all: there is no y, only a reward for the action you happened to take.

Making labels out of the data

import numpy as np

# self-supervised: the label is carved out of the input. Nothing is annotated.
tokens = tokenizer(corpus)                   # (n_docs, seq_len)
x, y = tokens[:, :-1], tokens[:, 1:]         # next-token: y is x shifted by one

mask = np.random.rand(*tokens.shape) < 0.15  # BERT masks 15% of positions
x_in = np.where(mask, MASK_ID, tokens)
y_out = np.where(mask, tokens, IGNORE_IDX)   # loss only on the hidden positions

# from here it is an ordinary supervised loop: forward, cross-entropy, step

Where this bites in production

BERT masks 15% of its input tokens and predicts them. SimCLR (Chen et al., 2020) takes two random crops of one photograph and pulls their embeddings together. Neither uses a single human annotation to pretrain, and SimCLR closed most of the gap to fully supervised ImageNet training. Yann LeCun has argued for years that the name matters — calling it unsupervised hides the fact that there is a target, and that the data supplied it.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Is self-supervised learning a kind of unsupervised learning?
No. Unsupervised learning has no target and optimises a proxy such as reconstruction error or within-cluster variance. Self-supervised learning constructs a target from the input — a masked token, the next token, a second crop — and then minimises an ordinary supervised loss against it. The labels are free, not absent.
You have no labels and a stakeholder wants a model next month. What do you ask?
Where the labels will come from and how long they take to arrive. Label latency sets the whole plan: a click lands in seconds, a chargeback in weeks, a default in months. If nothing arrives in time, the honest options are weak supervision with programmatic rules, a small hand-labelled seed plus pseudo-labelling, or an unsupervised proxy you can defend to the business.
When is reinforcement learning the right frame rather than supervised learning?
When the label depends on the action you took. Supervised learning needs a correct answer that exists independently of your model. If you only ever observe the outcome of the action you chose, and that action changes what you observe next, you have a bandit or an RL problem. Exhaust the supervised framing first — it is cheaper, more stable and far easier to evaluate offline.

Say this back tomorrow

supervised = someone labelled it  ·  self-supervised = the data labelled it  ·  unsupervised = nothing did
  • The taxonomy is about where the target comes from, not about the algorithm
  • Self-supervised manufactures a target, then trains in the ordinary supervised way
  • Label latency, not label count, is usually what decides the project

  • label latency
  • masked prediction
  • contrastive learning
  • weak supervision

02foundation

The Loss Function

Choosing a loss is choosing what you believe about the noise.

A loss is the sentence you write down that says how bad a wrong answer is. That sounds like bookkeeping. It is not. Squaring the miss says that a miss twice as large is four times as bad, so one wild outlier can drag the entire model towards itself. Taking the plain size of the miss says twice as large is twice as bad, and the outlier stops shouting. A third option behaves like the first near the middle and like the second out in the tails, so you get the smooth version where the data is well behaved and the calm version where it is not. And you can make the charge lopsided on purpose, when being wrong in one direction costs far more than the other.

Like a parking fine. A flat charge per minute is one policy. A charge that squares with the minutes is another, and under it a single driver who left the car all weekend dominates the council’s entire revenue plan. Neither is more correct than the other. They encode different beliefs about which offences you actually want to stop.

A loss encodes two assumptions: what the noise looks like, and how the two directions of error compare. Minimising squared error is maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise, and its minimiser is the conditional mean — which is why one outlier moves it so far. Minimising absolute error gives you the conditional median, and that is the actual reason it is robust. Huber is quadratic inside a band and linear outside it, so you keep a smooth gradient near zero and bounded influence in the tails. For classification you want a loss on probabilities: cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli or a categorical, and paired with a sigmoid or softmax its gradient with respect to the logits is exactly p−y. Hinge stops caring once you are past the margin. Focal down-weights easy examples by (1−pt​)γ, default γ=2.

Why not squared error for classification? Two reasons, and an interviewer wants both. Pushed through a sigmoid it is no longer convex in the parameters, so you inherit local minima you did not previously have. And its gradient carries a factor of σ′(z), which collapses toward zero exactly when the model is confidently wrong — your worst predictions learn slowest. Cross-entropy cancels that factor and leaves p−y, so a confident mistake produces the largest push available.

You reach for it when

  • A regression is being dragged around by a handful of extreme rows
  • A false negative costs the business far more than a false positive
  • Choosing a training objective for a heavily imbalanced detector
  • Someone asks why the model predicts the average and never the peak

The trap

Not knowing what each loss actually estimates. Squared error predicts the conditional mean and absolute error predicts the conditional median — that, not a vague appeal to squaring, is why absolute error is outlier-robust. The second trap is reaching for squared error on a classification head: through a sigmoid it stops being convex, and its gradient vanishes exactly when the model is most confidently wrong.

The math what each one estimates

MSE⇒E[y∣x]  ·  MAE⇒median(y∣x)  ·  BCE=−n1​∑[ylogp+(1−y)log(1−p)]The right-hand side of the first two is the part people miss. Squared loss is maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise and its minimiser is the conditional mean; absolute loss is maximum likelihood under Laplace noise and its minimiser is the conditional median. With softmax and cross-entropy, ∂L/∂z=p−y — no activation derivative survives, which is precisely why that pairing is standard.

The mean and the median, demonstrated

import numpy as np

def huber(r, delta=1.0):                  # r = y - y_hat
    small = np.abs(r) <= delta
    return np.where(small, 0.5 * r**2, delta * (np.abs(r) - 0.5 * delta))

# one dataset, one outlier. Watch which constant each loss would fit.
y = np.array([1., 2., 3., 4., 100.])
print(y.mean())      # 22.0  <- the MSE minimiser: the conditional MEAN
print(np.median(y))  #  3.0  <- the MAE minimiser: the conditional MEDIAN

# that single line is the whole robustness argument, and it is the follow-up

Where this bites in production

Focal loss arrived with RetinaNet (Lin et al., 2017). One-stage detectors were scoring on the order of 100,000 candidate boxes per image, almost all trivially background, and the easy negatives swamped the gradient before the hard ones were heard. Down-weighting confident examples with the focal term, defaults gamma 2 and alpha 0.25, is what let a one-stage detector match two-stage accuracy. It is a loss-function fix for a data-imbalance problem.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why not use MSE for classification?
Two reasons, and you need both. Composed with a sigmoid it is no longer convex in the parameters, so you inherit local minima that cross-entropy does not have. And its gradient carries the sigmoid derivative, which collapses toward zero exactly when the model is confidently wrong — your worst predictions learn slowest. Cross-entropy cancels that term and leaves p−y.
Your model predicts near the average and never the spikes. What is the loss doing?
Squared error is doing exactly what it promises. Its minimiser is the conditional mean, so on a skewed or heavy-tailed target it sits at the mean and books the spike as error. If you care about the typical case, move to absolute error or Huber. If you care about the spike, the answer is a quantile loss or a different target, not a bigger model.
When would you deliberately make the loss asymmetric?
Whenever the two directions of error cost different amounts. Under-forecasting demand means a stockout and a lost sale; over-forecasting means holding stock. A pinball loss at the 0.9 quantile prices that asymmetry inside the objective, which is far more honest than fitting on squared error and then nudging every prediction upward by hand afterwards.

Say this back tomorrow

squared loss buys the mean  ·  absolute loss buys the median  ·  cross-entropy buys a clean p - y
  • A loss is an assumption about the noise and about cost asymmetry, written down
  • MSE predicts the conditional mean, MAE predicts the conditional median
  • Squared error through a sigmoid is non-convex and vanishes when confidently wrong

03foundation

Gradient Descent & Its Batch Sizes

Everyone knows the update rule. The question is what you watch while it runs.

You are standing somewhere on a hillside in fog and you want to reach the bottom. You feel which way the ground slopes and you take a step downhill. Then again. The only real decisions are how big a step to take and how much of the map you consult before taking it. Consult every single example first and your step points in exactly the right direction, but you took hours to make one step. Consult one example and you can step constantly, though each step wobbles. Consult a few hundred and you get most of the accuracy for a fraction of the wait, which is why almost everybody does that. The wobble turns out to help: it shakes you off the flat ledges you would otherwise settle on.

Think of a supermarket queue. You could time all forty tills before choosing one, and be right, and still be standing there. You could glance at a single till and commit, and often pick badly. Or you glance at five, take the shortest, and move. You are wrong sometimes and you are through the checkout first.

Full-batch descent computes the exact gradient over the whole set: one update per epoch, deterministic, and above a few hundred thousand rows the memory alone rules it out. Stochastic descent uses one example per update — very high variance, but it converges in wall-clock terms because it updates constantly. Mini-batch is the practical middle, usually 32 to 512, and the real reason is hardware: a batch is one matrix multiply, so an accelerator is saturated at 256 and idle at 1. The gradient noise is not a defect you tolerate. It is what lets the iterate escape saddle points, which dominate high-dimensional loss surfaces far more than local minima do, and it acts as a regulariser — which is exactly why the large-batch generalisation gap exists.

What to monitor, in order: training loss per step, validation loss per epoch, the gradient norm, and accelerator utilisation. The last one is the one candidates never mention and it is usually the answer. If utilisation sits at 30%, your model is not slow — your input pipeline is, and no architecture work will help. Oscillation means the learning rate is too high, the batch too small, or the features unscaled. A plateau means the learning rate is too low, you are sitting on a saddle, or the gradients have vanished. Print the gradient norm before choosing between those three.

You reach for it when

  • Training loss is bouncing and nobody has touched the learning rate
  • An epoch takes eleven minutes and the GPU sits at 30% utilisation
  • Choosing a batch size for a model that barely fits in memory
  • Explaining why the loss stopped moving at epoch four

The trap

Assuming a slow epoch is the model’s fault. Nine times out of ten the accelerator is starved and the constraint is the input pipeline — decoding, augmentation, one worker, a synchronous read from object storage. Check utilisation before you touch the architecture. The second trap is describing stochastic noise as a cost you put up with. It is a feature: it escapes saddle points and it regularises, which is precisely why very large batches generalise worse.

The math one step, any batch size

θt+1​=θt​−η∇θ​∣B∣1​∑i∈B​ℓ(fθ​(xi​),yi​)Only ∣B∣ changes between the three variants. The gradient estimate is unbiased at every batch size; what changes is its variance, which falls like 1/∣B∣. So quadrupling the batch halves the noise and costs four times the compute per step — that diminishing return is the entire argument for mini-batch.

The loop, and where it actually stalls

import torch

loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(ds, batch_size=256, shuffle=True,
                                     num_workers=8, pin_memory=True,
                                     persistent_workers=True)   # the usual bottleneck

for xb, yb in loader:
    opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    loss = criterion(model(xb), yb)
    loss.backward()
    gn = torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)  # oscillating? clip
    opt.step()

# gn near 0 -> plateau or vanishing. utilisation under 40% -> fix num_workers, not the model

Where this bites in production

Goyal et al. (2017) trained ImageNet in one hour on 256 GPUs at batch size 8192, and it only worked with a linear learning-rate scaling rule plus a five-epoch warmup — without those, the large-batch run did not reach the same accuracy at all. That paper is the large-batch generalisation gap in one experiment: less gradient noise, a sharper minimum, worse test error unless you buy the noise back some other way.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why mini-batch rather than full batch?
Hardware first, noise second. A mini-batch is one matrix multiply, so an accelerator is saturated at 256 and idle at 1, and you get far more updates per unit of wall-clock time than one exact step per epoch. The gradient estimate stays unbiased at any batch size; only its variance rises, and that variance is what carries you off saddle points.
The loss oscillates, then it plateaus. What do you change, in order?
The learning rate both times, in opposite directions. Oscillation means the step is too large for the local curvature — lower it, clip the gradient norm, and check the features are scaled. A plateau means the step is too small, you are on a saddle, or the gradients have vanished. Print the gradient norm before you touch anything: those three have different fixes.
An epoch takes eleven minutes. Where do you look first?
At accelerator utilisation, not at the model. If it sits at 30% the GPU is waiting on data, and the fix is more dataloader workers, prefetching, pinned memory or a decoded cache — not a smaller architecture. Only once utilisation is high do mixed precision, a larger batch or a lighter model become the right lever.

Say this back tomorrow

batch size trades gradient noise for hardware efficiency  ·  the noise is doing useful work
  • The gradient is unbiased at every batch size; only its variance changes
  • SGD noise escapes saddles and regularises — large batches lose both
  • Check accelerator utilisation before you blame the model

  • saddle points
  • input pipeline
  • gradient clipping
  • large-batch gap

04foundation

Bias & Variance

Two numbers on a screen. Which of the two problems do you have?

A model can be wrong in two different ways, and they want opposite fixes. It can be too rigid to ever match the shape of the answer, so it misses in the same direction no matter which examples you feed it. Or it can be so flexible that it bends itself around whichever examples it happened to see, so a fresh sample hands you a completely different model. The first is stubborn wrongness. The second is jumpy wrongness. You can tell them apart from two numbers: how well it does on the data it trained on, and how much worse it does on data it has never seen. A strong first number with a large drop is the second problem. Both numbers poor is the first.

Like a darts player. One player groups tightly, a hand’s width to the left of the bullseye, every single throw: consistent, and consistently wrong. Another sprays the board, averaging out near the middle but never landing there. The first has bias. The second has variance. Practice helps the second player. Only a new grip helps the first.

For squared loss, expected error decomposes exactly into bias2+variance+σ2. Bias is the error from the hypothesis class being unable to represent the true function; variance is the sensitivity of the fit to the particular sample drawn; σ2 is irreducible. In a room you read it off two numbers rather than computing it. High training error is bias, whatever the gap looks like. Low training error with a wide gap is variance. The levers are opposites: bias wants capacity, interactions, better features, less regularisation; variance wants more rows, more regularisation, bagging, early stopping. Before any of that, on a gap wider than about twenty points, check the split — a grouped or temporal leak produces the same signature and no amount of regularisation will touch it.

Two caveats to say out loud. The decomposition is exact only for squared loss; for 0-1 loss and cross-entropy the intuition carries but the algebra does not. And it is not always a trade. More data cuts variance at no cost in bias, better features cut bias at no cost in variance, and past the interpolation threshold heavily overparameterised models show a second descent — so the classic U-curve describes the underparameterised regime and nothing beyond it.

You reach for it when

  • You have a train number and a validation number and nothing else
  • A colleague proposes a bigger model to fix a poor validation score
  • Deciding between buying more labels and adding regularisation
  • The leaderboard moved for everyone else and not for you

The trap

Reciting the definition. It is asked as a debugging question: given two numbers, which one do you have and what do you change first. The second trap is calling it a trade in every case — more data cuts variance at no bias cost, so “get more labels” is a legitimate answer that costs nothing on the other axis. The third is quoting the decomposition without saying it is exact for squared loss only.

The math squared loss only

E[(y−f^​(x))2]=bias2(E[f^​]−f)2​​+varianceE[(f^​−E[f^​])2]​​+σ2Exact for squared loss and nothing else. For 0-1 loss and cross-entropy there is no clean additive split — the intuition survives, the algebra does not. Saying that unprompted is a differentiator, and so is naming double descent: past the interpolation threshold the variance term stops behaving the way the U-curve predicts.

Read it off a learning curve

from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve
import numpy as np

n, tr, va = learning_curve(model, X, y, cv=5, scoring='neg_log_loss',
                          train_sizes=np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 8))

floor = -tr.mean(1)[-1]              # error on data it has already seen
gap   = tr.mean(1) - va.mean(1)      # how much worse on data it has not

# floor high              -> bias:     more capacity, better features
# gap wide at n_max       -> variance: more rows, more regularisation
# gap enormous            -> suspect the split before you touch the model
print(round(floor, 3), gap[-1].round(3), va.std(1)[-1].round(3))

Where this bites in production

Google Flu Trends is the public case. Ginsberg et al. (2009) selected 45 search terms out of 50 million candidates against 1,152 weekly data points, and the fit was excellent. By the 2012–13 season the system was predicting more than double the doctor visits the CDC actually recorded, and Lazer et al. (Science, 2014) traced it to a model that had fitted seasonal search behaviour rather than influenza. A near-perfect fit on 1,152 points is not evidence.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

0.98 train and 0.71 validation. Your next three moves, in order?
That signature is variance, but check the split before anything else. A twenty-seven point gap is more often a grouped or temporal leak than a genuinely flexible model, so run GroupKFold or a time-ordered split first. Then regularise: lower the depth, raise the penalty, add early stopping. Then get more rows — the only lever that cuts variance without adding bias.
Is bias against variance always a trade-off?
No. More training data cuts variance and leaves bias untouched. Better features can cut bias without adding variance. And past the interpolation threshold very large models show a second descent, so the classic U-curve describes the underparameterised regime only — which is worth one sentence, because it signals you have read post-2019 work.
Why does bagging cut variance but not bias?
Because averaging cancels independent errors, not systematic ones. Each bagged tree is low-bias and high-variance, and averaging B of them divides the variance term while every tree carries the same bias straight into the mean. That is also why a random forest adds feature subsampling — it decorrelates the trees so the averaging does real work.

Say this back tomorrow

high train error = bias  ·  wide gap = variance  ·  enormous gap = a broken split
  • Treat it as a lookup on two numbers, not as a definition to recite
  • More data cuts variance for free; nothing cuts bias for free
  • Exact for squared loss only, and double descent breaks the naive U-curve

  • GroupKFold
  • irreducible error
  • regularisation

05foundation

Overfitting, Underfitting & Learning Curves

Look at the curve before you touch the model.

Overfitting is when a model has learned the particular examples rather than the pattern behind them, so it looks brilliant on the data it trained on and ordinary on anything else. Underfitting is when it never learned the pattern at all and looks ordinary everywhere. The disciplined move is not to guess which one you have. It is to plot how well the model scores on training data and on held-out data as you feed it more and more rows, and then to read the shape. If both lines sit high and flat together, you have the second problem. If the two lines are still far apart when you run out of rows, you have the first. If they have already met at a level you are unhappy with, more rows will not save you and the problem sits somewhere upstream.

Like a student who memorised the past papers. Ask them last year’s question and they are flawless. Change one number in it and they are lost, because they learned the answers rather than the method. The tell is never their mock score. It is the size of the drop when you hand them a question they have not seen before.

The diagnostic is a learning curve: training and validation score against training-set size, not against epochs. Three shapes, three verdicts. Both curves high and converged means high bias — the hypothesis class cannot represent the function and more rows change nothing. A wide gap still narrowing at the right-hand edge means variance, and more data is the cheapest fix available to you. Converged at an error floor you are unhappy with means you are limited in a different dimension entirely: the ceiling is label noise, a missing feature, or a mismatched population, and neither regularisation nor capacity will move it. Only after reading the shape do you pick a lever. Dropout, weight decay, augmentation and early stopping act on the second shape and on nothing else.

Separating overfitting from a leak or a shift is a different test, and interviewers push here. Overfitting degrades smoothly, and its gap narrows as you add rows. A leak looks like an implausibly good validation score that collapses in production — you find it by dropping or permuting one suspect column and watching the score fall off a cliff. A distribution shift shows train and validation both healthy while production is not, and the test for it is adversarial validation: train a classifier to tell training rows from production rows, and if it succeeds, your populations differ.

You reach for it when

  • Validation sits far below training and nobody has plotted anything
  • Deciding whether buying 50,000 more labels is worth the money
  • A model is fine offline and mediocre the week after it ships
  • Someone proposes dropout as the first response to a poor score

The trap

Reaching for dropout or a bigger network before plotting anything. Each is an answer to exactly one of the three shapes, and you have not established which one you are looking at. The deeper trap is treating capacity as the diagnosis when the curves have already converged — at that point the ceiling is label noise, a missing feature or the wrong population, and every hour spent on architecture is wasted.

The math what a healthy curve does

Ltrain​(n)↑Lval​(n)↓gap(n)→0As rows are added, training error rises (there is more to fit) and validation error falls, and the two approach a common limit. If the gap is still wide when you run out of rows, more rows are the cheapest thing you can buy. If the gap has closed above your target, capacity is not the binding constraint — what you are looking at is σ2, and it lives in the data.

Plot it before you tune it

from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve, cross_val_score
import numpy as np

n, tr, va = learning_curve(model, X, y, cv=cv, scoring='roc_auc',
                          train_sizes=np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 10))
print(np.c_[n, tr.mean(1), va.mean(1), tr.mean(1) - va.mean(1)])

# gap narrowing at the last row  -> more data pays for itself
# gap flat and wide              -> regularise, or reduce capacity
# both curves flat and equal     -> stop tuning, go and look at the features

# leak or overfit? drop the suspect column and see if the score collapses
print(cross_val_score(model, X.drop(columns=['signup_ts']), y, cv=cv).mean())

Where this bites in production

Zech et al. (2018) trained pneumonia detectors on chest X-rays and got excellent held-out scores, then found the models had partly learned the hospital-specific metadata token burned into the image. Performance dropped sharply on films from a hospital they had not trained on. The learning curve looked healthy the whole time. Training and validation came from the same few sites, so the model was fitting the site and the split could not see it.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

How would you know it is overfitting rather than a leak or a distribution mismatch?
Three different tests. Overfitting shows a gap that narrows as you add rows on a learning curve. A leak shows an implausibly high validation score that collapses when you drop one suspect column, so permute features one at a time and watch for a cliff. A shift shows train and validation both healthy while production is not — train a classifier to separate training rows from production rows, and if it succeeds your populations differ.
Your learning curves have converged and the error is still too high. What now?
Stop tuning the model. Converged curves mean capacity is not the binding constraint, so dropout, weight decay and a bigger network all move nothing. Go upstream: check label noise and annotator agreement, look for a feature the model cannot currently see, and confirm that your training population matches the one you actually serve.
Why plot against training-set size rather than against epochs?
Because they answer different questions. Against epochs you learn when to stop, which is early stopping. Against training-set size you learn whether more data would help at all, which is a budget decision worth far more than a hyperparameter. An interviewer who asks about learning curves almost always means the second one.

Say this back tomorrow

both high and flat = bias  ·  still a gap at the last row = buy data  ·  converged and bad = look upstream
  • Plot the curve first: each of the three shapes has a different lever
  • Dropout and capacity are answers to one shape out of three
  • Overfitting, a leak and a shift look alike and need three different tests

  • adversarial validation
  • data quality

06foundation

Regularisation: L1, L2 & Elastic Net

Two penalties, and picking one is a claim about your data.

Regularisation is you telling the model that large coefficients are suspicious. You add a charge for size to the thing being minimised, so the fit has to earn every unit of weight it takes. There are two ways to charge. Charge the square of each coefficient and everything shrinks towards nothing but never quite arrives, so you keep every feature in a quieter form. Charge the plain size instead and coefficients get pushed all the way to nothing and stay there, which hands you a far shorter list of features. Which one you want is a claim about the data. If you believe only a handful of your columns matter, take the second. If you believe most of them matter a little, take the first.

Think of packing hand luggage. One airline charges by the square of the weight, so the honest move is to trim a little off everything and still take it all. Another charges a flat rate per kilo, and under that rule you leave whole items at home. Same suitcase, same trip, two completely different packing lists.

Both add a penalty on coefficient size to the loss. Ridge adds λ∥β∥22​ and shrinks smoothly toward zero without ever arriving; lasso adds λ∥β∥1​ and produces exact zeros, so it does feature selection as a side effect of fitting. The geometry is the answer an interviewer is waiting for. Restate the penalty as a constraint region. Constrain the coefficients to a ball and the expanding loss contour touches it, almost surely, at a point where every coordinate is non-zero. Constrain them to a diamond and the corners sit on the axes, so the contour meets a corner — and at a corner a coordinate is exactly zero. Elastic net mixes the two. Two practical notes: penalise standardised features, because the penalty is not scale-invariant, and never penalise the intercept.

The Bayesian reading is the one that lands. Ridge is the MAP estimate under a Gaussian prior on the coefficients; lasso is the MAP estimate under a Laplace prior, whose sharp peak at zero is exactly the belief that produces exact zeros. Ridge also has a second life that has nothing to do with overfitting: X⊤X+λI is invertible even when X⊤X is not, so ridge still returns a solution when the features are collinear or you have more columns than rows.

You reach for it when

  • Two hundred features and you suspect a dozen of them matter
  • Correlated features whose coefficients keep flipping sign between refits
  • More columns than rows, and the unpenalised fit will not solve at all
  • A stakeholder wants the shortest defensible feature list

The trap

Answering “L1 does feature selection” and stopping. The follow-up is why, and it is geometric: the L1 constraint region is a diamond whose corners sit on the axes, so the loss contour touches a corner and a coordinate is exactly zero. The larger trap: L1 is unstable under correlated features. It picks one of a correlated group arbitrarily and zeroes the rest, and a resample picks a different one. That instability is the whole reason elastic net exists.

The math the only difference is the norm

β^​ridge​=argmin∥y−Xβ∥22​+λ∥β∥22​  ·  β^​lasso​=argmin∥y−Xβ∥22​+λ∥β∥1​Ridge has the closed form β^​=(X⊤X+λI)−1X⊤y, invertible even when X⊤X is singular. Lasso has no closed form, because the penalty is not differentiable at zero — and that non-differentiability is precisely what produces the exact zeros. As priors: ridge is MAP under β∼N(0,τ2), lasso is MAP under a Laplace prior.

Scale first, then penalise

from sklearn.linear_model import LassoCV, ElasticNetCV
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# scale INSIDE the pipeline: the penalty is not scale-invariant, and fitting a
# scaler on the full frame before splitting is the classic leak
lasso = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LassoCV(cv=5)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print((lasso[-1].coef_ != 0).sum(), 'of', X_tr.shape[1], 'features survive')

# correlated columns? lasso keeps one at random. elastic net keeps the group.
enet = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                     ElasticNetCV(l1_ratio=[.1, .5, .7, .9, .95, 1], cv=5)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

Where this bites in production

scikit-learn’s LogisticRegression applies an L2 penalty by default at C=1.0. It has never been an unpenalised fit, and people routinely report “plain logistic regression” coefficients that are already shrunk. That default is also what quietly rescues you from perfect separation, where the unpenalised likelihood has no finite maximum and the coefficients run away. Zou and Hastie introduced elastic net in 2005 for the correlated-group case, on gene expression data with thousands of columns and dozens of rows.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why does L1 produce exact zeros and L2 does not?
Corners. Write each penalty as a constraint region: L2 is a ball, L1 is a diamond with its corners on the axes. The loss contour expands until it first touches the region, and touching a diamond almost always happens at a corner, where one coordinate is exactly zero. A ball has no corners, so the contact point generically has every coordinate non-zero. The subgradient argument says the same thing: at zero the L1 subgradient is an interval, so zero can be stationary.
Your features are heavily correlated. Lasso or elastic net?
Elastic net. Lasso picks one member of a correlated group arbitrarily and zeroes the rest, and a different bootstrap sample picks a different member — so the “selected features” are not stable enough to report to anyone. The L2 component of elastic net has a grouping effect: correlated predictors get similar coefficients and enter or leave together.
What is the Bayesian reading of ridge and lasso?
Both are MAP estimates under different priors. Ridge is the maximum a posteriori estimate with a Gaussian prior on the coefficients; lasso is the MAP estimate with a Laplace prior. The Laplace density has a sharp peak at zero, and that peak is exactly the prior belief which puts mass on coefficients being exactly zero in the posterior mode.

Say this back tomorrow

L2 shrinks everything  ·  L1 has corners on the axes, so it zeroes things  ·  elastic net keeps correlated groups together
  • Pick from a hypothesis: a sparse signal wants L1, a diffuse one wants L2
  • L1 zeroes because its constraint region has corners sitting on the axes
  • L1 is unstable under correlation, and that is why elastic net exists

07foundation

Train / Validation / Test — and Data Leakage

The score was never real. The only question is which line of code invented it.

You hold rows back so you can find out how the model does on data it has never seen. That only works if the held-back rows really are unseen. The commonest way to break it is dull and almost invisible: you clean the whole table first, then split. The step that fills in the blanks, or rescales the columns, or compresses them, has already read every row, so the averages it used carry a trace of the rows you were about to hide. The score comes back a little too good and nobody can say why. The second way is nastier. A column that looks harmless quietly encodes the answer, because it only ever gets filled in after the outcome is already known.

Like marking your own mock exam. You skim the whole paper first, including the questions you meant to save for a timed run, then sit down and take it. You are not cheating on purpose. You simply already know roughly what is coming, and the mark you give yourself is worth nothing to anyone deciding whether you are ready.

Leakage is any information present in training that would not exist at prediction time. The one you see most is preprocessing before splitting: fitting a StandardScaler, a SimpleImputer, a PCA or a target encoder on the full frame and splitting afterwards. Every one of those has now absorbed test-row statistics, and the damage is small enough that the score is merely flattering rather than absurd, which is why it survives review. The structural fix is not discipline — it is a Pipeline handed to cross_val_score, so every transformer is refit inside every fold by construction. The second kind is proxy leakage: a column that is a consequence of the label rather than a cause. Number of collection calls predicts loan default beautifully, because you only ring people who have already defaulted.

Have the taxonomy ready, because interviewers ask for the kinds by name. Preprocessing before the split. Group leakage, where the same user, patient or session lands on both sides. Temporal leakage from a random split on ordered rows. Duplicate rows, which is group leakage wearing a different hat. And leakage from the data-generation process itself — a field only populated once the outcome is known. The detection routine never changes: rank the feature importances, take anything suspiciously dominant, drop it and refit. If the score falls off a cliff, you have found it.

You reach for it when

  • A validation score arrives far better than anyone expected
  • Reviewing a notebook that calls fit_transform above train_test_split
  • One feature has three times the importance of the next
  • Rows repeat per customer and the split was random

The trap

Fitting a scaler, imputer, PCA or encoder on the full dataset and splitting afterwards. Each of those has read the test rows, and the result is quietly optimistic rather than obviously broken, so it clears review. The second trap is missing proxy leakage: a column populated only after the outcome is known reads as an innocent feature and is really the label wearing a hat.

The math whose mean, whose spread

z=σtrain​x−μtrain​​  ·  never μall​, σall​The subscript is the entire lesson. Fit the transformer on the training fold, then apply it unchanged to validation and to test. Inside cross-validation that means refitting it once per fold — which is exactly what a scikit-learn Pipeline does for you, and exactly what a hand-rolled loop forgets on the day you are tired.

The leak, and the structural fix

from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

# WRONG: the scaler has read every test row before a split exists
X_all = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)        # <- the leak, one line long

# RIGHT: every transformer is refit inside each fold, by construction
pipe = Pipeline([('imp', SimpleImputer()),
                 ('sc',  StandardScaler()),
                 ('clf', clf)])
print(cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=cv).mean())  # structure, not discipline

Where this bites in production

Kapoor and Narayanan surveyed machine-learning-based science and found leakage in 294 papers across 17 fields, from medicine to political science (Patterns, 2023). The commonest failure was not exotic — preprocessing or feature selection applied before the split. In the civil-war-prediction literature, complex models reported to beat plain logistic regression stopped beating it once the leak was removed. That is the reason scikit-learn’s own documentation tells you to put every transformer inside a Pipeline.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Where exactly in your pipeline did the leak happen?
Name the line, not the concept. The answer an interviewer wants is a specific operation and a specific ordering — the imputer was fitted on the full frame at cell four, before the split at cell nine. If you cannot point at a line, you are describing leakage rather than debugging it, and the follow-up is designed to find that out.
One feature carries three times the importance of the next. What do you check?
Leakage first, cardinality bias second. Drop the column and refit: if the score collapses, it was carrying the answer, and it is usually a field written after the outcome. If the score barely moves, you are probably looking at impurity importance flattering a high-cardinality or continuous column, and permutation importance on held-out data will say so.
Why does a Pipeline inside cross-validation fix this when a careful analyst does not?
Because it makes the correct order structural rather than remembered. A Pipeline refits every transformer on the training fold at each split, so the honest ordering happens even when nobody is watching. Discipline fails at the exact moment discipline always fails: late, under deadline, refactoring someone else’s notebook.

Say this back tomorrow

fit on train, apply to test  ·  and a feature that looks too good is a leak until proven otherwise
  • Any information in training that will not exist at prediction time is a leak
  • Preprocessing before the split is the commonest one and the hardest to spot
  • A Pipeline inside cross-validation makes the right order structural, not remembered

  • proxy leakage
  • group leakage
  • target encoding
  • fit_transform

08foundation

Cross-Validation, and When k-Fold Is Wrong

It is the default, and the default is wrong for most real data.

Holding out one slice of data gives you one number, and that number depends on which rows happened to land in the slice. So you cut the data into five or ten parts, train on all but one, score on the one you left out, and go round until every part has had a turn. Now you have five numbers instead of one, and the spread between them tells you how stable the model really is. Report the spread, not just the average. The catch is that shuffling rows at random assumes any row could sit anywhere. If your rows are in time order, or several of them belong to the same customer, that assumption is false and the rounds quietly hand the model answers it should never have had.

Think of a taste test with five judges. One judge tells you almost nothing, because you might have drawn the one who hates coriander. Five judges give you an average and, far more usefully, a range. If four of them said eight and one said two, the average of seven is hiding the single thing you most needed to know.

k-fold gives you a mean and a standard deviation across folds, and you quote both. Five or ten folds is the convention; leave-one-out only below about a hundred samples, because it costs n fits and has high variance. The interesting half is when not to use it. Time-ordered rows go to walk-forward validation — TimeSeriesSplit — so you never train on rows that arrived after the test window. Repeated measures, several rows per customer, patient or session, go to GroupKFold, so a group never straddles the boundary. A heavily imbalanced target goes to StratifiedKFold, so no fold comes back with three positives in it. Grouped and imbalanced at once is StratifiedGroupKFold, which exists because that pairing is extremely common.

Two things worth saying unprompted. If you tune hyperparameters with one cross-validation loop and then report its best score, that score is optimistically biased, because you selected on it; nested cross-validation puts the tuning in an inner loop and the estimate in an outer one, and it is covered properly on the hyperparameter-tuning card. And a mean with no standard deviation is a red flag in the room. A mean of 0.84 built from 0.83 and 0.85 and a mean of 0.84 built from 0.72 and 0.95 are different models, and only one of them is safe to put in front of anybody.

You reach for it when

  • Rows are ordered by time and somebody reached for shuffle
  • Several rows per customer, patient, session or device
  • Under a thousand labelled rows and one holdout looks noisy
  • Two models are half a point apart and you have to pick one

The trap

Two of them, and both are common. Random folds on temporal data, which trains on the future and reports a number you will never see again once it ships. And reporting a cross-validation mean with no standard deviation — a documented red-flag answer, because the spread is the only evidence you have about fold stability, and a mean of 0.84 assembled from 0.72 and 0.95 is not a result anybody can act on.

The math always both halves

s=k1​∑i=1k​si​;±;sd(si​)The term after the plus-or-minus is the one candidates drop and the one that carries information. A wide spread means fold-to-fold instability: too few rows, a leaky group, or a model far too flexible for the data you have. Quote the mean on its own and you have thrown away the only stability evidence the procedure produced.

Pick the splitter from the data, not from habit

from sklearn.model_selection import (TimeSeriesSplit, GroupKFold,
                                     StratifiedGroupKFold, cross_val_score)

# imbalanced AND several rows per customer -> the combined splitter
cv = StratifiedGroupKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
s = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, groups=customer_id, cv=cv,
                    scoring='average_precision')

print(f'{s.mean():.3f} +/- {s.std():.3f}')   # never the mean on its own
print(s.round(3))                            # and look at the folds themselves

# time-ordered instead? TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, gap=30), and no shuffling at all

Where this bites in production

scikit-learn’s cross_val_score picks StratifiedKFold for a classifier and plain KFold for a regressor, and in both cases shuffle defaults to False — so the folds are contiguous blocks of your dataframe in whatever order it arrived. A file sorted by date is leaking before you have written a line. Medical datasets learned this early: CheXpert (Irvin et al., 2019) is split so that no patient appears in more than one of train, validation and test, because one patient contributes many images.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

When would you NOT use k-fold?
Four situations, and each has its own splitter. Time-ordered rows go to walk-forward validation with TimeSeriesSplit. Repeated measures per customer or patient go to GroupKFold. A heavily imbalanced target goes to StratifiedKFold so no fold comes back nearly empty of positives. Grouped and imbalanced together is StratifiedGroupKFold.
Your five folds are 0.91, 0.79, 0.88, 0.83 and 0.79. What do you report?
The mean and the spread, then go and find the cause. That is 0.84 with a standard deviation of about 0.05, which is wide enough that a rival model half a point ahead is indistinguishable from this one. Wide fold variance usually means too few rows, a group concentrated in one fold, or a model with more capacity than the data can support.
You tuned with GridSearchCV and reported its best cross-validated score. What is wrong with it?
It is optimistically biased, because you selected on it. Searching a hundred configurations and reporting the maximum is reporting the luckiest fold assignment, not the expected performance. Nested cross-validation fixes it: the inner loop tunes, the outer loop estimates, and the outer number is the one you quote.

Say this back tomorrow

five numbers, not one  ·  and never the mean without its standard deviation
  • The default assumes rows are exchangeable, and real rows usually are not
  • Time goes to TimeSeriesSplit, groups to GroupKFold, both to StratifiedGroupKFold
  • A mean with no standard deviation hides fold instability and reads as a red flag

  • StratifiedGroupKFold
  • nested CV
  • fold variance

09foundation

The Confusion Matrix & the Threshold

Four cells, two prices, and one number nobody told you that you were allowed to change.

Every classifier makes two kinds of mistake and they almost never cost the same. Miss a fraudulent payment and you refund it. Stop a genuine one and you have insulted a customer who may not come back. Write the four outcomes into a small square: caught, missed, wrongly stopped, correctly left alone. Then put a price on the two mistakes, because the business already has one even if nobody has written it down. Once the prices exist, the cut-off becomes a lever. Most models hand back a score somewhere between nothing and certainty, and somebody decided long ago to call anything past the halfway mark positive. That halfway mark is a convention, not a result, and moving it is usually the cheapest improvement available to you.

Like a smoke alarm. Set it sensitive and it shrieks every time you make toast, so within a fortnight somebody has taken the battery out. Set it dull and it stays politely quiet through an actual fire. There is no correct sensitivity in the abstract. There is only the one that matches what a false alarm costs you against what a missed fire costs you.

Start from the four cells and immediately attach money. On a fraud book at one percent positives, a false negative is the chargeback plus the write-off; a false positive is a declined payment, a support contact and some churn risk. Once those two numbers exist, the threshold is a free parameter you optimise rather than a constant you inherit, and there are four principled ways to pick it. Expected value: sweep the threshold and take the one maximising the value of true positives minus the cost of false positives. Maximum F-beta, when you can state the relative weight of the two errors but not their prices. Youden’s J, true positive rate minus false positive rate, which is correct only under symmetric costs. Or a constraint — precision at least 0.90, maximise recall — which is how review queues are actually specified.

Three practical notes. Tune the threshold on validation and quote it on test, otherwise you have simply relocated the overfitting. The optimal threshold moves when the base rate moves, so a fraud model shipped in November needs a re-tuned cut-off in December rather than a retrain. And thresholding changes decisions, not probabilities: if anything downstream consumes the score as a probability — an expected-loss calculation, a pricing rule — keep the calibrated score and apply the threshold at the point of action, not before.

You reach for it when

  • A model with excellent accuracy is catching almost nothing
  • Finance can price a chargeback and nobody has asked them
  • Setting the cut-off for a manual review queue
  • The base rate moved and alert volume tripled overnight

The trap

Describing the four cells and stopping there. It is a business question — which mistake costs more, and what does that do to the cut-off. The second trap is leaving the threshold at 0.5 because that is what predict returns. Nothing about 0.5 is optimal; it is the point where the model believes the two classes are equally likely, which is the right decision only when the two errors cost the same.

The math the threshold is a decision

t⋆=argmaxt​;[TP(t)⋅V;−;FP(t)⋅C]With symmetric costs this collapses to Youden’s J, true positive rate minus false positive rate. Under a service constraint it becomes: among all thresholds with precision at least 0.90, take the one with the highest recall. All three are the same move — sweep the threshold on validation, score every candidate against the objective you actually have, and pick one.

Sweeping the threshold on validation

import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve

p = model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]
prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve(y_val, p)

VALUE, COST = 220, 12                       # a fraud stopped, a customer annoyed
tp = np.array([((p >= t) & (y_val == 1)).sum() for t in thr])
fp = np.array([((p >= t) & (y_val == 0)).sum() for t in thr])
print(thr[np.argmax(tp * VALUE - fp * COST)])   # rarely anywhere near 0.5

ok = prec[:-1] >= 0.90                      # or a constraint instead of a price
print(thr[ok][np.argmax(rec[:-1][ok])])     # best recall that still clears 0.90

Where this bites in production

scikit-learn’s predict hard-codes 0.5 for a binary classifier, and for years that was the only operating point most deployed models ever ran at. Version 1.5, released in 2024, added TunedThresholdClassifierCV and FixedThresholdClassifier for precisely this reason: the library now treats the cut-off as something you fit on validation against a scoring function you supply, rather than a constant baked into a method call.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Which error is more expensive here, and what does that do to your threshold?
Ask what each mistake costs, then move the threshold towards the cheaper one. If a missed fraud costs 220 and a false alarm costs 12, you should be happy to raise roughly eighteen false alarms per fraud you catch, which means a threshold far below 0.5. State the two numbers out loud — the interviewer is checking whether you reach for the business before the model.
Name the four principled ways to choose a threshold.
Expected value, maximum F-beta, Youden’s J, or a constraint. Expected value needs prices for both errors and is the strongest when you can get them. F-beta needs only a relative weight. Youden’s J assumes symmetric costs, so it is the weakest of the four. A constraint — precision at least 0.90, maximise recall — is how most review queues are specified, because analyst hours are fixed.
Your model has 99% accuracy on a 1% fraud problem. What is your first sentence?
That a model predicting legitimate every single time scores 99% too. Accuracy is untrustworthy past roughly five to one imbalance and meaningless at a hundred to one, so the number carries no information about whether the model works. Ask instead for the confusion matrix, the precision and recall at the operating point, and the prevalence.

Say this back tomorrow

four cells, two prices, one lever  ·  and 0.5 was never a result
  • Attach a cost to a false positive and a false negative before you tune anything
  • The threshold is a free parameter, chosen on validation, not inherited from predict
  • Expected value, max F-beta, Youden’s J, or a constraint — pick one and say why

10foundation

Precision, Recall, F1 & F-beta

F1 is a choice about which mistake hurts more. It is not a neutral default.

Two questions, and they are not the same question. Of everything the model flagged, how much of it was real? And of everything that was real, how much did the model flag? A model that flags absolutely everything catches all of it and is almost never right. A model that flags the single case it is certain about is right every time and misses the rest. You can squash the two into one score, and people usually do, but that single score quietly assumes the two mistakes matter equally. Often they do not. If you are screening for a disease and the next step is a cheap second test, you want the catching side. If every flag costs an analyst an hour of their afternoon, you want the being-right side. Say which, and say why.

Like a fishing net. A fine net dragged across the whole lake brings up every trout you were after, along with a great deal of weed and half a bicycle. A single baited hook brings up a trout or nothing at all. Neither is better in the abstract. It depends entirely on whether you are paid by the trout or charged by the kilo of weed.

Precision is true positives over everything you flagged. Recall is true positives over everything that was actually positive. They trade against each other as the threshold moves, so either one quoted alone is meaningless. F1 is their harmonic mean, and the harmonic mean is chosen because it punishes the lopsided case — recall 0.95 with precision 0.05 gives an F1 of 0.095, where the arithmetic mean would have said 0.50. But F1 is a choice, not a neutral default. It fixes the relative weight of the two errors at one to one, and you have to defend that. F-beta lets you state the weight instead: beta above one favours recall, so F2 is the screening metric, and beta below one favours precision, so F0.5 is right when a false positive is expensive.

Two imbalance-robust alternatives worth naming unprompted. Matthews correlation coefficient uses all four cells of the confusion matrix, so unlike F1 it cannot be flattered by a huge true-negative block sitting outside the formula, and it stays near zero for a model barely better than chance. Balanced accuracy is the mean of sensitivity and specificity, easier to explain to a stakeholder but still generous when the negative class is enormous. And precision and recall mean nothing without a stated threshold: quoted with no operating point, they are one arbitrary row of a curve.

You reach for it when

  • Choosing the headline metric before anybody has modelled anything
  • A screening model where a miss is far worse than a false alarm
  • A review queue with a fixed number of analyst hours a day
  • Someone reports F1 and cannot say why the weights are equal

The trap

Reaching for F1 because it is what the docs use. F1 weights precision and recall equally, which is a claim about your business you have to defend out loud. If a missed case costs a hundred times a false alarm, F1 is the wrong objective and F2 is nearer. The second trap is answering the 0.95 and 0.05 question with a verdict instead of a question. The correct reply is: what happens to a flagged case, and who pays for it?

The math beta is a weight you chose

Fβ​=β2P+R(1+β2)PR​  ·  F1​=2TP+FP+FN2TP​Setting beta to one is not neutrality — it is the specific claim that a false negative and a false positive cost the same amount. Beta of two weights recall roughly four times as heavily, which is why F2 is the screening default. The second form makes the omission explicit: true negatives appear nowhere in F1, which is both why it survives imbalance and why MCC is the safer one-number summary.

The same predictions, scored five ways

from sklearn.metrics import (precision_recall_fscore_support, fbeta_score,
                             matthews_corrcoef, balanced_accuracy_score)

p, r, f1, _ = precision_recall_fscore_support(y, yhat, average='binary')
print(p, r, f1)                          # 0.050  0.950  0.095 <- harmonic mean bites

print(fbeta_score(y, yhat, beta=2))      # 0.207  screening: a miss costs more
print(fbeta_score(y, yhat, beta=0.5))    # 0.062  queue: a false alarm costs more

print(matthews_corrcoef(y, yhat))        # 0.216  uses all four cells
print(balanced_accuracy_score(y, yhat))  # 0.966  still generous. know why.

Where this bites in production

Kaggle’s Planet: Understanding the Amazon from Space competition (2017) was scored on mean F2, not F1, because it was multi-label land-use tagging where missing a tag mattered more than adding a spare one. That choice sat in the problem statement before anybody modelled anything, and it changed what every top solution optimised. The mirror image is a bank review queue, where analyst hours are fixed and the specification reads “precision at least 0.90, maximise recall” — an F0.5 world.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Your recall is 0.95 and precision 0.05 — is the model good?
Ask what happens to a flagged case before you answer. If a flag triggers a cheap automatic second test, catching 95% of cases for nineteen false alarms apiece may be excellent. If a flag consumes an analyst hour, you are asking for nineteen wasted hours per real find and the model is unusable. The number is not good or bad; the workflow behind it decides.
Why is F1 the harmonic mean rather than the arithmetic mean?
Because the harmonic mean refuses to reward a lopsided pair. Precision 0.05 with recall 0.95 has an arithmetic mean of 0.50, which would rank a useless model as average. The harmonic mean gives 0.095, because it is dominated by the smaller of the two. That is the whole reason for the choice, and it is a common follow-up.
When would you report MCC instead of F1?
When the negative class is large and you want a number that cannot be gamed. F1 ignores true negatives entirely, so it says nothing about how the model behaves on the bulk of the data. MCC uses all four cells, sits near zero for chance-level performance whichever way the imbalance runs, and is symmetric if you swap the class labels. F1 is not.

Say this back tomorrow

precision = of what you flagged  ·  recall = of what was there  ·  F1 is a choice, not a default
  • Neither number means anything without the other and without a stated threshold
  • F1 fixes the weight at one to one; F2 screens, F0.5 protects a queue
  • MCC uses all four cells, so it is the harder number to flatter

11foundation

ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC, and Why Accuracy Lies

What is the baseline PR-AUC? Almost everybody says 0.5.

Accuracy is the share of predictions you got right, and on a rare event it is close to useless. If one payment in a hundred is fraudulent, a model that waves everything through is right ninety-nine times out of a hundred and has caught nothing whatsoever. So people move from a single number to a curve. The first curve weighs how many real cases you caught against how many false alarms you raised as a share of all the ordinary cases — and when the ordinary cases outnumber the rare ones a hundred to one, that share barely budges no matter how badly you behave, so the curve flatters you. The second curve weighs catching against being right, and it has nowhere to hide.

Like judging a metal detector on a beach. Score it on how much of the sand it correctly ignored and it looks magnificent, because almost all of it is sand. The only two figures anyone doing the digging cares about are how many rings you found and how many times you knelt down for a bottle top.

Accuracy is untrustworthy past roughly five to one imbalance and meaningless at a hundred to one. ROC-AUC is the probability that a random positive scores above a random negative, and its random baseline is 0.5. PR-AUC has a random baseline equal to the positive-class prevalence — at one percent positives the baseline is 0.01, so a PR-AUC of 0.31 is thirty-one times chance and not a poor result. Almost everybody answers 0.5 to that, and it is the cleanest single discriminator in the whole metrics conversation. The reason ROC flatters under imbalance is the denominator of the false positive rate: it divides by every negative, so at ninety-nine percent negatives you can raise thousands of false alarms and shift that axis by a fraction of a point. Below roughly ten percent positives, report PR-AUC.

Then break the aggregate apart. Slice-based evaluation is the point Chip Huyen makes in Designing Machine Learning Systems and candidates never raise: one number across the whole test set hides a subgroup the model is failing badly, and the aggregate can improve in the same quarter that a slice collapses. Slice by whatever the business would be embarrassed by — device, region, tenure band, new versus returning, language — and report the worst slice next to the mean. The same holds for calibration: a model calibrated on the full test set is routinely miscalibrated inside every slice of it.

You reach for it when

  • Fewer than one positive in ten and somebody quoted accuracy
  • Two models both look excellent on ROC and you must choose
  • Picking the headline metric for a fraud, churn or screening model
  • The aggregate metric is flat and the support queue is not

The trap

Using ROC-AUC on a one-percent-positive problem. The false-positive-rate denominator is every negative, and the negatives are ninety-nine percent of the data, so thousands of false alarms move that axis barely at all and the curve looks superb. The second trap is answering 0.5 for the baseline PR-AUC. It is the positive-class prevalence — 0.01 on that same dataset — so a model scoring 0.31 is running thirty-one times better than chance.

The math two baselines, two different numbers

ROC-AUC=P(s(x+)>s(x−)), baseline 0.5  ·  PR-AUCrandom​=π=P(y=1)The second equality is the whole card. A random scorer traces a flat precision line at the prevalence, so the area beneath it is the prevalence. Quote a PR-AUC without the prevalence beside it and nobody can interpret the number, including you. The first line also explains why ROC-AUC is a pure ranking measure: it never looks at the calibration of the scores, only at their order.

Print the prevalence next to the number

import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, average_precision_score

prevalence = y_test.mean()               # 0.010 <- print this every single time
print(roc_auc_score(y_test, p),          # 0.94  against a baseline of 0.50
      average_precision_score(y_test, p)) # 0.31  against a baseline of 0.010

for name, mask in slices.items():        # device, region, tenure band, locale
    ap = average_precision_score(y_test[mask], p[mask])
    print(f'{name:>12} n={mask.sum():>6} AP={ap:.3f} base={y_test[mask].mean():.3f}')

# the aggregate can rise in the same week a slice falls off a cliff. report the worst.

Where this bites in production

Saito and Rehmsmeier (PLOS ONE, 2015) showed the failure directly: on imbalanced data a ROC plot can look near-identical for a good classifier and a badly degraded one, while the precision-recall plot separates them cleanly. Davis and Goadrich (ICML, 2006) had already proved the two are linked — a curve dominating in ROC space dominates in PR space — but the areas are not, so two models can swap places depending on which one you report.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What is the baseline PR-AUC?
The positive-class prevalence, not 0.5. A random scorer produces a flat precision line at the base rate, so the area under it equals the base rate. On a dataset with 1% positives the baseline is 0.01, which means a PR-AUC of 0.31 is thirty-one times chance. Most candidates transfer the ROC answer and say 0.5, and that single slip is what the question is built to catch.
Why does ROC-AUC flatter a model at 1% positives?
Because of the false-positive-rate denominator. FPR divides false positives by every negative, and the negatives are 99% of the data, so a model can raise several thousand false alarms and shift that axis by a fraction of a point. Precision divides by the flagged set instead, which is small, so it reacts immediately. Below about ten percent positives, report PR-AUC.
Your aggregate AUC held steady all quarter and complaints doubled. What did you not look at?
Slices. One number across the whole test set can stay flat while a subgroup degrades badly, because the subgroup is small enough to be invisible in the mean. Slice by device, region, tenure, locale and new versus returning, then report the worst slice beside the aggregate. The same applies to calibration, which is routinely fine overall and wrong inside every slice.

Say this back tomorrow

ROC baseline is 0.5  ·  PR baseline is the prevalence  ·  and the aggregate hides the slice
  • Accuracy is untrustworthy past roughly five to one imbalance
  • ROC flatters under imbalance because its denominator is all the negatives
  • Report the worst slice next to the mean, or the mean is doing the hiding

  • slice-based eval
  • class imbalance

12core

Linear Regression & Its Assumptions

A model is a list of assumptions, and each one has its own failure mode.

Fit a straight line through a cloud of points and you have made a set of promises without noticing. That the relationship really is a straight one. That the error on one row tells you nothing about the error on the next. That the spread of the errors is about the same all along the line, rather than fanning out as the values get larger. That your columns are not saying the same thing twice. Break the first promise and both the predictions and the confidence you report are wrong. Break the ones about the spread and the shape of the errors and the predictions are still fine on average — it is the intervals and the significance tests that quietly stop meaning anything at all.

Like a rental contract you signed without reading. Nothing goes wrong while the flat behaves. The clauses only matter on the day something breaks, and then it matters enormously which one you broke — one costs you the deposit, another costs you the flat. Reciting the clauses is not the skill. Knowing what each one costs when it fails is.

Six assumptions, one failure mode each. Linearity in the parameters: violate it and both prediction and inference are wrong, and it is the only one that breaks everything. Independence of errors: violate it with autocorrelated or clustered rows and the standard errors come out far too small, so everything looks significant. Homoscedasticity: violate it and the coefficients stay unbiased while the standard errors are wrong, so the p-values and confidence intervals are invalid and the point predictions are fine. Normality of residuals: needed for exact inference in small samples only, and at large n the central limit theorem carries you. Low multicollinearity: the fit is untouched, the coefficients become unstable and uninterpretable. And no high-leverage outliers, because squared loss lets one point drag the line.

The diagnostic order in practice. Plot residuals against fitted values first — curvature means you broke linearity, a widening cone means heteroscedasticity. Then a Q-Q plot of the residuals, and Durbin-Watson if the rows have an order. For collinearity, compute the variance inflation factor per predictor: above 5 is a concern by convention, above 10 is the loose version, and neither is a law. If heteroscedasticity is all you have and you only need inference, you do not need a different model — you need robust standard errors, which is one argument in statsmodels.

You reach for it when

  • A stakeholder wants to know which driver matters, not just the forecast
  • Two predictors correlate at 0.9 and their signs flip between refits
  • Residuals fan out as the fitted value grows
  • Somebody says the data has to be normally distributed

The trap

Saying the data must be normally distributed. It is the residuals, not the features and not the target, and normality is needed only for exact small-sample inference — ordinary least squares is still the best linear unbiased estimator without it. The second trap is treating multicollinearity as something that hurts the model. It does not touch predictive accuracy. It inflates the variance of the coefficients, so signs flip between refits and no interpretation survives.

The math the estimate, then its uncertainty

β^​=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y  ·  Var(β^​)=σ2(X⊤X)−1  ·  VIFj​=1−Rj2​1​The first expression never mentions a distribution, which is the entire answer to the trap — least squares is a projection and it does not need normality. The second one does: homoscedasticity is the assumption that makes a single σ2 the right thing to put in front, and it is exactly the term that goes wrong under a fan. Near-collinear columns make the inverse ill-conditioned, which is what the variance inflation factor measures.

Diagnose first, then fix the right thing

import statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor as vif

Xc = sm.add_constant(X)
fit = sm.OLS(y, Xc).fit()
print(fit.summary())          # these p-values assume constant error variance

# a cone in the residual plot? do not refit -- fix the standard errors
robust = sm.OLS(y, Xc).fit(cov_type='HC3')
print(robust.summary())       # identical coefficients, honest intervals

for j, name in enumerate(Xc.columns):     # VIF above 5 is a convention, not a law
    print(name, round(vif(Xc.values, j), 2))

Where this bites in production

Anscombe’s quartet (1973) is still the cleanest demonstration: four datasets with the same means, the same variances, the same correlation and the same fitted line, one of which is a clean linear relationship and three of which are emphatically not. Matejka and Fitzmaurice extended it in 2017 with the Datasaurus Dozen, twelve datasets identical to two decimal places, one of them a dinosaur. Both make the same operational point — a regression summary cannot tell you whether its own assumptions hold, and only the residual plot can.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Which assumption, if violated, invalidates your p-values but not your predictions?
Heteroscedasticity, and non-normal residuals in a small sample. Non-constant error variance leaves the coefficient estimates unbiased but makes the standard-error formula wrong, so every p-value and confidence interval on the output is invalid while the point predictions are fine. Non-linearity is the one that breaks both, because the fitted function is wrong everywhere.
Two predictors correlate at 0.95. What actually breaks?
The interpretation, not the prediction. The fitted values and the residual sum of squares are essentially unchanged; what inflates is the variance of the individual coefficients, so they become unstable, their signs flip between bootstrap samples, and no story you tell about them survives a refit. Check VIF, drop one, combine them, or move to ridge if you only need prediction.
Does linear regression require normally distributed data?
No, and it is the residuals anyway. Ordinary least squares needs linearity, independence and constant variance to be the best linear unbiased estimator, and normality appears nowhere in that. Normality of the residuals buys you exact t and F inference in small samples; at large n the central limit theorem gives you the same intervals without it.

Say this back tomorrow

non-linearity breaks predictions  ·  heteroscedasticity breaks p-values  ·  collinearity breaks interpretation
  • Know the failure mode per assumption, not the list of assumptions
  • It is the residuals that need normality, and only for small-sample inference
  • Multicollinearity leaves prediction intact and destroys every coefficient story

Unlocks

  • homoscedasticity
  • VIF
  • robust standard errors
  • residual plot
  • multicollinearity
