Logistic Regression & the Log-Odds

It is a linear model. Linear in the log-odds, and nowhere else.

Logistic regression builds the same weighted sum any linear model builds, then pushes it through a curve so the answer lands somewhere between impossible and certain. The word linear confuses people, because the picture is plainly a curve. What is straight is not the probability. It is the log of the odds — the chance the thing happens divided by the chance it does not, then logged. On that scale, one more unit of a feature adds the same fixed amount every time, wherever you started. On the probability scale the same feature moves the answer a great deal in the middle and almost nothing at the ends, because the curve has flattened out. So a coefficient is a statement about odds. On its own it says nothing about how far a probability will move.

Like a bookmaker’s price. A bookmaker never tells you a horse gained four percentage points. He says the price shortened from 5-to-1 to 5-to-2, and everyone understands that the odds have halved. That is a multiplicative statement and it means the same thing for a favourite and for an outsider. Percentage points do not: four points added to a near-certainty is a different event entirely from four points added to a long shot.

You model the log-odds as a linear function: log(p/(1−p))=β0​+β⊤x, and the sigmoid is just the inverse link that carries you back to a probability. So the linearity lives on the logit scale, which is exactly why the fitted curve is not a straight line. A coefficient is therefore a log odds-ratio: 0.7 exponentiates to about 2.01, so one more unit of that feature multiplies the odds by two, holding the other features fixed — not the probability. It is fitted by minimising log loss, which is the negative Bernoulli log-likelihood, and there is no closed form, so you use Newton–Raphson (IRLS) or gradient descent. Because log loss is a proper scoring rule, a well-specified logistic fit comes out close to calibrated for free.

Perfect separation is the failure worth naming out loud. If some feature or combination of features splits the classes cleanly, the likelihood is monotone in that coefficient — pushing it towards infinity keeps raising the likelihood, so the maximum likelihood estimate does not exist. You see it as a coefficient in the tens or hundreds with an enormous standard error, and a solver that will not converge. The fix is a penalty (ridge, or Firth’s bias-reduced likelihood), never more iterations. Note the contrast: a raw SVM emits a margin and a random forest emits a vote share, and neither is a probability, which is why both need Platt scaling or isotonic regression afterwards.

You reach for it when

  • A stakeholder asks what one feature is worth and expects a percentage
  • The solver returns a coefficient of 34 and refuses to converge
  • You need probabilities a pricing or triage rule will act on, not a ranking
  • Explaining a credit or risk model to someone who has to sign it off

The trap

Reading a coefficient as a change in probability. It is a change in the log-odds, so exponentiate it: 0.7 becomes roughly a two-fold change in the odds, and what that does to a probability depends entirely on where you started. The second trap is not recognising perfect separation — when a feature splits the classes cleanly the likelihood has no finite maximum, coefficients run away, and the answer is a penalty, not more iterations.

The math linear on the left-hand side only

log1−pp​=β0​+β⊤x  ·  p=σ(z)=1+e−z1​  ·  e0.7≈2.01Exponentiating a coefficient gives an odds ratio, which is why the interpretation is multiplicative and why it holds uniformly across the range. The fitting objective is −∑[ylogp+(1−y)log(1−p)], and with the sigmoid the gradient with respect to the logits is exactly p−y. Under perfect separation that gradient never reaches zero, so ∥β∥→∞ and the MLE simply does not exist.

Coefficients to odds, odds to probability

import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm

fit = sm.Logit(y, sm.add_constant(X)).fit()   # unpenalised, so it will warn honestly
print(np.exp(fit.params))                     # ODDS RATIOS, not probability changes
# tenure_years  coef 0.70  ->  exp(0.70) = 2.01x the odds per extra year

# what that buys you in probability depends on where you started
p0 = np.array([0.10, 0.50, 0.90])
odds = p0 / (1 - p0) * np.exp(0.70)
print(odds / (1 + odds))                      # 0.183, 0.668, 0.948

# sklearn hides separation behind its default L2 penalty. statsmodels tells you.

Where this bites in production

Credit scorecards are logistic regressions in disguise, and the industry scales them with a points-to-double-the-odds convention, commonly 20. Every 20 points on a FICO-style scale means the odds of repayment double — a scaling that only makes sense because the model is linear on the log-odds scale, so points can be added up. Scorecard documentation is full of this arithmetic. It is the plainest evidence that a coefficient lives on the odds scale.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What does a coefficient of 0.7 mean?
The odds multiply by about 2.01 per unit, holding the other features fixed. It is a log odds-ratio, so you exponentiate it, and the statement is multiplicative rather than additive. What it does to the probability depends on where you started: at even money it moves you to 0.668, at 0.90 it moves you to 0.948. Anyone who answers “it raises the probability by 0.7” has not understood the link function.
Your solver returns a coefficient of 34 with a standard error of 12,000. What happened?
Perfect separation. Some feature or linear combination splits the classes cleanly, so the likelihood keeps rising as that coefficient grows and the maximum likelihood estimate does not exist. Check for a column that is effectively the label, then add an L2 penalty or use Firth’s bias-reduced likelihood. More iterations and a looser tolerance will not help — there is nothing finite to converge to.
Why is logistic regression well calibrated when a random forest is not?
Because it is fitted by minimising log loss, which is a proper scoring rule. The objective is minimised only when the predicted probabilities match the true conditional probabilities, so calibration is what the fit is directly buying. A random forest outputs a vote share and an SVM outputs a distance to a margin; neither was optimised to be a probability, which is why both need Platt scaling or isotonic regression bolted on afterwards.

linear in the log-odds  ·  a coefficient multiplies the odds, never the probability
  • The linearity is on the logit scale, which is why the fitted curve bends
  • Exponentiate a coefficient to read it: 0.7 is about a two-fold change in the odds
  • Perfect separation has no finite solution — regularise, do not iterate

  • log loss
  • calibration

Decision Trees: Entropy & Gini

A split is an exhaustive search over every feature and every cut point, scored by impurity.

A tree asks one question at a time. Is tenure under a year? Yes goes left, no goes right. To choose that question it tries every feature and every cut point available, scores each candidate by how much purer the two resulting groups are than the group it started with, and keeps the winner. Then it does the same thing again inside each group, and again, until it runs out of rows or hits a limit you set. Nothing in that procedure cares what units a feature is measured in, because only the order of the values ever matters. That is why trees need no scaling, and why they pick up bends and interactions between features without anybody telling them those exist.

Like twenty questions. A good question is one whose answer leaves you far more certain than you were before, so you never ask something that splits the field evenly when a sharper question is on the table. You ask, the field shrinks, you ask again. And you stop well before the questions get so specific that they only ever identify the one person sitting in front of you.

CART is greedy and recursive. At each node it searches every feature and every candidate threshold, scores each split by the weighted impurity of the children, and takes the best one — then recurses, never revisiting an earlier choice. Entropy is −∑pi​log2​pi​, one bit at a 50/50 node; Gini is 1−∑pi2​, maximum 0.5. Information gain is the parent impurity minus the row-weighted child impurity. Because the splits only compare values, the whole thing is invariant to any monotone transform of a feature, so scaling, log transforms and outlier winsorising change nothing. Interactions come free, since the second question is asked inside the answer to the first. For regression the impurity is variance and the same machinery applies.

Pruning is where the interview goes, and there are two families. Pre-pruning stops growth early: max_depth, min_samples_leaf, min_samples_split. It is cheap, but it is myopic — it can refuse a weak split whose children would have been excellent. Post-pruning grows the tree out and then cuts back, minimising Rα​(T)=R(T)+α∣T∣, which in scikit-learn is ccp_alpha with cost_complexity_pruning_path to enumerate the candidates. Cross-validate over that path rather than guessing a depth. One more thing worth knowing: the built-in feature importance is impurity-based, and it is biased towards high-cardinality and continuous columns.

You reach for it when

  • You need a model a compliance officer can read line by line
  • Training accuracy is 1.00 and nobody set a depth
  • A feature is on a wild scale and someone reaches for a scaler first
  • Explaining why an interaction term is unnecessary here

The trap

Adding a StandardScaler in front of a tree. Splits compare values, they never measure distances, so any monotone transform of a feature produces an identical tree. The bigger trap is leaving pruning out of the answer. An unconstrained tree grows until every leaf is pure and has memorised the table, and “I would set max_depth” is only half of it — the other half is cost-complexity pruning, cross-validated over the alpha path.

The math one split, worked by hand

H=−∑i​pi​log2​pi​  ·  G=1−∑i​pi2​  ·  IG=1.000−(10040​(0.544)+10060​(0.811))=0.296The left child is 35 churned out of 40: −0.875log2​0.875−0.125log2​0.125=0.544. The right is 15 out of 60, giving 0.811. Weight each by its share of the rows, sum to 0.704, subtract from the parent’s 1.000. Gini scores the same split 0.500−0.313=0.188 and ranks it first as well — which is the entire answer to “gini or entropy”.

Grow it, then cut it back

from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

# defaults: max_depth=None, min_samples_leaf=1 -> grows until every leaf is pure
base = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(base.score(X_tr, y_tr), base.score(X_va, y_va))   # 1.000 and 0.71

# post-pruning: enumerate the cost-complexity path, then cross-validate over it
path = base.cost_complexity_pruning_path(X_tr, y_tr)
for a in path.ccp_alphas[::10]:
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(ccp_alpha=a, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(round(a, 5), t.tree_.node_count, round(t.score(X_va, y_va), 3))

# note what is absent: no scaler, no encoder for ordered ints, no interaction terms

Where this bites in production

scikit-learn ships DecisionTreeClassifier with max_depth=None and min_samples_leaf=1, so the default tree grows until every leaf is pure — training accuracy 1.00 and a model that has memorised the table. On the other question, Raileanu and Stoffel analysed Gini against information gain in 2004 and found they disagree on only about 2% of splits. Argue about depth and ccp_alpha instead; those actually move the score.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Gini or entropy — does it matter?
Almost never. They are both concave impurity measures with the same maximum at a 50/50 node, and the analysis puts their disagreement at roughly 2% of splits. Entropy costs a logarithm per candidate, so Gini is the default in scikit-learn on speed grounds alone. The levers that do change the tree are max_depth, min_samples_leaf and ccp_alpha.
Do decision trees need feature scaling?
No, and this is a clean signal to an interviewer. A split is a comparison against a threshold, so any strictly monotone transform of a feature — scaling, logging, ranking — produces exactly the same tree with a relabelled threshold. That is also why a tree tolerates skew and outliers in the features. kNN, SVM, PCA, k-means and anything gradient-based do need scaling; trees and tree ensembles do not.
Your tree scores 1.00 on train and 0.71 on validation. What do you change?
Prune it, and prefer post-pruning. Pre-pruning with max_depth or min_samples_leaf is quick but myopic — it will veto a weak split whose children would have been excellent. Grow the tree out, get the cost-complexity path with cost_complexity_pruning_path, and cross-validate over the alpha values. If a single pruned tree still is not enough, that is the argument for an ensemble.

Say this back tomorrow

a split is the largest weighted drop in impurity  ·  gini and entropy agree  ·  pruning is the real knob
  • Greedy and recursive: the best split now, never revisited later
  • No scaling, ever — splits compare order, they do not measure distance
  • Pre-prune by depth, post-prune by cost-complexity, cross-validate the alpha

Unlocks

  • information gain
  • gini impurity
  • ccp_alpha
  • cost-complexity
  • axis-aligned splits

Bagging & Random Forests

Not parallel versus sequential. Averaging cuts variance, and only decorrelation lowers the floor.

Grow one deep tree and it fits the training rows almost perfectly, then changes completely if you hand it a slightly different sample. It is jumpy. Averaging many of them calms that down, so you draw sample after sample from your data with replacement, grow a tree on each, and average the answers. The catch is that all those trees have seen nearly the same rows, so they nearly all make the same mistake, and averaging near-identical mistakes cancels almost nothing. The fix is to force the trees apart. At every single split, hide most of the columns and let the tree choose only from the handful it can still see. Now the trees genuinely differ, their errors stop lining up, and the average is far steadier.

Think of a panel of forecasters. Twenty pundits who all read the same newspaper give you one opinion twenty times over, and averaging them buys you nothing at all. Make each of them read a different handful of sources and they start disagreeing for real reasons. The average of genuinely independent guesses is much steadier than any single one. Independence is what the averaging is paying for, not headcount.

Bagging is bootstrap aggregating: draw B samples with replacement, fit a high-variance low-bias learner on each, average. The identity that matters is Var(fˉ​)=ρσ2+B1−ρ​σ2. More trees kill the second term and nothing else, so the first term is a floor set by how alike the trees are. Plain bagged trees stay strongly correlated, because every tree still sees every column and the dominant feature wins the root split every time. The extra ingredient in a random forest is feature subsampling at each split — max_features, defaulting to p​ for classification and p/3 for regression. That lowers ρ, and lowering ρ is what actually delivers the variance reduction.

Out-of-bag error is validation you get for nothing. Each bootstrap sample leaves out about 1/e≈36.8% of the rows, so every row can be scored by the subset of trees that never saw it. On a small dataset that saves you a holdout entirely, and oob_score_ tracks 5-fold cross-validation closely. It fails in the usual places: it is still a random split, so it leaks under grouped or time-ordered data exactly as a random KFold would. And a note on importances — the built-in impurity importance is biased towards high-cardinality and continuous features, so report permutation importance on held-out data instead.

You reach for it when

  • A single tree is accurate on train and unstable on every refit
  • You have 3,000 rows and cannot afford to give up a holdout
  • One dominant feature wins the root split in every tree you fit
  • Someone asks for a strong baseline before any tuning happens

The trap

Answering “bagging is parallel, boosting is sequential” and stopping there. That is a scheduling fact, not a mechanism. Bagging averages independent high-variance low-bias learners, so it cuts variance; boosting stacks weak high-bias learners on the residuals, so it cuts bias. The direct version of this trap is the question “is a random forest bagging or boosting?” — it is bagging, plus feature subsampling at each split.

The math why decorrelation is the whole game

Var(fˉ​)=ρσ2+B1−ρ​σ2  ·  OOB share=(1−n1​)n→e−1≈0.368B appears in the second term only, so adding trees drives that term to zero and then stops helping — which is why a forest does not overfit as you add trees, it just stops improving. The first term is a floor you cannot average away, and ρ is the average pairwise correlation between trees. max_features is the only knob that lowers it. The second identity is the out-of-bag share: roughly 37% of rows are unseen by any given tree.

One parameter is the whole difference

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, max_features='sqrt',
                            oob_score=True, n_jobs=-1, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
print(rf.oob_score_)     # free validation: each row scored by the trees that missed it

# plain bagging is the SAME call with every column offered at every split
bag = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, max_features=None,
                             oob_score=True, n_jobs=-1, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
print(bag.oob_score_)    # usually worse - the trees agree, so averaging cancels less

# careful: RandomForestRegressor defaults to max_features=1.0, which IS plain bagging

Where this bites in production

scikit-learn’s RandomForestRegressor defaults max_features to 1.0 — every column offered at every split. Out of the box the regressor is plain bagging, and people who never touch that parameter report “random forest” results built from fully correlated trees. The classifier defaults to sqrt. Breiman introduced the subsampling in 2001 for exactly this reason: bagged trees on a dominant feature all split the same way at the root.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Is a random forest bagging or boosting?
Bagging. Every tree is fitted independently on its own bootstrap sample and the predictions are averaged, so the trees never see each other’s errors. Boosting is the opposite construction: each learner is fitted to what the running ensemble still gets wrong. The forest adds one thing on top of bagging — feature subsampling at each split — and that is a decorrelation device, not a sequential one.
Random forest versus plain bagging — what is the extra ingredient?
Feature subsampling at every split, not just at every tree. max_features defaults to the square root of the feature count for classification and a third of it for regression. Its job is to lower the correlation between trees, because the variance of an average is the correlation times the individual variance plus a term that more trees already remove. Only decorrelation touches the floor.
How do you validate a forest when you cannot spare a holdout?
Out-of-bag error. Each bootstrap sample omits about 37% of the rows, so every row can be predicted by the subset of trees that never saw it, and oob_score_ tracks 5-fold cross-validation closely for free. The caveat is that it is a random split under the bonnet, so it leaks in exactly the same way a random KFold does on grouped or time-ordered data.

bagging averages away variance  ·  only feature subsampling lowers the correlation floor
  • More trees remove the 1/B term and nothing else — the floor is the correlation
  • max_features at each split is the ingredient that makes a forest a forest
  • OOB error is a free validation estimate, with a random KFold’s leaks

Boosting: AdaBoost, GBM & XGBoost

Each learner is fitted to what the last one got wrong. That cuts bias — and it will not stop on its own.

Boosting starts with something deliberately feeble — a stump that asks a single question — and lets it be wrong. Then it fits a second one, not to the original target, but to what the first one missed. Then a third to what the first two still miss, each correction added on top with the volume turned down. Because every learner starts out far too simple to capture the pattern, the whole stack spends its life closing that gap, which is the opposite problem from a forest. And that is exactly the danger: nothing stops it. Keep adding corrections and it eventually starts fitting the noise in the leftovers, at which point the score on unseen data begins climbing back up while the training score keeps falling.

Like a tailor with a chalk line. The first fitting gets the jacket roughly right and leaves it baggy at the shoulder. The second fitting addresses only the shoulder. The third addresses only what the second left behind. Each pass is small and each is aimed squarely at the remaining error — and if you keep going, you end up tailoring to the way the customer happened to stand that morning.

Boosting is a stagewise additive fit: Fm​=Fm−1​+νhm​, where hm​ is a weak high-bias learner. AdaBoost reweights the samples, upweighting the ones the running ensemble misclassifies, which is equivalent to a stagewise fit under exponential loss. Friedman’s gradient boosting fits hm​ to the negative gradient of the loss at the current predictions instead, which is why it generalises to any differentiable loss — squared error, log loss, quantile, Cox. XGBoost goes one order further and takes a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss around Fm−1​, so each tree is a Newton step, and it adds explicit penalties on leaf weights and on the number of leaves. That objective is what “regularised boosting” actually names.

The asymmetry with a forest is the follow-up people fumble. A forest averages independent estimates of the same quantity, so adding trees drives one variance term to zero and then does nothing — the curve flattens, it does not turn up. Boosting keeps reducing training loss by construction, and after some round it is reducing it by fitting noise. So the number of rounds is a capacity parameter, and you do not choose it: you set a low learning rate, pass a validation set, and let early stopping choose it. Learning rate 0.05 to 0.1, max_depth 6 to 8, subsample and colsample 0.7 to 0.9.

You reach for it when

  • A tabular baseline needs to beat a random forest this week
  • Validation loss is creeping up while training loss keeps falling
  • Someone set n_estimators to a round number and never revisited it
  • Picking a loss that is not squared error or log loss

The trap

Carrying “more trees never hurts” across from random forests. It is true there and false here. A forest averages independent estimates, so extra trees shrink one variance term and then do nothing. Boosting fits every new tree to the current residuals, so extra rounds keep reducing training loss, and past some point they do it by fitting noise. Round count is a capacity parameter, and early stopping is the thing that picks it.

The math the XGBoost objective, second order

L(t)≃∑i​[gi​ft​(xi​)+21​hi​ft​(xi​)2]+γT+21​λ∑j​wj2​gi​ and hi​ are the first and second derivatives of the loss at the current prediction, so each tree is a Newton step rather than a gradient step. Minimising for a fixed structure gives the optimal leaf weight wj∗​=−Gj​/(Hj​+λ) and the split gain that follows from it. γT charges you per leaf and λ shrinks the leaf weights — those two terms, not the subsampling, are what “regularised boosting” refers to.

Let early stopping choose the round count

import xgboost as xgb

model = xgb.XGBClassifier(n_estimators=5000,        # a ceiling, not a choice
                          learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=6,
                          subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8,
                          reg_lambda=1.0, gamma=0.0,
                          eval_metric='logloss', early_stopping_rounds=50)
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr, eval_set=[(X_va, y_va)], verbose=False)

print(model.best_iteration)      # 320 - THIS is your n_estimators, and you did not pick it
print(model.best_score)

# ship best_iteration. Without early stopping the validation curve turns back up.

Where this bites in production

Chen and Guestrin’s 2016 XGBoost paper reports that 17 of the 29 winning solutions published on Kaggle in 2015 used XGBoost, 8 of them on its own. The same paper is where the second-order objective and the leaf-weight penalty are written down. The failure to name in the room is just as concrete: n_estimators does not stop itself, so you pass early_stopping_rounds and read back best_iteration, or you ship the overfitted count.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

A random forest barely overfits with more trees. Why does boosting?
Because boosting trees are not independent estimates of the same quantity. A forest averages independent fits, so extra trees remove one variance term and then stop mattering. Boosting fits each new tree to the residuals of everything before it, which keeps reducing training loss by construction — and once the signal is exhausted it reduces it by fitting noise. The round count is capacity, so early stopping has to choose it.
What did AdaBoost do, and what did gradient boosting generalise?
AdaBoost reweights the samples; gradient boosting fits the gradient of the loss. AdaBoost upweights misclassified examples each round, which turns out to be a stagewise additive fit under exponential loss — a single, fixed loss. Friedman replaced the reweighting with fitting the negative gradient of the current loss, so the same machinery works for squared error, log loss, quantile loss or a Cox partial likelihood.
What does “regularised boosting” actually mean in XGBoost?
Two explicit penalty terms inside the objective, plus a Newton step. XGBoost takes a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss around the current prediction, so it uses both the gradient and the curvature to choose splits and leaf values. The objective then carries γT for the number of leaves and 21​λ∑wj2​ for the leaf weights. Shrinkage and column subsampling help too, but the name points at those terms.

Say this back tomorrow

bagging averages to cut variance  ·  boosting stacks corrections to cut bias  ·  only one of the two needs early stopping
  • Weak high-bias learners fitted to residuals: the family attacks bias, not variance
  • AdaBoost reweights samples, GBM fits the gradient of any differentiable loss
  • Round count is capacity — early stopping picks it, you do not

  • stagewise additive
  • shrinkage
  • early stopping
  • second-order Taylor
  • leaf-weight penalty

LightGBM & CatBoost: Which One and Why

Three libraries, one algorithm. What differs is how the tree grows and how a category is encoded.

All three build the same object: a stack of small trees, each correcting the last. What differs is bookkeeping, and the bookkeeping decides which one you should reach for. The first grows every tree evenly, one whole layer at a time, which is cautious and makes a sensible default. The second always extends whichever leaf promises the largest improvement, so it runs deep down one branch and stays shallow everywhere else. That is much faster and much easier to overfit on a small table. The third has a different obsession: columns holding thousands of distinct labels, like a postcode or a product code. Replacing those labels with the average outcome per label leaks the answer unless you are careful, and the third one is careful by default.

Think of two decorators in the same house. One paints every room a single coat before anybody starts the second coat, so the house is always evenly finished and nothing gets ahead of itself. The other finds the wall that will look best painted, paints it until it is perfect, then goes looking for the next one. The second is quicker to something impressive, and far likelier to leave you one immaculate wall in a shabby house.

XGBoost grows level-wise, splits on a histogram of binned features, and ships conservative defaults around max_depth 6 — a good baseline you rarely regret. LightGBM grows leaf-wise: it always splits the leaf with the highest gain, so for a fixed number of leaves it reaches a lower loss than a level-wise tree, and it is several times faster on a million rows. The lever is num_leaves, not depth, and it overfits a small table more readily — keep num_leaves below 2max_depth and raise min_data_in_leaf. CatBoost uses symmetric (oblivious) trees, the same split across a whole level, which regularises and makes inference very fast. Its real differentiator is ordered target statistics for categoricals.

Target encoding replaces a category with the mean outcome for that category, and computed naively each row’s feature contains its own label — the classic leak. Two fixes. Do it out of fold with smoothing, x^c​=(nc​yˉ​c​+myˉ​)/(nc​+m), so a category seen twice is pulled almost all the way to the global mean. Or use CatBoost, whose ordered target statistics compute each row’s encoding from only the rows preceding it in a random permutation, which is the same idea taken to its limit and applied per row rather than per fold. That is why CatBoost is the default when high-cardinality categoricals dominate.

You reach for it when

  • Four million rows and twenty tuning runs to fit into an afternoon
  • A postcode, SKU or customer-ID column with thousands of levels
  • LightGBM beats XGBoost on train and loses on validation
  • Choosing the first library for a tabular baseline nobody has built yet

The trap

Picking a library on reputation instead of on the shape of the data. The three answers are: XGBoost as the conservative baseline, LightGBM when rows or tuning runs are the constraint, CatBoost when high-cardinality categoricals dominate. The concrete failure underneath is target encoding computed in fold — each row’s feature then contains its own label, validation looks superb, and production does not. Out-of-fold with smoothing, or let CatBoost do it.

The math smoothed target encoding

x^c​=nc​+mnc​yˉ​c​+myˉ​​nc​ is the number of rows in category c, yˉ​c​ its mean outcome, yˉ​ the global mean, and m the smoothing weight, usually 10 to 100. A category seen twice is dragged almost entirely to the global mean; a category seen ten thousand times keeps its own. This must be computed out of fold. CatBoost’s ordered target statistics apply the same idea per row, using only the rows before it in a random permutation.

The two calls, and the two levers

import lightgbm as lgb
from catboost import CatBoostClassifier

# LightGBM grows leaf-wise, so num_leaves is the overfitting lever - not max_depth
gbm = lgb.LGBMClassifier(num_leaves=31, max_depth=8, min_data_in_leaf=100,
                         learning_rate=0.05, n_estimators=5000)
gbm.fit(X_tr, y_tr, eval_set=[(X_va, y_va)],
        categorical_feature=['postcode'], callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(50)])

# CatBoost: hand it the raw string column. Ordered target statistics, no fold leak.
cb = CatBoostClassifier(iterations=5000, learning_rate=0.05, depth=6,
                        cat_features=['postcode'], early_stopping_rounds=50)
cb.fit(X_tr, y_tr, eval_set=(X_va, y_va), verbose=False)

Where this bites in production

LightGBM ships with num_leaves=31 and max_depth=-1 — depth is unlimited and leaf count is the only thing holding the tree back, which is precisely why it overfits a small table faster than XGBoost’s depth-6 default. The documentation says it outright: keep num_leaves under two to the power of max_depth. CatBoost’s ordered target statistics come from Prokhorenkova et al. (NeurIPS 2018), which named the leak they remove.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Four million rows and twenty tuning runs. Which library?
LightGBM. Leaf-wise growth plus histogram binning of the continuous features makes it several times faster than XGBoost at this size, and when you are fitting twenty configurations that difference is the difference between one afternoon and three. Set num_leaves deliberately and raise min_data_in_leaf, because leaf-wise growth with an unlimited depth is what makes it overfit.
You have a postcode column with 20,000 levels. What breaks first?
The encoding, and specifically target encoding computed in fold. One-hot at that cardinality is unusable and ordinal invents an order that is not there, so you reach for the category mean — and computed naively each row’s feature contains its own label. Do it out of fold with smoothing, or hand the raw column to CatBoost and let ordered target statistics handle it per row.
Why does LightGBM overfit a small table faster than XGBoost?
Leaf-wise growth with no depth cap. It always splits the leaf with the highest gain, so it will run deep down one branch chasing a handful of rows, while a level-wise tree at max_depth=6 simply cannot. The default max_depth=-1 means unlimited. The fixes are num_leaves kept below two to the power of the depth you want, a larger min_data_in_leaf, and early stopping.

Say this back tomorrow

level-wise is cautious  ·  leaf-wise is fast and greedy  ·  ordered target statistics are why CatBoost eats categoricals
  • XGBoost for a safe baseline, LightGBM for size and speed, CatBoost for categoricals
  • num_leaves is LightGBM’s capacity knob, because depth is unlimited by default
  • Target encoding must be out of fold with smoothing, or it leaks the label

  • histogram binning

Why Boosting Still Beats Deep Learning on Tables

Three structural mismatches, not a matter of taste.

On a spreadsheet of customers, a stack of boosted trees usually wins, and it is not because the field has failed to catch up. Three properties of a table fight a neural network. First, the relationship between a column and the answer is often jagged: nothing happens until an account is ninety days overdue, and then everything does. A tree cuts at exactly that point; a network draws a smooth curve and rounds the corner off. Second, a network is happy to mix the columns together freely, but in a table every column means one specific thing and blending them destroys that meaning. Third, real tables carry columns that are pure noise. A tree simply never splits on them. A network has to learn to ignore them, and it does that badly.

Like reading a spreadsheet rather than a photograph. Shift, rotate or slightly blur a photograph and it is still the same cat, so a model that assumes smoothness and mixes neighbouring pixels is right to. Rotate a spreadsheet and you get nonsense: half a postcode added to a third of an age. The assumptions that make a network excellent at photographs are precisely the ones that fail on a table.

Grinsztajn, Oyallon and Varoquaux (NeurIPS 2022) benchmarked tree ensembles against neural networks on 45 mid-sized tabular datasets and gave the trees’ advantage three named causes. One: neural networks are biased towards smooth solutions. Smoothing the target function badly damaged the tree models and barely touched the networks, which shows the networks were already ignoring the irregular part — and tabular targets are irregular. Two: multi-layer perceptrons are approximately rotation-invariant, so a random rotation of the features left them roughly unchanged and destroyed the trees. That invariance is a liability when each column carries its own meaning; axis-aligned splits are the right prior. Three: uninformative features degrade networks far more than trees, which never split on them at all.

The honest counterpoint matters as much as the finding. Deep learning wins on tables when the table stops being only a table. Very high-cardinality categoricals are one case: learned entity embeddings give you a dense, transferable representation that a tree cannot build. Multimodal joins are another — if the row has free text or an image attached, the tabular part becomes one tower of a jointly trained network. So does transfer and multi-task learning across related tables, where a shared encoder amortises across problems that individually have too few rows. And at the small end, TabPFN v2 (Nature, 2025) beat tuned gradient boosting on datasets under ten thousand rows, in seconds, with no tuning at all.

You reach for it when

  • A stakeholder asks why you are not using deep learning on the customer table
  • Choosing the first model for a 200-column, 500,000-row warehouse extract
  • A row has free text or an image attached to it as well as columns
  • Someone reports a neural net beating boosting and you want to know what changed

The trap

Answering this as a question about fashion — “trees are just what people use for tabular data”. It is a question about inductive bias, and there are three specific claims to make: tabular targets are irregular and networks smooth them, networks are rotation-invariant in a way that throws away the per-column meaning trees exploit, and uninformative columns hurt networks while trees never split on them. The mirror trap is claiming deep learning never wins on tables. It does, and you should say where.

The math the inductive bias, in one line

trees: 1[xj​>t], axis-aligned  ·  MLP: w⊤x, near-invariant to x↦RxA split reads one coordinate, so a tree is tied to the basis the data arrived in — which is the right prior when column j means “days overdue”. The first layer of an MLP takes arbitrary linear combinations, so a rotation R of the features is almost free for it. That is the experiment in the paper: rotate the data, and tree performance collapses while the network barely notices. Invariance you do not need is capacity you are wasting.

Reproducing the uninformative-features result

import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

for k in (0, 20, 100):                       # bolt on k columns of pure noise
    Xk = np.hstack([X, np.random.randn(len(X), k)])
    gb = cross_val_score(HistGradientBoostingClassifier(), Xk, y, cv=5).mean()
    nn = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                                       MLPClassifier(max_iter=600)), Xk, y, cv=5).mean()
    print(k, round(gb, 3), round(nn, 3))

# the tree line barely moves, the MLP line falls. Grinsztajn's second claim, in ten lines

Where this bites in production

Grinsztajn, Oyallon and Varoquaux benchmarked 45 mid-sized tabular datasets for NeurIPS 2022, and tree ensembles won even after the neural networks were given a far larger hyperparameter budget. The counter-example is equally concrete: Guo and Berkhahn took third place in the Rossmann store-sales competition using entity embeddings of high-cardinality categoricals fed to a small network, and those learned embeddings then improved the tree models they were handed to.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why do gradient-boosted trees still beat neural networks on tabular data?
Three inductive-bias mismatches, not fashion. Tabular targets are irregular and piecewise, which axis-aligned splits fit exactly and a network smooths over. Networks are approximately rotation-invariant, so they cannot exploit the fact that each column means one specific thing — and rotating the features proves it, wrecking the trees and leaving the network alone. And uninformative columns degrade a network badly, while a tree simply never splits on them.
When would you actually use a neural net on a table?
When the table stops being only a table. Very high-cardinality categoricals you want as learned embeddings rather than encodings; a multimodal join where free text or an image sits alongside the columns and one network can be trained end to end; and transfer or multi-task across related tables, where a shared encoder amortises over problems that individually have too few rows. Add very large row counts, and small-data foundation models like TabPFN.
What does “not rotation invariant” actually mean here, and why is it a good thing?
It means the model is tied to the basis the data arrived in, and on a table that basis is meaningful. A split reads one coordinate, so a tree can only cut along the columns as given. An MLP’s first layer takes arbitrary linear combinations, so a rotation of the features costs it almost nothing. Rotate the data and the trees collapse while the network is unmoved — the invariance is capacity spent on a symmetry a table does not have.

Say this back tomorrow

irregular targets  ·  meaningful axes  ·  noisy columns — three structural reasons, not a preference
  • Tabular targets are jagged; trees cut at the jump, networks smooth it away
  • Rotation invariance throws away the per-column meaning a table carries
  • Deep learning does win: embeddings, multimodal joins, transfer across tables

Unlocks

  • inductive bias
  • rotation invariance
  • uninformative features
  • entity embeddings
  • Grinsztajn 2022

Support Vector Machines & the Kernel Trick

Not any separating line. The one with the widest empty street around it.

Two groups of points, and a whole family of lines that separate them. Pick the one with the widest empty corridor around it, because a boundary that keeps its distance from both sides is the one most likely to survive a point it has never seen. Only the points touching the edge of that corridor matter. Move a point far from the boundary and nothing changes at all. Then there is a knob for how strict you are: turn it down and the corridor widens while a few points are allowed to sit inside it, or on the wrong side of it entirely. And when no straight boundary exists, there is a shortcut that answers how similar two points would be in a far richer space, without ever building that space or listing a single one of its coordinates.

Think of paving a road between two villages. Plenty of routes get you through, but the one you want is the route with the most clearance on either side, because a lorry that drifts a little still stays on the tarmac. Only the buildings nearest the verge decide where the road goes. A cottage half a mile back has no vote at all.

A hard-margin SVM maximises the distance from the boundary to the closest point of either class. That margin is 2/∥w∥, so maximising it means minimising ∥w∥2. Only the points on or inside the margin appear in the solution — those are the support vectors, and every other row could be deleted without moving the boundary a millimetre. Real data is not separable, so the soft margin adds slack with a penalty C: large C makes a violation expensive, giving a narrow margin that hugs the data, and small C buys a wider margin at the cost of more points inside it. C is an inverse regularisation strength. The kernel trick is not a projection: the dual touches the data only through inner products, so you swap xi⊤​xj​ for K(xi​,xj​) and get the inner product in the richer space directly.

Three practicalities that decide whether you would actually ship one. SVM scores are signed distances to the boundary, not probabilities; SVC(probability=True) fits a separate Platt sigmoid on internal cross-validated folds, which multiplies training cost and can even disagree with predict. Features must be scaled, because an RBF kernel is a Euclidean distance and one column in pounds will swamp one in years. And the fit scales roughly O(n2) to O(n3) in the number of samples, which is the plain reason SVMs lost large tabular problems to gradient boosting.

You reach for it when

  • A few thousand rows, many columns, and a non-linear boundary
  • Text or gene expression, where the data is wide and clean
  • Someone hands you SVM scores and calls them probabilities
  • Choosing between an SVM and gradient boosting on a two-million-row table

The trap

Saying the kernel projects the data into a high-dimensional space. It never computes the projection — it returns the inner product in that space directly, which is the entire point, and the RBF kernel’s space is infinite-dimensional so no projection could be computed at all. The second trap is reading decision_function as a probability. It is a signed distance; probability=True bolts a Platt sigmoid on top via internal folds.

The math the soft margin, and the kernel

minw,b​21​∥w∥2+C∑i​ξi​  ·  margin =2/∥w∥  ·  K(x,x′)=exp(−γ∥x−x′∥2)C prices a violation. Large C makes slack expensive, so the margin narrows and the boundary bends to catch every training point; small C buys a wider margin and tolerates points inside it. γ is the inverse radius of the RBF bump — large γ means each point’s influence dies off quickly and the boundary breaks into wiggly islands. Both knobs overfit in the same visual way, which is why you tune them together on a log grid.

Scale it, and do not trust the score

from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV

# scaling is not optional: the RBF kernel is a Euclidean distance
svm = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(C=1.0, gamma='scale')).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(svm[-1].n_support_, 'support vectors out of', len(X_tr))   # usually a small fraction

raw = svm.decision_function(X_te)   # a SIGNED DISTANCE, not a probability

# if the business needs a probability, fit the calibrator yourself and see the bill
cal = CalibratedClassifierCV(SVC(C=1.0), method='sigmoid', cv=5).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

Where this bites in production

scikit-learn’s SVC wraps LIBSVM, and its own documentation states that fit time scales at least quadratically with the number of samples and becomes impractical beyond tens of thousands of rows — the recommended escape hatch is LinearSVC or SGDClassifier. The same page warns that with probability=True the Platt-scaled output can disagree with predict, because the sigmoid is fitted on separate internal folds. Cortes and Vapnik published the soft margin in 1995.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What does C do, and what does gamma do in an RBF kernel?
C prices margin violations; gamma sets each point’s radius of influence. Large C makes slack expensive, so the margin narrows and the boundary bends to catch every training point — C is an inverse regularisation strength. Large gamma shrinks the reach of each point, so the boundary collapses into wiggly islands around individuals. Both directions overfit, so tune the pair together on a log grid rather than one at a time.
Does the kernel trick project your data into a higher-dimensional space?
No — it computes inner products in that space without ever building it. The dual formulation touches the data only through xi⊤​xj​, so replacing that term with a kernel gives you the inner product in the implicit space at the cost of one function call. For the RBF kernel that space is infinite-dimensional, so the coordinates could not be constructed even if you wanted them.
Your SVM has 0.94 AUC and the business wants probabilities. What do you say?
That AUC is a ranking measure and the SVM does not produce probabilities. decision_function returns a signed distance to the hyperplane. Setting probability=True fits a Platt sigmoid on cross-validated folds, which is slow and can disagree with predict. Fit the calibration yourself on a held-out set, check a reliability curve, and only then let anyone build a threshold rule on the number.

Say this back tomorrow

widest empty street  ·  only the points on the kerb vote  ·  the kernel returns the inner product, never the coordinates
  • Maximising the margin means minimising the norm of the weights
  • Only support vectors enter the solution; the rest of the data is inert
  • The kernel computes an inner product in a space it never constructs

  • maximum margin
  • support vectors
  • RBF kernel
  • Platt scaling
  • soft margin

k-Nearest Neighbours & the Curse of Dimensionality

There is no training. You pay the entire bill at query time.

There is nothing to train. You keep the whole training set, and when a new point arrives you find the closest stored examples and let them vote. All of the cost sits at the moment somebody asks, not before. The number of neighbours you consult is a dial: consult one and you copy whatever noise happens to sit nearest, consult hundreds and you smooth the answer into the local average. The problem arrives when each example carries a great many columns. In a high number of dimensions the points spread out into a thin shell, and the distance to the closest one and the distance to the furthest one drift towards each other. Once nearest and furthest are almost the same number, the word nearest has stopped carrying information, and so has the model.

Like asking your neighbours who to vote for. On a street it works, because the three nearest houses genuinely share your circumstances. Now imagine a country where every address is the same distance from every other. Asking your nearest neighbours is then identical to stopping three people at random, and the answer has stopped being about you at all.

kNN is a lazy learner: fitting is storing the array, and a brute-force query costs O(nd) against the whole training set, so the entire bill arrives at inference time. k is the bias-variance dial written down directly — k=1 has zero training error, a jagged boundary and maximum variance, while a large k smooths the boundary towards the global majority class. The metric is not a hyperparameter you sprinkle on afterwards, it is the model: Euclidean, Manhattan and cosine define genuinely different neighbourhoods, and on unscaled features whichever column carries the largest units becomes the metric on its own. Then the curse. Beyer et al. (1999) showed that under broad conditions the ratio of the furthest to the nearest distance converges to one as dimension grows, so every point is roughly equidistant from every other and “nearest” is noise.

This is also the reason vector search is approximate. A kd-tree degenerates to a linear scan above roughly twenty dimensions, and a 768-dimensional embedding index has no exact structure that beats brute force — so production systems trade a small recall loss for a large latency win with HNSW or IVF-PQ. The saving grace is that real embeddings sit on a low-dimensional manifold inside that space, which is why nearest-neighbour retrieval still works at 768 dimensions when the uniform-data theory says it should not.

You reach for it when

  • A small dataset with genuine local structure and no time to train anything
  • A baseline you can stand up in an afternoon and beat later
  • Someone proposes kNN on three hundred raw columns
  • Choosing a distance metric for deduplication or retrieval

The trap

Handing kNN unscaled features. Distance is the model, so a salary column in pounds beside an age column in years means the neighbourhood is decided by salary alone and age contributes nothing at all. The related trap is treating the metric as a detail: Euclidean, Manhattan and cosine define different neighbours, and swapping one for another moves the predictions further than changing the number of neighbours does.

The math the vote, and the curse

y^​(x)=mode{yi​:xi​∈Nk​(x)}  ·  dmin​dmax​−dmin​​→0 as d→∞The second expression is the Beyer result: as dimension grows, the spread between the furthest and the nearest neighbour shrinks relative to the nearest distance itself, so their ratio tends to one. The other half of the story is cost. A brute-force query is O(nd) per prediction, and nothing whatsoever is amortised at training time, which is why the model that is free to fit is the expensive one to serve.

Scale it, then watch the curse arrive

import numpy as np
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# without the scaler, the neighbourhood is decided by whichever column
# happens to be measured in the largest units
knn = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                    KNeighborsClassifier(15, weights='distance')).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

for d in (2, 10, 100, 1000):                    # the curse, measured
    P = np.random.rand(2000, d)
    dist = np.linalg.norm(P - P[0], axis=1)[1:]
    print(d, round(dist.min() / dist.max(), 2))  # ~0.02  0.31  0.74  0.91

Where this bites in production

Meta’s FAISS, and the HNSW indexes in pgvector, Qdrant and Elasticsearch, all exist because exact nearest-neighbour search over 768-dimensional embeddings has no structure left to exploit — a kd-tree degenerates to a full scan above roughly twenty dimensions. So every production vector database is approximate by design, trading a few points of recall for orders of magnitude of latency. The A in ANN is there because of the curse of dimensionality.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why does kNN break in high dimensions?
Because the ratio of the furthest neighbour to the nearest tends towards one. Beyer et al. (1999) showed that under broad conditions the contrast between distances vanishes as dimension grows, so every stored point is roughly equidistant from your query. The vote is then taken among neighbours chosen by rounding error, and adding more irrelevant columns actively makes it worse.
How do you choose the number of neighbours?
By cross-validation, because it is the bias-variance dial in plain sight. One neighbour gives zero training error, a jagged boundary and maximum variance. A very large value smooths towards the global majority class and towards pure bias. Use an odd number for binary problems to avoid ties, and prefer distance weighting so a neighbour twice as far counts for less.
Why is vector search approximate rather than exact?
Because at 768 dimensions exact search is a full scan. Tree indexes lose to brute force above roughly twenty dimensions, and the curse guarantees there is no partition that prunes usefully. HNSW and IVF-PQ therefore accept a small, measurable recall loss for a very large latency win — and you should quote the recall figure, because it is a tuning knob and not a constant.

Say this back tomorrow

no training, all query  ·  the metric is the model  ·  in high dimensions nearest and furthest converge
  • Fitting is free and every prediction costs a pass over the training set
  • Scaling is mandatory and the distance metric is a modelling decision
  • As dimension grows the nearest-to-furthest ratio goes to one, so kNN dies

  • distance metric
  • approximate search
  • HNSW

Naive Bayes

The assumption is false. The classifier works anyway, and you should be able to say why.

You want to know which class a document belongs to. The honest calculation asks how likely this exact combination of words is under each class, and there are far too many combinations for you to have ever seen. So you pretend every word arrived independently of every other, multiply the individual word probabilities together, and take whichever class comes out highest. The pretence is plainly wrong. In real text “new” and “york” arrive together, and counting them separately counts the same piece of evidence twice. What saves you is that you only need the ranking to be right, not the numbers. Double counting inflates every class, usually in the same direction, so the winner is still the winner. The scores that come out, though, are almost always far more confident than they have any right to be.

Like a panel of judges who never speak to each other. Each scores the dish on one thing alone — salt, texture, plating — and nobody adjusts for the fact that an over-salted dish is usually over-seasoned all round. The same fault is counted three times and the total is nonsense. The dish that wins is still, very often, the right dish.

Naive Bayes applies Bayes’ rule and then assumes the features are conditionally independent given the class, which collapses P(x1​,…,xd​∣y) into ∏j​P(xj​∣y). That turns an intractable joint into d one-dimensional counting problems, so it trains in a single pass and needs very little data. The assumption is false for almost any real feature set, and it still classifies well because the decision depends only on which class has the largest posterior, not on the value of that posterior. Correlated features are double counted and the products go badly wrong in magnitude — but they go wrong in roughly the same direction for every class, so the argmax survives. Two details always get asked: additive smoothing, so one unseen feature does not zero the whole product, and summing logs rather than multiplying probabilities.

Naive Bayes is generative: it models the joint P(x,y) and could in principle produce data. Logistic regression is discriminative: it models P(y∣x) directly and never commits to how the features are distributed. Ng and Jordan (2001) made the tradeoff precise — the generative model has the higher asymptotic error but approaches its own ceiling in roughly O(logd) examples rather than O(d), so it wins on small data and loses once data is plentiful. Its wrong assumption is functioning as a prior. That sentence is what separates a memorised answer from an understood one.

You reach for it when

  • A text classifier you need working as a baseline this afternoon
  • Four hundred labelled rows and several thousand features
  • Spam or topic filtering where one pass over the data is the budget
  • An interviewer asks for the difference between generative and discriminative

The trap

Reporting Naive Bayes probabilities as though they were calibrated. Multiplying hundreds of correlated word probabilities drives the posterior to 0.999 or 0.001 with almost nothing in between, so a threshold of 0.9 does not mean 90% confidence in anything. Use the ranking, or fit isotonic or Platt calibration on held-out data before anyone writes a business rule on the number. The other trap is forgetting smoothing: a single unseen token zeroes the entire product.

The math the assumption, and the smoothing

y^​=argmaxy​P(y)∏j​P(xj​∣y)  ·  P^(xj​∣y)=ny​+αdnjy​+α​The product is the conditional-independence assumption written down — it is the only step in the derivation that is not exact. In practice you compute logP(y)+∑j​logP(xj​∣y), because a thousand-token document multiplies a thousand numbers below one and underflows a 64-bit float long before it finishes. α=1 is Laplace smoothing, α<1 is Lidstone, and scikit-learn defaults to α=1.0.

Smooth it, log it, then calibrate it

import numpy as np
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV

nb = MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0).fit(X_counts, y)   # alpha=1.0 IS Laplace smoothing
# with alpha=0, one token never seen in a class zeroes that whole product

lp = nb.predict_log_proba(X_te)     # log space, or a 1000-token doc underflows
print(np.exp(lp).max(1)[:5])        # [1.000 0.999 1.000 0.998 1.000] -- no middle

# want a number a business can threshold? calibrate it on held-out folds first
cal = CalibratedClassifierCV(MultinomialNB(), method='isotonic', cv=5).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

Where this bites in production

Paul Graham’s “A Plan for Spam” (2002) and its follow-up put naive Bayesian filtering into everyday use, reporting on the order of 99.5% of spam caught at a false-positive rate near 0.03% — on a personal corpus of a few thousand messages, which is exactly the small-data regime where a generative model wins. scikit-learn’s MultinomialNB still defaults to alpha=1.0, so Laplace smoothing is on unless somebody deliberately turns it off.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Independence is obviously false for text. Why does it still work?
Because classification needs the argmax, not the posterior. Correlated words are counted more than once, which corrupts the magnitude of every class score. It corrupts them in roughly the same direction, so the ordering between classes survives even when the numbers do not. Ranking is preserved; calibration is destroyed. Say both halves — the second half is the one candidates miss.
Naive Bayes or logistic regression on four hundred labelled rows?
Naive Bayes, and the reason is the generative-discriminative tradeoff. Ng and Jordan showed the generative model has the higher asymptotic error but reaches its ceiling in far fewer examples — roughly logarithmic in the number of features rather than linear. Its independence assumption acts as a prior that buys you variance reduction when you have no data to spend.
Your Naive Bayes classifier outputs 0.9999. What does that tell you?
Almost nothing about probability. The posterior is a product of hundreds of correlated per-feature terms, so it saturates at the extremes by construction — that number is not a 99.99% chance of anything. It is still usable as a rank, so ROC-AUC and top-k precision remain meaningful. If the value itself has to mean something, fit isotonic regression on a held-out set.

Say this back tomorrow

wrong probabilities, right argmax  ·  smooth the counts, and sum the logs
  • Conditional independence is false and mostly harmless, because you need only the argmax
  • Generative beats discriminative on small data: the assumption acts as a prior
  • The posteriors are badly overconfident — calibrate before thresholding

  • Laplace smoothing
  • generative model
  • log-space
  • calibration

k-Means & Its Failure Modes

Three lines of algorithm, and five assumptions nobody states out loud.

Decide how many groups you want. Drop that many markers at random positions. Then repeat two steps until nothing moves: send every point to its nearest marker, and shift each marker to the average of the points that chose it. That is the whole algorithm. It is quick and it always returns something, which is the danger, because it will hand you groups whether or not any exist. It assumes the groups are round, roughly the same size and roughly the same spread. Give it two long thin streaks, or a small dense clump beside a huge diffuse one, and it slices them the wrong way with complete confidence. It is also sensitive to where the markers started, so two runs on identical data give two different answers unless you fix the seeding procedure.

Like siting ice cream vans on a beach. Park them anywhere, send every sunbather to the closest van, then move each van to the middle of its own crowd, and repeat until the vans settle. It works beautifully on a wide open beach. On a long narrow one the right answer is a line of vans down the sand, and the algorithm insists on circles.

Lloyd’s algorithm in three lines: initialise k centroids, assign each point to the nearest one, recompute each centroid as the mean of its members, repeat until the assignments stop changing. It minimises the within-cluster sum of squares, it always converges, and it converges to a local optimum of a non-convex objective. Random initialisation can drop two centroids inside one true cluster and leave another unclaimed, which is why k-means++ seeds them one at a time with probability proportional to the squared distance from the nearest existing centroid. The assumptions are the entire interview: isotropic clusters of similar variance and similar size, a Euclidean metric and therefore mandatory scaling, sensitivity to the seed, and a mean that outliers drag around. It will happily return k clusters from pure noise.

The discriminating fact: k-means is a constrained Gaussian mixture. Fix every component’s covariance to σ2I with the same σ, fix the mixing weights equal, and replace the soft responsibilities of the E-step with a hard assignment — and EM becomes Lloyd’s algorithm exactly. That framing hands you the escape route as well: relax the covariance and a full Gaussian mixture handles elongated clusters, relax the shape entirely and DBSCAN handles arbitrary ones. On choosing k: add silhouette and the gap statistic to the elbow, and be honest that in commercial work k is usually set by what the business can act on — five segments because there are five campaign budgets.

You reach for it when

  • A first look at unlabelled customer or telemetry data
  • Vector quantisation, colour reduction, or building a codebook
  • Somebody presents five segments and cannot say why five
  • The scatter plot shows arcs, streaks or nested rings

The trap

Trusting the elbow. On real data the within-cluster sum of squares falls smoothly with no kink to read, so people pick a number anyway and justify it afterwards. The deeper trap is being unable to name the assumptions when asked what k-means gets wrong: isotropic clusters of similar variance and similar size, a Euclidean metric, mandatory scaling, a local optimum that depends on the seed, and a mean that any outlier can drag.

The math inertia, and the silhouette

minC​∑k​∑x∈Ck​​∥x−μk​∥2  ·  s=max(a,b)b−a​The objective is the within-cluster sum of squares, and it falls monotonically as k rises — which is precisely why the elbow is unreliable, and why k=n scores perfectly. The silhouette compares a, the mean distance to your own cluster, with b, the mean distance to the nearest other cluster. It runs from −1 to 1 and, unlike inertia, it can be compared across different values of k.

Never read the elbow on its own

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)   # Euclidean objective: scaling is not optional

for k in range(2, 9):
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, init='k-means++', n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(Xs)
    print(k, round(km.inertia_), round(silhouette_score(Xs, km.labels_), 3))

# inertia falls monotonically, so it can never choose k on its own
# n_init exists because one random start lands in one local optimum
# elongated clusters? swap in GaussianMixture(covariance_type='full')

Where this bites in production

scikit-learn seeds with k-means++ by default and, until version 1.4, repeated the entire fit ten times and kept the lowest inertia. The default is now n_init='auto' — one run for k-means++ and ten for random init — because good seeding is what made the repeats unnecessary. Arthur and Vassilvitskii’s 2007 k-means++ paper proves a logarithmic competitive bound on the objective and reports fits that were both faster and better than random restarts.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

The elbow is ambiguous. Now what?
Stop hunting for a kink and use something comparable across k. Silhouette scores every k on the same scale, the gap statistic compares your inertia against a uniform null, and the downstream task metric beats both when one exists. Then say the honest thing: in commercial work k is usually fixed by what the business can act on, and five segments because there are five budgets is a defensible answer.
Name three shapes k-means will get wrong.
Elongated, nested, and very unequally sized clusters. The objective minimises squared distance to a centre, so it carves Voronoi cells and cuts a long streak across its length rather than following it. Nested rings share a centre, so no partition by distance can separate them. And a large diffuse cluster beside a small tight one gets split, because splitting the big one lowers inertia more.
How is k-means related to a Gaussian mixture?
It is a constrained special case. Tie every component’s covariance to the same isotropic matrix, fix the mixing weights equal, and replace the soft responsibilities of the E-step with a hard assignment — EM then reduces to Lloyd’s algorithm. That is also the fix: relax the covariance constraint and you have a mixture that handles elongated, unequally sized clusters and returns a soft membership too.

Say this back tomorrow

assign, recompute, repeat  ·  it assumes round, equal and separate  ·  it is a hard-assignment isotropic Gaussian mixture
  • Lloyd’s algorithm converges, but only to a seed-dependent local optimum
  • It assumes isotropic, similar-size, similar-variance clusters and needs scaling
  • Inertia cannot choose k: use silhouette, the gap statistic, or the business

Unlocks

  • Lloyd's algorithm
  • k-means++
  • silhouette
  • inertia
  • Gaussian mixture

DBSCAN & Hierarchical Clustering

When the clusters are not blobs, and when you would rather not pick a number at all.

Instead of asking which centre a point is nearest, ask how crowded its own neighbourhood is. Draw a small circle around every point. If enough others fall inside it, that point sits in a dense region and belongs to a cluster, and anything reachable through a chain of such points joins the same cluster. Points that are close to a dense one without being crowded themselves sit on the border. Points that are neither get labelled noise and left out, which is the honest thing to do with an outlier rather than forcing it into the nearest group. Because clusters grow by contact they can be any shape at all: rings, crescents, long ribbons. The weakness is that one circle size has to serve the whole dataset, so a tight group and a diffuse group cannot both be found with a single setting. The other family never asks for a number. Start with every point alone, repeatedly merge the two closest groups, and draw the entire merge history as a tree that you cut wherever you like, afterwards.

Think of finding towns from house lights at night. A town is anywhere the lights are packed close, whatever shape it sprawls into, and a lone farmhouse stays a farmhouse rather than becoming a suburb of the nearest town. Now try one packing rule for a city and for the Highlands. Set it for the city and the Highlands reads as empty countryside.

DBSCAN takes a radius eps and a count min_samples. A point with at least min_samples neighbours inside eps is a core point; clusters are the connected components of core points; border points are non-core points that fall inside a core point’s radius; everything else is labelled noise rather than assigned anywhere. You never specify the number of clusters, and because membership propagates by density connection the clusters can take any shape — concentric rings and interleaved crescents, where k-means is hopeless. The failure is the mirror image of the strength: one global eps cannot describe a dense cluster and a sparse cluster at the same time, so you either merge the tight ones or lose the diffuse one to noise. HDBSCAN fixes precisely this by building the clustering over all values of eps and extracting the most persistent clusters.

Agglomerative clustering starts with every point as its own cluster and merges the closest pair repeatedly, and the linkage is the whole decision. Single linkage uses the minimum distance between members, so it follows thin bridges and produces the chaining effect — helpful for elongated shapes, disastrous when two clusters touch at one point. Complete linkage uses the maximum and returns compact round clusters. Ward merges the pair that raises the within-cluster variance least, which is the k-means objective run bottom-up, and it is the sensible Euclidean default. The deliverable is the dendrogram: you compute it once and cut it at any height afterwards, so nothing forces you to commit to a number in advance. It costs O(n2) memory, so it stops at tens of thousands of rows.

You reach for it when

  • The scatter plot shows rings, crescents or long ribbons
  • You genuinely do not know how many groups there are
  • Outliers must be excluded rather than forced into a group
  • A stakeholder wants the merge history, not a fixed number of segments

The trap

Tuning eps by hand until the picture looks about right. There is a principled way: sort every point by the distance to its min_samples-th nearest neighbour, plot that sorted curve, and read eps off the knee. The second trap is selling DBSCAN as strictly better than k-means. One radius cannot serve two densities, it degrades in high dimensions where all distances converge, and it is entirely at the mercy of the metric you picked.

The math two knobs, and neither is k

core point: ∣Nε​(x)∣≥minPts  ·  minPts≥d+1, commonly 2d  ·  Ward merges the pair raising ∑∥x−μ∥2 leastε is read off the k-distance curve at k=minPts, not guessed. minPts sets how much evidence a point needs before it counts as dense, and the usual rule is at least d+1, commonly 2d. Note what neither parameter is: a number of clusters. Hierarchical clustering removes even these — the dendrogram is computed once and cut afterwards, at whatever height you choose to defend.

Read eps, do not guess it

import numpy as np
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN, AgglomerativeClustering

# read eps off the k-distance curve instead of guessing at it
d, _ = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=4).fit(Xs).kneighbors(Xs)
kdist = np.sort(d[:, -1])          # plot this: eps is the knee, min_samples = 4

db = DBSCAN(eps=0.42, min_samples=4).fit(Xs)
print((db.labels_ == -1).sum(), 'points labelled noise')   # -1 is not a cluster id

# no k in advance: build the whole tree, cut it wherever you like
ward = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=None, distance_threshold=2.5,
                               linkage='ward').fit(Xs)

Where this bites in production

DBSCAN came out of Ester, Kriegel, Sander and Xu at KDD 1996 and won that conference’s test-of-time award in 2014. Its varying-density weakness was well enough known that HDBSCAN lived as a separate package for years before scikit-learn absorbed it as sklearn.cluster.HDBSCAN in version 1.3. One library convention is worth carrying into an interview: DBSCAN returns -1 for noise, and that is a label meaning “not clustered”, not a cluster index.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

How do you pick eps and minPts?
minPts from the dimensionality, eps from the k-distance curve. Set minPts to at least one more than the number of features, commonly twice it. Then compute every point’s distance to its minPts-th nearest neighbour, sort those distances, plot them, and take eps at the knee where the curve turns upward. Hand-tuning eps until the picture looks right is the answer that loses the round.
When would you not reach for DBSCAN?
When the clusters have different densities, or the data is high-dimensional. A single eps cannot fit a tight cluster and a diffuse one at once, so you either merge the tight ones or lose the diffuse one to noise — HDBSCAN exists for exactly this. And above a few dozen dimensions distances concentrate, so the density estimate that DBSCAN is built on stops discriminating.
Single linkage or Ward?
Ward, unless you specifically want chains. Single linkage merges on the minimum pairwise distance, so it follows thin bridges and will happily join two clusters that touch at one noisy point. Ward merges the pair that increases within-cluster variance least, giving compact clusters — it is the k-means objective run bottom-up, and it requires a Euclidean metric to be meaningful.

Say this back tomorrow

density, not distance to a centre  ·  noise is a legitimate answer  ·  one eps cannot serve two densities
  • Core, border and noise: DBSCAN is allowed to leave a point unassigned
  • Arbitrary shapes and no k, paid for by one global eps that cannot vary
  • The dendrogram lets you choose the number of clusters after the fact

  • core points
  • k-distance plot
  • HDBSCAN
  • Ward linkage
  • dendrogram
