Feature Engineering: Scaling, Encoding & Missing Values

The model is a week of work. This is the other three.

Three questions come up on every table you will ever model. Does the scale of a column matter? For anything that measures distance or follows a gradient, yes, and a column in pounds will drown a column in years. For trees it does not matter at all, because a split only cares about the order of the values. How do you turn words into numbers? If there are a handful of categories, give each one its own column. If the categories have a real order, keep the order. If there are fifty thousand of them, replace each with the average outcome you have seen for it — but work that average out on folds the row is not in, or the column quietly contains the row’s own answer. And what do you do about blanks? That depends entirely on why they are blank, and often the fact that a value is missing is the most useful thing in the whole row.

Think of a form with a blank box. Sometimes the printer smudged it, and writing in the typical answer is harmless. Sometimes an entire ward was handed a different version of the form, so the blank tells you which ward. And sometimes people leave it blank precisely because their answer is embarrassing — then filling in the average erases the only signal that box ever carried.

Scaling: anything that measures distance or follows a gradient needs it — kNN, SVM, k-means, PCA and any penalised linear model, because the penalty is not scale-invariant. Trees never need it, since a split is invariant to any monotone transform of a feature. Encoding: one-hot for low cardinality, ordinal only when the order is genuinely real, and target encoding for high cardinality, replacing each level with a smoothed mean of the target, x^c​=(nc​yˉ​c​+myˉ​)/(nc​+m), where m pulls rare levels back towards the global mean. Target encoding must be computed out of fold, or each row’s feature contains its own label. For unbounded vocabularies — URLs, device IDs, product SKUs — the hashing trick maps the string into a fixed number of buckets, so a level never seen in training still lands somewhere at serving time instead of throwing.

Missing values are a mechanism question before they are a technique question. MCAR means the missingness is independent of everything, so dropping rows or mean-imputing is unbiased and only costs you power. MAR means it depends on other observed columns, so a model-based imputation conditioned on those columns is the honest fix. MNAR means it depends on the unobserved value itself — income missing because it is high, a lab test missing because nobody thought the patient needed one — and no imputation recovers what was never recorded. In all three cases add a binary indicator for was-it-missing, because under MNAR that indicator routinely carries more signal than the imputed value does.

You reach for it when

  • A postcode or SKU column holding forty thousand levels
  • A column that is 40% null and nobody has asked why
  • Moving a notebook model onto a serving path that will meet unseen categories
  • Deciding whether the pipeline needs a scaler at all

The trap

Mean-imputing a column that is missing for a reason. If income is blank because the applicant declined to state it, the blank is a fact about the applicant, and replacing it with the population mean deletes that fact and invents a fake typical customer. Add a was-it-missing indicator before you impute anything. The other reliable trap is target encoding fitted on the full training set, so every row’s feature quietly contains its own label.

The math smoothed target encoding, and the hash

x^c​=nc​+mnc​yˉ​c​+myˉ​​  ·  j=hash(s)modBnc​ is the number of rows in category c, yˉ​c​ its mean target and yˉ​ the global mean, and m is the smoothing weight — a level seen twice is pulled almost entirely to the global mean, a level seen ten thousand times is left alone. Compute the numerator on folds that exclude the row itself, or the feature contains its own label. The hash sends any string, including one never seen in training, into B buckets; collisions are the price and the model usually absorbs them.

Everything inside one fitted pipeline

from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder, TargetEncoder
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ('num', make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(add_indicator=True), StandardScaler()), num_cols),
    ('cat', OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore', min_frequency=20), low_card),
    ('hi',  TargetEncoder(smooth='auto'), high_card),   # cross-fitted internally
])

# add_indicator keeps the was-it-missing column, which is the signal under MNAR
# handle_unknown='ignore' is what stops an unseen category crashing the serving path
# everything fits INSIDE the pipeline, so no statistic crosses the split

Where this bites in production

scikit-learn added TargetEncoder in version 1.3 and made fit_transform cross-fit internally by default, precisely because target encoding fitted on the full training set leaks so reliably that the library would not ship the naive version. CatBoost’s answer is ordered target statistics, computed over a random permutation of the history so a row never sees its own label. Vowpal Wabbit made the hashing trick standard at web scale, hashing raw feature strings into a fixed table rather than building a vocabulary at all.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

One-hot, ordinal or target encoding — which and why?
Cardinality picks the encoder; a real order picks the middle one. One-hot below roughly fifty levels, because it makes no ordering claim. Ordinal only when the order is genuine, such as small-medium-large, since a tree can split it and a linear model reads it as a number. Target encoding above that, computed out of fold with smoothing — or let CatBoost do it with ordered target statistics.
A column is 40% missing. What do you do first?
Ask why it is missing, because the mechanism decides the fix. If it is missing completely at random, dropping or mean-imputing is unbiased. If it depends on other observed columns, impute conditionally on them. If it depends on the unobserved value itself, no imputation can recover it — add an indicator column and let the model use the missingness, which is often the strongest feature in the row.
Your model meets a category at serving time that was never in training. What happens?
It depends entirely on which encoder you chose, and you should know before you ship. One-hot with handle_unknown='ignore' emits an all-zero row; without it, the transform raises and takes the request down. Target encoding falls back to the global mean. The hashing trick maps it into a bucket like everything else, which is the reason it is used for unbounded vocabularies.

Say this back tomorrow

trees ignore scale  ·  target encoding must be out-of-fold  ·  the blank itself is a feature
  • Distance and gradient models need scaling; trees are invariant to it
  • Target encoding leaks unless it is computed on folds excluding the row
  • MCAR, MAR and MNAR need different fixes, and missingness is often predictive

  • target encoding
  • hashing trick
  • MNAR
  • missing indicator
  • ColumnTransformer

ADVANCED · 14 topics

Neural networks and the statistics under them

Calibration and imbalance first, because they decide whether a model is usable at all. Then a neural network built from the perceptron up — every piece of it is here because something before it failed. Ends with the three ways to squash high-dimensional data into a picture, and the one you must never re-fit on new points.

Read it first
You are my AI/ML interview tutor. This session covers ONE block of machine learning: Advanced — Neural networks and the statistics under them

The topics in this block are:
1. Class Imbalance in Practice — Usually a threshold and a metric problem wearing a data problem’s clothes
2. Calibration — AUC grades the order. Calibration asks whether the number means anything
3. Hyperparameter Tuning & Nested CV — The search is the easy half. Reporting it honestly is the half people fail
4. Ensembling & Stacking — Diversity is the ingredient. Five copies of the same model buy you almost nothing
5. The Perceptron & the Multilayer Perceptron — One neuron draws one straight line. Everything after that follows from the limitation
6. Backpropagation — The chain rule, cached, run right to left. That is the whole idea
7. Activation Functions & Vanishing Gradients — The bend between two layers, and the arithmetic that kills a deep stack
8. Optimisers: SGD, Momentum, Adam & AdamW — Four algorithms, and each one exists because the one before it failed at something
9. Initialisation & Learning-Rate Schedules — Where the weights start, and how fast you move them. The second is the setting to tune first
10. Batch Norm vs Layer Norm — The same formula. The axis it reduces over decides where each one can be used
11. Dropout & Early Stopping — One trains a crowd of smaller networks. The other stops before the crowd memorises
12. Convolutions, Pooling & the Receptive Field — One small detector, slid everywhere — and a window that widens with every layer
13. RNNs, LSTMs & Why They Lost — The gates are the famous part. The reason they lost has nothing to do with them
14. PCA, t-SNE & UMAP — Two of these are pictures, not preprocessing. Only one of them belongs in a pipeline

25advanced

Class Imbalance in Practice

Usually a threshold and a metric problem wearing a data problem’s clothes.

Ninety-nine out of a hundred transactions are fine and one is fraud. The first question is not which sampling trick to reach for. It is whether the imbalance is a problem at all. A model can rank the rare cases perfectly well and still look broken, because you are reading the wrong number and cutting at the wrong place. Accuracy stops meaning anything once one class is much rarer than the other: a model that always says no scores brilliantly and catches nothing. Most of the time the fix is to stop quoting accuracy and to move the cut-off, which costs nothing and changes nothing about the model itself. Only when that runs out do you start reweighting, and only after that do you start inventing rows.

Like a smoke alarm. Real fires are rare, so an alarm that never sounds is right almost every night. Nobody fixes that by rebuilding the sensor, and nobody fixes it by lighting fake fires in the kitchen to train it on. You turn the sensitivity dial until it catches the real thing without going off every time you make toast.

Ask three questions before touching the data. Is the imbalance real, or an artefact of how you sampled? Does the metric reflect it — accuracy is untrustworthy past roughly five to one, so move to PR-AUC, F-beta or MCC, and quote the PR-AUC baseline, which is the prevalence and not 0.5. And is the threshold tuned? 0.5 is an arbitrary cut on a probability, and it is a free parameter. Only then do you touch the distribution: class_weight="balanced" reweights the loss so a minority error costs more, then random undersampling throws data away, random oversampling duplicates it, and SMOTE interpolates between a minority point and its nearest neighbours. A 2024 study over 15 models and 30 datasets — about nine thousand runs — put threshold tuning first at mean F1 0.617, against SMOTE 0.605, class weights 0.594 and an untouched baseline 0.556.

Three specific problems with SMOTE, and an interviewer wants them named. It interpolates in feature space, so on one-hot, ordinal or bounded columns it invents points that could not exist — half a category, a negative age — which is why SMOTE-NC exists. It must be fitted inside each training fold, never before the split, or synthetic points built from validation neighbours walk straight into your estimate. And it changes the base rate the model was fitted to, so every probability it emits is inflated. Anything that rebalances the training distribution decalibrates you. That is the cost threshold tuning does not have.

You reach for it when

  • Fraud, churn or default with a positive rate under five per cent
  • Someone proposes SMOTE before the metric has been agreed
  • A model reports 99% accuracy and catches nothing
  • A downstream decision needs the probability, not just the ranking

The trap

Reaching for SMOTE first, and then reporting the validation score computed on the resampled data. That is two mistakes in one move. The oversampling has to happen inside each training fold, or synthetic points built from validation neighbours leak into your estimate. And a validation set you rebalanced no longer carries the production base rate, so its precision is fiction. Fix the metric and the threshold first.

The math the two numbers people skip

PR-AUCchance​=π  ·  t⋆=argmaxt​[v⋅TP(t)−c⋅FP(t)]The left-hand line is the baseline everyone forgets: ROC-AUC starts at 0.5 whatever the prevalence π, but PR-AUC starts at the prevalence, so 0.30 on a 1% problem is a thirty-fold lift and not a poor score. The right-hand line is the threshold, chosen by expected value when you can price the two errors, by max Fβ​ or Youden’s J when you cannot, or by a hard constraint such as precision at least 0.90. And if you did resample from π to π′, every score is shifted: subtract log1−π′π′​ and add log1−ππ​ in log-odds space to get back a number you can quote.

SMOTE inside the fold, threshold outside

from imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_predict
from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve

# SMOTE INSIDE the pipeline -> refit on each training fold, never on the whole set
pipe = Pipeline([("smote", SMOTE(random_state=0)), ("clf", clf)])
p = cross_val_predict(pipe, X, y, cv=StratifiedKFold(5), method="predict_proba")[:, 1]

# the threshold is a free parameter. 0.5 came from nowhere.
prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve(y, p)
f2 = 5 * prec * rec / (4 * prec + rec + 1e-12)   # recall-heavy: screening
print(thr[f2[:-1].argmax()], y.mean())           # tune this BEFORE you resample

# y.mean() is your PR-AUC baseline. Quote it next to any PR-AUC you report.

Where this bites in production

The ULB credit-card fraud dataset on Kaggle — 284,807 transactions, 492 of them fraudulent, 0.172% positives — is where most people first meet this. Predicting “legitimate” for every row scores 99.83% accuracy on it. It is also where SMOTE-first became folklore: hundreds of public notebooks oversample before splitting, report near-perfect recall on a rebalanced holdout, and would catch almost nothing behind a real payment gateway.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Would you use SMOTE here? Defend it.
Rarely, and never as the first move. It interpolates between a minority point and its neighbours in feature space, so on one-hot or ordinal columns it manufactures rows that could not exist. It has to be fitted inside each training fold or it leaks. And it shifts the base rate, which decalibrates every probability the model emits. Tune the threshold first — that costs nothing and it preserves calibration.
Your fraud model reports 99.8% accuracy. What do you say?
Nothing, until I know the base rate. At 0.2% positives the constant “not fraud” scores 99.8%, so that number is entirely consistent with a model that catches no fraud whatsoever. Ask for the confusion matrix, for PR-AUC against a baseline equal to the prevalence, and for recall at whatever precision the manual review queue can actually absorb.
Why does resampling hurt if you need probabilities?
Because it changes the prior the model was fitted to. Train on a fifty-fifty set built by oversampling and the model has learned a world in which half of all transactions are fraud, so every score it emits is inflated relative to production. The 2024 nine-thousand-run study found SMOTE produced the worst log loss and Brier of any strategy tested. Either leave the data alone and move the threshold, or resample and then correct the prior.

Say this back tomorrow

imbalance is usually a metric and a threshold problem  ·  resample last, if at all
  • Ask whether the imbalance is real before you change anything about the data
  • Threshold tuning beat every resampling strategy in the 2024 nine-thousand-run study
  • Every rebalancing method decalibrates the probabilities; threshold moving does not

  • PR-AUC baseline
  • class weights
  • SMOTE leakage
  • MCC

26advanced

Calibration

AUC grades the order. Calibration asks whether the number means anything.

Take every case where the model said seventy per cent, and count how many of them actually happened. If it is about seventy in a hundred, the number means what it says. If only forty happened, the model is bluffing. This is a different question from whether the model puts the right cases at the top. A model can order every case perfectly and still quote numbers that are systematically too confident, and you would never see it in a ranking score. It matters the moment somebody multiplies the number by money — an expected loss, a bid, a review queue with a fixed cost per case. If a person or a spreadsheet consumes the number rather than the order, this is the thing to check.

Like a weather forecaster. Gather every day she said thirty per cent chance of rain. If it rained on about thirty of every hundred such days, she is calibrated, and you can plan a wedding on her word. A second forecaster ranks wet days above dry ones flawlessly but says ninety per cent every single time. Perfect order, useless numbers.

A model is calibrated when, among all cases it scored p, the event happens a fraction p of the time. You measure it three ways: a reliability diagram, which bins the predictions and plots mean predicted against observed frequency; the Brier score, which is mean squared error on probabilities; and expected calibration error, which is the reliability diagram collapsed into one bin-weighted average gap, with under 0.05 the usual heuristic. Three post-hoc fixes. Platt scaling fits a two-parameter sigmoid, so it is stable on small data and is the classic repair for an SVM. Isotonic regression fits any monotone step function, which is more flexible and will overfit under a few thousand points. Temperature scaling divides the logits by one learned scalar, which is standard for neural networks because it cannot change the ranking or the accuracy.

Which models arrive calibrated is worth knowing cold. Logistic regression and gradient boosting trained on log loss optimise a proper scoring rule, so they land close. An SVM optimises hinge loss and its margin is not a probability at all. A random forest averages votes, so it is pulled toward the middle and comes out under-confident at both extremes. Modern deep networks are the opposite — more accurate than their ancestors and far more over-confident. Whatever calibrator you fit, fit it on data the model has not seen: CalibratedClassifierCV with cv=5 does that by using out-of-fold predictions.

You reach for it when

  • A score is multiplied by a cost, a bid or an expected loss
  • AUC is high and the business says the numbers look wrong
  • You rebalanced the training set and the probabilities moved
  • Setting one threshold that has to hold for a year

The trap

Calibrating once, on the whole test set, and never looking again. One aggregate curve can look immaculate while the model is confidently wrong on a single region, device type or age band — the over-shoot in one slice cancels the under-shoot in another and the average hides both. Calibration also decays: the base rate moves, the population moves, and the ranking holds while the numbers quietly stop meaning anything.

The math the two numbers to quote

Brier=N1​∑i​(pi​−yi​)2  ·  ECE=∑b=1B​Nnb​​​acc(b)−conf(b)​Brier is the mean squared error of a probability. It decomposes into uncertainty plus resolution minus reliability, which means a good Brier can hide poor calibration when sharp resolution is carrying it — so never quote Brier alone. ECE bins the predictions, takes the gap between confidence and accuracy in each bin, and weights by bin size; under 0.05 is a convention, not a law, and it is sensitive to the number of bins. Temperature scaling is softmax(z/T) with a single T fitted on a validation set: monotone in z, so accuracy and AUC are provably unchanged.

Calibrating without leaking

from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV, calibration_curve
from sklearn.metrics import brier_score_loss

# cv=5 fits the calibrator on OUT-OF-FOLD predictions - never on data the model saw
# method="sigmoid" is Platt: 2 parameters, the right choice under ~1000 points
cal = CalibratedClassifierCV(clf, method="isotonic", cv=5).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

p_raw = clf.fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
p_cal = cal.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
print(brier_score_loss(y_te, p_raw), brier_score_loss(y_te, p_cal))

observed, predicted = calibration_curve(y_te, p_cal, n_bins=10)
print(abs(observed - predicted).max())   # worst bin. Now repeat it PER SLICE.

Where this bites in production

Guo et al. (2017), “On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks”, put the number on it. LeNet from 1998 was close to calibrated on CIFAR-100; ResNet-110, far more accurate, was badly over-confident, with expected calibration error several times worse. Depth, batch normalisation and weight decay all pushed it further. The fix that won was the cheapest one on the shelf: a single temperature parameter fitted on a validation set, which cannot reorder a single prediction.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

AUC is 0.91 and the business says the probabilities are wrong. What is happening?
AUC only grades the order. It is the probability that a random positive outscores a random negative, so any monotone squashing of your scores leaves it untouched while destroying their meaning. Plot a reliability diagram, quote Brier and ECE, then fit a calibrator on held-out data. If it is a neural network, try temperature scaling first — it cannot change the ranking, so the AUC is safe.
Platt, isotonic or temperature — pick one and say why.
The size of the calibration set decides it. Platt fits a two-parameter sigmoid, so it is stable on a few hundred points and is the classic repair for an SVM’s uncalibrated margins. Isotonic fits any monotone step function, which is more flexible and will happily overfit below a few thousand points. Temperature scaling is one scalar on the logits, which is why it is standard for deep nets: accuracy and ranking are untouched by construction.
Which models come out calibrated and which do not?
Anything optimising a proper scoring rule tends to. Logistic regression and gradient boosting on log loss land close. An SVM optimises hinge loss and its margins are not probabilities at all. A random forest averages votes, so it is pulled toward the middle and is under-confident at both extremes. Modern deep networks are the mirror image — accurate and badly over-confident.

Say this back tomorrow

calibrated = of everything you called 0.7, about 70% happened
  • Ranking metrics are blind to calibration; a monotone squash leaves AUC untouched
  • Platt for small data, isotonic for large, temperature for neural networks
  • Measure it by slice and on a schedule — the aggregate curve hides both failures

Hyperparameter Tuning & Nested CV

The search is the easy half. Reporting it honestly is the half people fail.

There are two loops here and people collapse them into one. The inner loop tries settings and keeps whichever did best. The outer loop asks how well the whole procedure does on data it has never touched. If you use the same split for both, the winning setting was chosen partly because it happened to suit that split, and the score you then quote includes all of that luck. Run enough trials and you will always find a setting that looks brilliant on your validation set for no reason whatsoever. As for the search itself: trying every combination on a neat lattice sounds thorough, but most of the knobs barely matter, and the lattice spends nearly every trial re-testing the same value of the one that does.

Think of a hiring panel. You interview two hundred candidates, pick whoever scored highest, and then quote that interview score as your estimate of how well they will do the job. It is inflated, by exactly the amount the search could exploit. An honest estimate needs a second assessment that the selection never saw.

Grid search takes the product of your value lists, so cost multiplies with every axis you add and most of the trials go on parameters that do not matter. Random search samples from distributions instead, and Bergstra and Bengio’s 2012 result is the reason it wins: real objective functions have low effective dimensionality, so with n trials random search gives you n distinct values of every parameter, while a grid gives you only the number of levels on that axis. Bayesian methods — Gaussian processes or TPE — fit a surrogate to what they have seen and sample where the expected improvement is highest, which earns its overhead when each trial is expensive. Successive halving starts many configurations on a small budget, keeps the top fraction and multiplies the budget; Hyperband runs successive halving at several aggressiveness levels so a slow starter is not always killed.

Then the part most candidates miss. Using one cross-validation loop for both tuning and reporting is optimistically biased, because the selection and the estimate share a split. Nested cross-validation separates them: the outer loop estimates generalisation, and inside each outer training fold a complete inner search picks its own hyperparameters. You end up with k different winners across the outer folds, and that is correct — nested CV estimates the performance of the procedure, not of one configuration. Report the mean across outer folds and the standard deviation; a mean with no spread hides fold instability. It costs kouter​×kinner​× trials, so on a large budget a single untouched test set is the honest cheap alternative.

You reach for it when

  • A sweep is about to run for two days on a shared cluster
  • Quoting a tuned score to someone who will make a decision on it
  • Each training run costs an hour and you have twenty of them
  • Model choice and hyperparameters are being picked on the same split

The trap

Reporting the best score from a five-hundred-trial sweep as your expected test performance. The maximum of five hundred noisy estimates is not an unbiased estimate of anything — it is the luckiest draw, and the search selected for exactly that luck. The bias grows with the trial count and shrinks with the size of the validation set. Either nest the loops, or hold out a test set the search never touches.

The math why the winner is inflated

E[maxi​s^i​]>maxi​E[s^i​]Each configuration’s cross-validation score s^i​ is a noisy estimate of its true performance. Taking the maximum over many of them selects for the noise as well as the signal, so the winner’s score is biased upward and the gap widens with every extra trial. Nested cross-validation removes it by scoring the chosen configuration on an outer fold that played no part in choosing it. One more number worth carrying: about 60 random trials give you a 95% chance of landing in the top 5% of the search space, since 1−0.9560≈0.95.

Nested CV, and the number you may quote

from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold

inner = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
outer = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=1)

search = GridSearchCV(pipe, param_grid, scoring="average_precision", cv=inner)

# the outer loop never sees the tuning. THIS is the number you are allowed to quote.
scores = cross_val_score(search, X, y, cv=outer, scoring="average_precision")
print(scores.mean(), scores.std())   # always report the spread, never the mean alone

search.fit(X, y)                     # only now, to produce the model you ship
print(search.best_score_)            # optimistic. Not a generalisation estimate.

Where this bites in production

scikit-learn ships successive halving as HalvingGridSearchCV, and it still sits behind from sklearn.experimental import enable_halving_search_cv — a fair marker of how recently it reached mainstream tooling. Optuna defaults to TPE for sampling and a median pruner for early stopping, which is successive halving in spirit. The industrial version of the bias is the Kaggle public leaderboard: a held-out set queried hundreds of times becomes a validation set, and the shake-up on private scores is the correction arriving.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why is random search better than grid search?
Because only a few hyperparameters matter and the grid keeps re-testing the same values of them. With nine trials over two axes, a grid gives you three distinct values of each; random search gives you nine of each. Bergstra and Bengio showed the gap widens as you add parameters that turn out not to matter. Random search also stops on demand — any prefix of a random sweep is still a valid sweep.
You ran 500 trials and the best CV score was 0.91. What do you expect on test?
Less than 0.91, and that number cannot tell you how much less. The maximum of 500 noisy estimates is biased upward by whatever the search could exploit, and the bias grows with the trial count and shrinks with validation-set size. Quote a nested-CV mean with its standard deviation, or a score from a test set the search never touched. Anything else is the selection reporting on itself.
What does nested cross-validation actually estimate?
The performance of the whole procedure, not of one configuration. Each outer fold runs its own complete inner search, so different outer folds may well choose different hyperparameters — that is expected, not a bug. You refit the search on everything afterwards to get the model you ship. Report the mean across outer folds and the spread, because a mean on its own hides fold instability.

Say this back tomorrow

inner loop picks the settings  ·  outer loop is the only honest score
  • Random search beats grid because only a few hyperparameters carry the objective
  • Successive halving and Hyperband buy budget back by killing weak trials early
  • One CV loop for both tuning and reporting is optimistically biased — nest them

  • nested CV
  • optimistic bias

Ensembling & Stacking

Diversity is the ingredient. Five copies of the same model buy you almost nothing.

If several people guess a number badly but in different directions, the average of their guesses can beat every one of them, because the errors partly cancel. That only works if they are wrong in different ways. Five people who read the same newspaper and made the same mistake will average to that same mistake, and you have paid five times over for it. So the useful question is never how many models you have. It is how differently they are wrong. You can average them, take a vote, weight them by how much you trust each one, or train a small model whose only job is to learn when to listen to which. That last one is delicate, because it is easy to train the judge on answers it should never have been shown.

Like a panel of doctors. A second opinion is worth having when the second doctor trained somewhere else and looks at different signs. Five consultants from the same department who all read the same scan the same way are not a panel; they are one opinion with a bigger bill. And the bill is real — five models to serve, five to monitor, five to retrain.

Average M models of equal error variance with average pairwise error correlation ρ and the ensemble variance is M1​σ2+MM−1​ρσ2. At ρ=1 that collapses back to σ2: identical models, no gain, M times the serving cost. So correlation, not count, sets the floor, and diversity is the thing you are actually buying. In practice: hard voting takes the majority label, soft voting averages probabilities and usually wins when those probabilities are calibrated, weighted blending fits the weights on a holdout, and stacking trains a meta-learner on the base models’ predictions. The meta-features must be out-of-fold — every prediction used as a feature for a row has to come from a base model fitted without that row. Keep the meta-learner small; a regularised logistic regression over five columns is usually the right size.

The classic stacking leak is worth being able to describe in one breath. Fit the base models on all the training data, predict on that same data, feed those predictions to the meta-learner. Those in-fold predictions are far too good, because an overfitted base model looks near-perfect on rows it memorised, so the meta-learner learns to trust it completely and then collapses in production. Blending is the simpler cousin: one holdout instead of folds, less code and less leakage risk, but it wastes data and the weights are noisier. And price the thing before you propose it — a serving budget of 50ms does not stretch to twelve models.

You reach for it when

  • A single model has plateaued and the deadline has not
  • A 50ms serving budget and someone proposes a twelve-model stack
  • Building meta-features for a stacker
  • Two candidates with similar scores and different failure modes

The trap

Stacking five gradient-boosting models with different seeds and calling it an ensemble. Their errors correlate at around 0.97, so the variance falls by roughly one per cent while you now serve, monitor and retrain five models. The other trap is the leak: meta-features built from base models that had already seen the row they are predicting. Those columns look superb in training and are worth nothing at serving time.

The math the whole argument for diversity

Var(fˉ​)=M1​σ2+MM−1​ρσ2Average M models of equal error variance σ2 with average pairwise error correlation ρ. The first term falls like 1/M and is the part people remember. The second term does not vanish however many models you add — at ρ=1 the whole expression is just σ2 and you have bought nothing. Two models at ρ=0.97 cut variance by 1.5%; two at ρ=0.29 cut it by 35%. This is also exactly why a random forest subsamples features at every split: it is manufacturing decorrelation on purpose.

Stacking without the leak

import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import StackingClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict

# diversity is the ingredient: different inductive biases, not different seeds
base = [("gbm", LGBMClassifier()), ("lin", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
        ("knn", KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=25))]

# price it before you propose it: how correlated are the ERRORS?
oof = np.column_stack([cross_val_predict(m, X, y, cv=5, method="predict_proba")[:, 1]
                       for _, m in base])
print(np.corrcoef((oof - y[:, None]).T))   # above ~0.9 -> do not bother

# cv=5 builds the meta-features OUT OF FOLD. cv="prefit" is the classic leak.
stack = StackingClassifier(base, final_estimator=LogisticRegression(), cv=5)

Where this bites in production

The Otto Group Kaggle competition in 2015 was won with a three-level stack: 33 models in the first layer, their out-of-fold predictions plus eight engineered features in the second, a weighted average in the third. It won on a fraction of a point of log loss, and nobody would put it behind an API. scikit-learn’s StackingClassifier defaults to cv=5 precisely because the out-of-fold rule is the part people get wrong.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why do ensembles work at all?
Because errors that are not perfectly correlated partially cancel. Averaging models of equal error variance leaves one term that falls like one over the number of models and a second term that does not fall at all, scaled by their average error correlation. That second term is the floor. It is why different inductive biases, different features and different preprocessing buy more than another copy of your best model.
How do you build meta-features for a stacker without leaking?
Out-of-fold predictions, always. Split the training set into folds and, for every row, take the prediction from a base model that was fitted without that row. In-fold predictions hand the meta-learner numbers an overfitted base model produced on rows it had memorised, so it learns to trust that model completely and then collapses in production. StackingClassifier builds them for you when you pass cv.
A twelve-model stack adds 0.3 AUC points against a 50ms budget. What do you do?
Ship one model, or two at the outside. Three tenths of a point of AUC rarely survives contact with a real online metric, and it never justifies twelve models to serve, monitor, retrain and be paged about. Take the single best model, spend the effort on features and on the operating threshold, and keep a two-model blend in reserve only if the latency budget genuinely has room for it.

ensembles are paid for in disagreement  ·  meta-features must be out-of-fold
  • Error correlation, not model count, sets how much an ensemble can win
  • Stacking meta-features must come from base models that never saw the row
  • Price latency, monitoring and retraining against a fraction of a point of AUC

The Perceptron & the Multilayer Perceptron

One neuron draws one straight line. Everything after that follows from the limitation.

A single artificial neuron does two things. It adds up its inputs, each with its own importance, and then it bends the result through a fixed shape. On its own it can only split the world with a straight cut. That is enough for a great many problems and hopeless for others. The famous hopeless one is a rule that says yes when exactly one of two switches is on: no straight line separates those four cases, and you may try for as long as you like. Put a layer of neurons in between, with a bend applied after each, and the cuts compose into a shape with corners. Leave the bends out and the whole stack folds back down into a single straight cut, however many layers you piled up.

Like folding paper before you cut it. One straight snip through a flat sheet gives you one straight edge, and no amount of care changes that. Fold the sheet first and the same single snip produces a shape with corners in it. The folding is the non-linearity. Skip it and every extra cut still lands on the same straight line.

A unit computes z=w⊤x+b and then a=ϕ(z). One unit with a sigmoid, trained on log loss, is logistic regression — same model, same objective, fitted by gradient descent rather than by a solver. A single layer can only realise a linear decision boundary, which is why XOR is unlearnable by one: the four points are not linearly separable, and Minsky and Papert’s 1969 book made that limitation famous enough to stall the field. Add a hidden layer with a non-linearity and you compose half-planes into arbitrary regions. The shapes: input (batch,features), first weight (features,units), hidden (batch,units), output (batch,classes). Universal approximation (Cybenko 1989, Hornik 1991) says one hidden layer of sufficient width approximates any continuous function on a compact set to any accuracy.

Say what the theorem does not say, unprompted. It is an existence result: it puts no bound on the required width, and it offers no guarantee that gradient descent will find those weights from your initialisation and your data. Depth also beats width in practice — some functions need exponentially many units in one hidden layer and only polynomially many when you go deeper, which is why nobody builds the single wide layer the theorem describes. And without the activation, a stack of linear layers is a product of matrices, which is one matrix: depth buys exactly nothing. That sentence is the fastest way to show you know what the non-linearity is for.

You reach for it when

  • Explaining why a network needs activations at all
  • Someone proposes an MLP for a tabular problem a tree already solves
  • A deep model is behaving exactly like a linear one
  • Sizing the shapes for a first PyTorch model

The trap

Treating universal approximation as a reason to use an MLP. The theorem is an existence result on a compact set: it promises a sufficient width exists, says nothing about how large, and gives no guarantee that gradient descent will find those weights. On tabular problems a gradient-boosted ensemble still usually wins. The neighbouring trap is stacking linear layers with no activation between them — that is one linear layer wearing a costume.

The math why the bend is not optional

a=ϕ(Wx+b)  ·  with no ϕ:   W2​(W1​x)=(W2​W1​)xTwo linear layers with nothing between them multiply out to a single matrix, so depth without activations buys nothing at all. Shapes for a batch of 64 rows, 20 features, 128 hidden units and 3 classes: input (64,20), first weight (20,128), hidden (64,128), second weight (128,3), logits (64,3). The parameter count is 20×128+128+128×3+3=3075, and being able to produce that number on a whiteboard is worth more than knowing the theorem’s name.

The whole thing, in five lines

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

net = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(20, 128),   # (batch, 20)  -> (batch, 128)
    nn.ReLU(),            # drop this line and the whole stack IS one linear layer
    nn.Linear(128, 3),    # (batch, 128) -> (batch, 3) logits, NOT probabilities
)

x = torch.randn(64, 20)
print(net(x).shape)                                 # torch.Size([64, 3])
print(sum(p.numel() for p in net.parameters()))     # 3075

# one unit + sigmoid + log loss == logistic regression. Same model, same objective.

Where this bites in production

Minsky and Papert’s Perceptrons (1969) showed that a single-layer perceptron cannot represent XOR, and the funding winter that followed ran into the 1980s — the field stalled on a limitation one hidden layer removes. The theorem that answered it, Cybenko’s in 1989, is an existence proof and nothing more. Grinsztajn et al. (2022) then benchmarked trees against neural networks across 45 tabular datasets and the trees still won.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What can a single-layer perceptron not learn?
Anything that is not linearly separable, and XOR is the standard example. The four points sit at the corners of a square with the two positives on one diagonal, so no straight line separates them. Minsky and Papert made exactly this point in 1969. One hidden layer with a non-linearity composes two half-planes into a region that does separate them, which is why the fix is depth and not a better solver.
How does a one-unit, one-layer network relate to logistic regression?
It is logistic regression. A weighted sum plus a bias, a sigmoid on top, trained with log loss — the same model and the same objective, fitted by gradient descent rather than by a solver. Saying this out loud is worth a lot: it shows you see a neural network as a generalisation of something you already understand rather than as a separate species.
Universal approximation says an MLP can fit anything. Should you use one?
No, because the theorem does not say what people think it says. It guarantees that a sufficiently wide hidden layer exists, with no bound on the width and no promise that gradient descent will find it from your initialisation. On tabular data a gradient-boosted ensemble usually wins, trains in minutes and needs almost no tuning. Reach for an MLP when the input has structure a network can exploit.

Say this back tomorrow

one neuron is one straight cut  ·  the non-linearity is the only thing that makes depth mean anything
  • A single unit with a sigmoid and log loss is exactly logistic regression
  • Linear layers with no activation between them collapse into one linear layer
  • Universal approximation bounds nothing — not the width, not the trainability

Backpropagation

The chain rule, cached, run right to left. That is the whole idea.

Every layer of a network is one step in a long calculation, and each step feeds the next. To improve a weight buried near the start, you need to know how a nudge to it changes the final score, and that means multiplying together the sensitivities of every step in between. The trick is the order. Start at the end, where there is a single number, and work backwards, keeping each partial result to reuse for the layer before it. Going the other way would mean redoing the same multiplications once for every weight, and there are millions of weights. The forward run has to remember what each layer produced, because the backward run needs those values, and that is why training a network costs far more memory than using one.

Think of tracing a delay back down a supply chain. The lorry arrives four hours late. You do not ask every supplier how long they took; you start at the loading bay, find the two hours lost there, hand the remaining two hours back one step, and keep going. Each stage only needs the delay handed to it plus what it wrote down on the way out.

Backpropagation is reverse-mode automatic differentiation applied to a scalar loss. The forward pass computes and caches each layer’s activation; the backward pass walks the same graph in reverse and at each node multiplies the incoming gradient by that node’s local Jacobian. Reverse mode is chosen because its cost scales with the number of outputs rather than inputs: with millions of parameters and one scalar loss, a single backward sweep produces every partial derivative, where forward mode would need one sweep per parameter. Softmax with cross-entropy is the standard pairing because the gradient with respect to the logits is exactly p−y — the activation derivative cancels, so a confident mistake produces the largest available push instead of the smallest. And backpropagation is not an optimiser. It computes gradients; SGD or Adam consumes them.

The memory follows directly from the caching. Activation memory scales with batch size times the number of stored tensors times their size, which is why a smaller batch is the first fix for an out-of-memory error, and why depth costs memory as well as compute. Gradient checkpointing keeps only a subset of the activations and recomputes the rest during the backward pass — roughly one extra forward pass of compute for a large drop in memory, and torch.utils.checkpoint is the switch. One more detail worth knowing: backward() accumulates into .grad rather than overwriting it, which is why zero_grad() exists and why forgetting it silently sums gradients across steps.

You reach for it when

  • An out-of-memory error at a batch size that used to fit
  • Explaining why training needs far more memory than inference
  • Someone calls backpropagation an optimiser
  • Deciding whether gradient checkpointing is worth the extra compute

The trap

Describing it as “the network learns from its mistakes and adjusts its weights”. That sentence contains no mechanism at all. What an interviewer wants is the chain rule, the direction — right to left, because there are many parameters and one scalar loss — and the cached forward activations that make the reuse possible. The related trap is calling backpropagation an optimiser. It produces gradients. SGD and Adam are what consume them.

The math the chain rule, and the reason for that pairing

∂W1​∂L​=∂a2​∂L​∂a1​∂a2​​∂W1​∂a1​​  ·  softmax with cross-entropy: ∂z∂L​=p−yEvaluate the product right to left and you are doing forward mode: one sweep per parameter. Evaluate it left to right and you are doing reverse mode: one sweep for every parameter at once, because you start from the single scalar and carry a vector backwards instead of a matrix forwards. The second identity is why softmax and cross-entropy are always paired — every activation derivative cancels and what survives is the prediction minus the target, so a confidently wrong prediction produces the largest gradient available rather than a vanishing one.

One backward sweep

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

h = torch.relu(x @ w1)          # h is CACHED - the backward pass needs this value
logits = h @ w2
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, y)   # takes LOGITS: fused log-softmax + NLL, stable

loss.backward()   # one sweep, right to left, fills every .grad on the graph
opt.step()        # backprop produced the gradients. THIS is the optimiser.
opt.zero_grad()   # backward() ACCUMULATES - forget this and steps silently add up

# out of memory? torch.utils.checkpoint drops activations and recomputes them:
# ~1 extra forward pass of compute, for a large cut in activation memory.

Where this bites in production

PyTorch’s cross_entropy takes logits rather than probabilities precisely so it can fuse log-softmax with negative log-likelihood — computing softmax separately and taking its log overflows on large logits, and the fused form is both stable and yields the clean prediction-minus-target gradient. On memory, Chen et al. (2016) showed gradient checkpointing gives roughly square-root memory in depth for about 30% extra compute. It is one flag in Hugging Face’s Trainer.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What is the memory cost of backpropagation, and why?
You must store the forward activations, so memory scales with batch size and depth. Each layer’s backward step needs the value that layer produced on the way forward, so those tensors stay resident until they are consumed. That is why halving the batch is the first fix for an out-of-memory error, and why gradient checkpointing exists — keep a subset, recompute the rest, pay roughly one extra forward pass.
Why does backpropagation run right to left?
Because there are many parameters and exactly one scalar loss. Reverse-mode automatic differentiation costs one sweep per output; forward mode costs one sweep per input. With a million weights and a single loss, reverse mode hands you every partial derivative in one pass while forward mode would need a million. If you ever had one input and many outputs, the arithmetic would flip the other way.
What is the gradient of softmax with cross-entropy?
Prediction minus target. The softmax Jacobian and the log inside cross-entropy cancel exactly, leaving p−y on the logits. That is why the pairing is standard: no activation derivative survives to shrink the signal, so a confidently wrong prediction produces the largest push available rather than the smallest. It is also why frameworks fuse the two into a single call that takes logits.

  • Reverse mode wins because there are many inputs and a single scalar output
  • Cached forward activations are the entire reason training memory scales with batch and depth
  • Softmax with cross-entropy gives prediction minus target — that is why they are paired

Activation Functions & Vanishing Gradients

The bend between two layers, and the arithmetic that kills a deep stack.

Between every two layers sits a small fixed bend, and the shape of that bend decides whether a deep network can be trained at all. The old choice was a squashing curve that flattens at both ends. Flat means the layer barely reacts to a nudge, and when you chain many layers you multiply all those small reactions together. The steepest that curve ever gets is a quarter, so ten layers of it multiply ten numbers no larger than a quarter, and what reaches the first layer is about one part in a million. The modern choice leaves positive inputs completely alone, so the reaction stays at full strength, and flattens only the negative side. That has its own failure: a unit pushed permanently negative stops reacting forever.

Like a chain of gearboxes. Each one passes on a fraction of the turn it receives. If every box in the chain gives back at most a quarter, the tenth one along barely twitches however hard you spin the first, and no amount of patience fixes it. Swap them for boxes that pass the turn straight through and the far end finally moves.

Sigmoid squashes to (0,1) and its derivative is σ(z)(1−σ(z)), which maxes at 0.25 at z=0. Backpropagation multiplies one such factor per layer, so ten sigmoid layers scale the gradient by at most 0.2510≈10−6 before it reaches the first weight matrix, and the early layers stop learning. Tanh maxes at 1 and is zero-centred, so it is better on both counts and still saturates. ReLU is max(0,z): the derivative is exactly 1 for positive pre-activations, so nothing is multiplied down on that side, and it costs one comparison. Its own failure is dying ReLU — a unit whose pre-activation is negative for every input in the data gets zero gradient forever and never recovers, often after one oversized step. Leaky ReLU gives the negative side a small slope; ELU makes it smooth.

Name the architectural fixes too, because the activation is only part of the answer: residual connections give the gradient a path that skips the multiplications entirely, normalisation keeps pre-activations in the responsive part of the curve, and gradient clipping by global norm handles the mirror failure on the exploding side. GELU is zΦ(z), the input times the probability a standard normal falls below it, so it is a soft probabilistic gate rather than a hard cut. SiLU, also called Swish, is zσ(z) and is very close to it. Both are smooth, both pass a small negative gradient, so no unit dies. BERT, GPT-2 and Vision Transformers all use GELU, and Llama uses SwiGLU, a gated SiLU. The reason is empirical rather than theoretical — at transformer depth, with LayerNorm and residuals already handling the vanishing problem, the smooth negative region simply trains a little better. For a convolutional network ReLU is still the right default.

You reach for it when

  • Choosing an activation for a network deeper than a few layers
  • A deep model trains but the early layers barely move
  • A large share of units output zero for every row and never recover
  • Explaining why a transformer does not use plain ReLU

The trap

Answering “ReLU, because it is faster” and stopping there. The speed is real and it is the least interesting thing about it. ReLU unlocked depth because its derivative is exactly 1 for positive pre-activations, so nothing shrinks on the way back. Give the number for the alternative — sigmoid caps at 0.25, ten layers is one part in a million — and then name ReLU’s own failure, which is that a unit stuck negative is dead for good.

The math the arithmetic that kills depth

σ′(z)=σ(z)(1−σ(z))≤0.25  ·  l=1∏10​σ′(zl​)≤0.2510≈10−6The first identity is the one to have on a whiteboard: the sigmoid’s derivative is largest at z=0, where σ=0.5 and the product is exactly 0.25. The second is what backpropagation does with it — one such factor per layer, multiplied. Tanh’s derivative is 1−tanh2(z), which maxes at 1, so tanh is strictly better and still saturates at the tails. ReLU’s is 1 for z>0 and 0 for z<0: nothing shrinks, and nothing recovers. GELU is zΦ(z) and SiLU is zσ(z), both smooth and both non-zero on the negative side. The mirror failure is exploding gradients, where the factors exceed 1; the standard answer there is clipping by global norm, conventionally at 1.0.

The 0.25, measured

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

z = torch.linspace(-6, 6, 1201, requires_grad=True)
for name, f in [("sigmoid", torch.sigmoid), ("tanh", torch.tanh),
                ("relu", torch.relu), ("gelu", nn.functional.gelu)]:
    g, = torch.autograd.grad(f(z).sum(), z, retain_graph=True)
    print(name, round(g.max().item(), 3))   # 0.25   1.0   1.0   1.13

print(0.25 ** 10)     # 9.5e-07 - this IS the vanishing-gradient argument

# dying ReLU: units whose pre-activation is negative for EVERY row in the batch
dead = (pre_act <= 0).all(dim=0).float().mean()
print(dead.item())    # drifting up past ~0.4 -> lower the LR or use LeakyReLU

Where this bites in production

AlexNet (2012) is the standard citation. Krizhevsky et al. reported a four-layer convolutional network with ReLU reaching 25% training error on CIFAR-10 roughly six times faster than the identical network with tanh, and the paper is explicit that no saturating unit could have trained the full model in the time available. On the other side, PyTorch’s nn.TransformerEncoderLayer still defaults to activation="relu" — which is why nearly every real transformer config overrides it to GELU.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why exactly does sigmoid cause vanishing gradients?
Because its derivative never exceeds 0.25. The derivative is the output times one minus the output, which is largest at a pre-activation of zero, where it equals a quarter. Backpropagation multiplies one of those factors per layer, so ten layers scale the gradient by at most 0.25 to the tenth, about one in a million, and the early layers stop moving. Tanh maxes at 1 and is zero-centred, so it is better and still saturates.
ReLU fixed vanishing gradients. What did it break?
Dying ReLU. A unit whose pre-activation is negative for every input in the data receives exactly zero gradient, so it can never come back — and one oversized step is enough to put it there permanently. Watch the fraction of units that are zero for the whole batch. The fixes are a smaller learning rate, Leaky ReLU or ELU for a non-zero negative slope, or GELU and SiLU, which are smooth and never fully off.
Fixing the activation is not the whole answer. What else?
Residual connections, normalisation, and clipping for the other direction. A residual gives the gradient a path that skips the chain of multiplications entirely, which is what actually made hundred-layer networks trainable. Normalisation keeps pre-activations in the responsive part of the curve. And the mirror failure — factors above 1, so the gradient explodes — is handled by clipping the global norm, conventionally at 1.0.

Say this back tomorrow

sigmoid’s slope caps at 0.25  ·  ten layers of that is one part in a million
  • Sigmoid’s derivative maxes at 0.25, so depth multiplies the gradient away
  • ReLU’s derivative is exactly 1 on the right, and exactly 0 forever on the left
  • GELU and SiLU are the smooth transformer defaults; ReLU still owns convolutions

Unlocks

  • 0.25 ceiling
  • dying ReLU
  • GELU
  • SiLU / Swish
  • gradient clipping

Optimisers: SGD, Momentum, Adam & AdamW

Four algorithms, and each one exists because the one before it failed at something.

Plain gradient descent steps straight downhill from wherever it is standing. That fails in a long narrow valley, because the steepest direction points across the valley rather than along it, so the path bounces between the walls and creeps forward. Momentum fixes that by carrying a running average of recent steps: the side-to-side moves cancel and the forward drift builds up. The second failure is that one step size has to serve every weight at once, when some weights are getting large nudges and others tiny ones. The fix is to give each weight its own scale, based on how big its own recent nudges have been. Adam does both at the same time, and it is the default nearly everywhere. Then one more version fixes how Adam handles the penalty that keeps weights small.

Like walking down a narrow gorge in fog. Step straight downhill each time and you cross from wall to wall, gaining almost nothing along the floor. Keep a memory of your last few steps and the sideways moves cancel each other while the forward ones add up, so you drift down the gorge instead of ricocheting across it.

SGD takes θ←θ−ηg and struggles in ravines, where the curvature across the valley is far larger than along it. Momentum keeps vt​=βvt−1​+gt​ with β=0.9, damping the oscillating component and accumulating the consistent one; Nesterov evaluates the gradient after the momentum step rather than before. RMSProp attacks the other failure — one global learning rate for parameters whose gradient magnitudes differ by orders of magnitude — by dividing each step by a running root mean square of that parameter’s own gradients. Adam is both together, plus bias correction: m and v are initialised at zero, so the early estimates are biased toward zero, and dividing by 1−β1t​ and 1−β2t​ undoes it. The defaults are β1​=0.9, β2​=0.999, ϵ=10−8 and a learning rate of 10−3.

Adam is not AdamW, and this is the discriminating question. Classic L2 regularisation adds 2λ​∥θ∥2 to the loss, so its gradient λθ flows through the same adaptive denominator as everything else. A parameter with large historical gradients has a large v^​, so its decay is divided down — the penalty you asked for is applied unevenly, and least of all to the parameters carrying the largest gradients. Loshchilov and Hutter’s fix is to decouple it: leave the loss alone and subtract ηλθ from the weights directly, outside the adaptive step. Say the other half too. Adam is not always better: SGD with momentum and a tuned schedule still generalises better than Adam on several vision benchmarks, which is why the reference ResNet and EfficientNet recipes are SGD recipes.

You reach for it when

  • Choosing an optimiser for a model you have not trained before
  • A config sets Adam with weight decay and expects L2 behaviour
  • Reproducing a vision result whose recipe is SGD with momentum
  • The loss bounces while the average direction barely advances

The trap

Saying “Adam, because it is always better”. It is the right default and it is not always better — SGD with momentum and a tuned schedule still generalises better on several vision benchmarks, which is why the standard ResNet and EfficientNet recipes are SGD recipes. The other half of the trap is reading Adam(weight_decay=0.01) as L2 regularisation. It is not. That penalty goes through the adaptive denominator and comes out uneven.

The math Adam, term by term

mt​=β1​mt−1​+(1−β1​)gt​  ·  vt​=β2​vt−1​+(1−β2​)gt2​  ·  m^t​=1−β1t​mt​​, v^t​=1−β2t​vt​​  ·  θt​=θt−1​−ηv^t​​+ϵm^t​​mt​ is the momentum term, an exponential average of the gradient. vt​ is the RMSProp term, an exponential average of the squared gradient, and dividing by its square root is what gives every parameter its own effective step size. Both start at zero, so early on they are biased toward zero; the hats undo that, and at t=1 with β2​=0.999 the correction is a factor of a thousand. AdamW changes exactly one line: θt​=θt−1​−η(m^t​/(v^t​​+ϵ)+λθt−1​), with λθ sitting outside the denominator so the decay is the same proportion for every weight. That is the whole of decoupling.

AdamW, and the parameter groups

import torch

# torch.optim.Adam pushes weight_decay THROUGH the adaptive step -> not L2
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4, weight_decay=0.01,
                        betas=(0.9, 0.999), eps=1e-8)

# never decay biases or norm gains - there is no scale for them to shrink toward
decay, plain = [], []
for n, p in model.named_parameters():
    (plain if p.ndim < 2 or "bias" in n else decay).append(p)

opt = torch.optim.AdamW([{"params": decay, "weight_decay": 0.1},
                         {"params": plain, "weight_decay": 0.0}], lr=3e-4)

# and keep the honest baseline in the sweep, especially on vision:
# torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1, momentum=0.9, nesterov=True)

Where this bites in production

Loshchilov and Hutter’s “Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization” is the paper, and the tooling moved with it: PyTorch shipped torch.optim.AdamW as a separate class rather than a flag, and Hugging Face’s Trainer defaults to AdamW, not Adam. The GPT-3 paper sets the second-moment decay to 0.95 rather than the usual 0.999, a useful reminder that the defaults are only defaults. The reference ResNet-50 recipe, meanwhile, is still SGD with momentum 0.9.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What is the difference between Adam and AdamW?
Where the weight decay is applied. In Adam an L2 penalty is added to the loss, so its gradient passes through the adaptive denominator and each parameter gets a different effective amount of decay — least of all the ones with the largest gradients. AdamW decouples it: the loss is untouched and the decay is subtracted from the weights directly. That is why AdamW is standard and why the two are separate classes.
Why does Adam need bias correction?
Because both moment estimates start at zero. The first and second moments are exponential averages initialised at zero, so for the first steps they are pulled toward zero and badly underestimate the true values. Dividing by one minus the decay rate raised to the step number removes exactly that bias. Without it the very first updates are enormous, which is also part of why warmup helps.
Is Adam always the right choice?
No, and saying it is is the trap. It is the right default, especially for transformers and sparse gradients, but SGD with momentum and a tuned schedule still generalises better on several vision benchmarks — the reference ResNet and EfficientNet recipes are SGD recipes for that reason. Keep SGD with momentum in the sweep whenever the task is vision and the training budget allows two runs.

Say this back tomorrow

momentum for ravines  ·  RMSProp for scale  ·  AdamW takes the decay out of the loss
  • Each optimiser exists because the previous one failed at something specific
  • Bias correction exists because both moments are initialised at zero
  • Adam’s adaptive denominator corrupts an L2 penalty; AdamW decouples it

  • momentum
  • bias correction
  • decoupled decay
  • AdamW
  • SGD baseline

Initialisation & Learning-Rate Schedules

Where the weights start, and how fast you move them. The second is the setting to tune first.

Two things have to be right before a network can learn anything at all. The first is where the weights start. Set them all to zero and every unit in a layer receives the same input, produces the same output and takes the same correction, so they stay identical forever and a layer of a hundred units does the work of one. Set them too large and the signal grows as it passes through the layers until the squashing curves flatten out and nothing moves. The right size depends on how many inputs each unit has. The second thing is the step size, and it has a larger effect on the final result than almost anything else you can change. Keep it small for the first few hundred steps, then let it fall smoothly toward nothing as training goes on.

Think of a choir that has to sing in parts. Hand every singer the same sheet of music and you get one voice, however many people are standing there. Break that sameness and you get harmony. Then the volume: come in too loud and nobody can find the pitch, so you start quietly, settle at the right level, and fade out at the end.

All-zero initialisation fails on symmetry: every unit in a layer computes the same activation and receives the same gradient, so they never differentiate and the layer has the capacity of a single unit. Too large fails on variance: the activation variance is multiplied at each layer, so it grows or decays geometrically with depth, saturating tanh or overflowing the forward pass. Both fixes are variance-preserving arguments. Xavier/Glorot sets Var(w)=2/(nin​+nout​), balancing the forward and backward passes for activations symmetric about zero — tanh and sigmoid. He/Kaiming sets Var(w)=2/nin​, where the factor of 2 compensates for ReLU zeroing half the distribution and so halving the variance. Biases start at zero, which is fine because the weights already broke the symmetry. Use He with ReLU and Xavier with tanh, and give the reason rather than the name.

Warmup exists because the first steps are the worst informed. Adam’s second-moment estimate is built from a handful of gradients, so its per-parameter scaling is noisy exactly when the weights are most fragile, and with a large batch the initial gradient is large and consistent enough to push the model somewhere it never recovers from. Ramping the rate linearly over the first few hundred to few thousand steps removes both problems. After warmup: cosine decay is the modern default and needs one number, the total step count; step decay drops by a fixed factor at set epochs; one-cycle raises the rate and then lowers it while inverting the momentum; ReduceLROnPlateau reacts to a stalled validation metric instead of following a curve. To find the peak rate, run Smith’s range test — increase the rate exponentially over a single epoch, plot the loss against it, and take roughly a tenth of the value where the loss was falling fastest.

You reach for it when

  • Starting a training run and picking the one number to tune first
  • A deep network’s loss is flat from the very first step
  • Training diverges in the first few hundred steps at a large batch size
  • Porting a recipe from a small batch size to a much larger one

The trap

Spending a two-day sweep on dropout, hidden width and weight decay while the learning rate stays at whatever the tutorial used. The learning rate moves the result more than everything else on that list put together, and a rate wrong by an order of magnitude cannot be rescued by any of them. Run a range test, fix the rate and its schedule, then tune the rest. The other half is initialising every weight to zero and calling it neutral.

The math Xavier, He, and the cosine

Var(w)=nin​+nout​2​  ·  Var(w)=nin​2​  ·  ηt​=ηmax​Tw​t​, then 2ηmax​​(1+cosT−Tw​π(t−Tw​)​)The first is Xavier/Glorot, which splits the difference between preserving the variance forward and preserving it backward, and suits activations symmetric about zero. The second is He/Kaiming: the numerator 2 is there because ReLU zeroes half the distribution and therefore halves the variance, so you double the weight variance to compensate. Both are stated for the normal form; the uniform forms are U[−6/(nin​+nout​)​,+6/(nin​+nout​)​] and U[−6/nin​​,+6/nin​​]. The third pair is the schedule: a linear ramp over Tw​ warmup steps, then a cosine from the peak down to zero over the remaining budget. Cosine needs the total step count T in advance, which is the one thing people forget when they change the epoch count.

He init, warmup, cosine

import math
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.optim.lr_scheduler import LambdaLR

# He for ReLU, Xavier for tanh. PyTorch's Linear default is neither:
# it calls kaiming_uniform_(w, a=math.sqrt(5)), which lands close to Xavier.
for m in model.modules():
    if isinstance(m, nn.Linear):
        nn.init.kaiming_normal_(m.weight, nonlinearity="relu")
        nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)

warm, total = 500, 20_000
sched = LambdaLR(opt, lambda t: t / warm if t < warm
                 else 0.5 * (1 + math.cos(math.pi * (t - warm) / (total - warm))))
# sched.step() goes AFTER opt.step(), once per batch for a step-based schedule

Where this bites in production

PyTorch’s nn.Linear does not default to He or Xavier: it calls kaiming_uniform_ with a=math.sqrt(5), a legacy of the old Torch code that happens to land close to Xavier. Hugging Face’s Trainer defaults to linear decay with zero warmup steps, which is why nearly every published config overrides warmup_ratio. And Goyal et al. (2017) needed five epochs of gradual warmup to train ImageNet at batch size 8192 in an hour at all.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Xavier or He — which, and why?
He with ReLU, Xavier with tanh or sigmoid. Both preserve activation variance through the layers so the signal neither dies nor explodes with depth. Xavier uses two over the sum of fan-in and fan-out, balancing forward and backward for activations symmetric about zero. He uses two over fan-in, and the factor of two is there because ReLU zeroes half the distribution and so halves the variance. Give the variance argument, not the name.
Why does warmup exist?
Because the first few hundred steps are the worst informed ones. Adam’s second-moment estimate is built from a handful of gradients, so its per-parameter scaling is at its noisiest exactly when the weights are most fragile. With a large batch the initial gradient is also large and consistent, so a full-size step can move the model somewhere it never recovers from. A linear ramp removes both.
What breaks if you initialise every weight to zero?
Symmetry never breaks. Every unit in the layer sees the same inputs, produces the same output and receives the same gradient, so they stay identical for the whole run and a hundred-unit layer has the capacity of one unit. Random values break it; the scale of those values is what Xavier and He decide. Biases can safely start at zero, because the weights have already done the breaking.

Say this back tomorrow

zero init means one unit forever  ·  He for ReLU  ·  tune the learning rate before anything else
  • All-zero weights never break symmetry; the scale of the random values is what Xavier and He set
  • He doubles the variance because ReLU discards half the distribution
  • Warmup protects against noisy adaptive estimates and large-batch first steps

  • Xavier
  • warmup

  • LR range test
