Batch Norm vs Layer Norm

The same formula. The axis it reduces over decides where each one can be used.

Both do the same arithmetic: take a set of numbers, subtract their average, divide by their spread, then apply a learned scale and shift. The only difference is which set. One takes a single feature and looks at every example in the batch. The other takes a single example and looks at all of its own features. That sounds like a detail and it decides everything. Normalising across the batch means each example’s output depends on whichever examples happened to be sitting alongside it, which is fine on large batches and awkward everywhere else. At prediction time there may be one example and no batch at all, so the layer has to fall back on averages it recorded during training. Normalising within a single example has no such problem.

Like marking exam papers. One examiner takes a single question and grades it across all two hundred scripts, marking each answer relative to the rest of the pile. The other takes one script and marks it against itself, question by question. The first needs the pile to exist. Hand it a single script and it has nothing to compare against.

Both compute x^=(x−μ)/σ2+ϵ​ and then γx^+β; the entire argument is about which axis μ and σ2 reduce over. Batch norm reduces over the batch — and, in a convolution, over the spatial positions too — producing one mean and variance per channel, statistics that depend on the other examples in the batch. Layer norm reduces over the feature dimension within each example, producing one mean and variance per example and no dependence on the batch at all. That independence is why transformers and RNNs use LayerNorm: sequence lengths vary, batches are small, and an RNN would otherwise need separate statistics per timestep. GroupNorm splits channels into groups and normalises within each group, which is the small-batch answer for vision.

Two facts carry the interview. First, batch norm behaves differently at training and inference. It accumulates running estimates of the mean and variance while training and uses those fixed numbers at inference, because there may be no batch to compute over. That is a genuine train/test discrepancy and a real source of bugs: forget model.eval() and the layer keeps normalising with statistics taken from whatever happens to be in the evaluation batch, so your metric depends on how you shuffled. Second, batch norm degrades badly at small batch sizes — the estimates get noisy below about eight and are worthless at two — and that is the actual reason LayerNorm and GroupNorm exist. Batch noise also acts as a mild regulariser, which is why batch norm and dropout stacked together often hurt. RMSNorm drops the mean subtraction and keeps only the rescaling, which is cheaper and is what Llama and most recent LLMs use; the LLM module takes it from there.

You reach for it when

  • Choosing a normalisation layer for a sequence model
  • Training at a batch size of two because the model barely fits
  • Validation is far worse than training and nothing else changed
  • Fine-tuning a vision model whose batch statistics no longer match the new data

The trap

Forgetting model.eval() before evaluating. Batch norm then keeps normalising with statistics taken from the evaluation batch rather than its running averages, so your validation number moves with the shuffle, and dropout is still firing at the same time. The second trap is claiming batch norm works “because it reduces internal covariate shift” — Santurkar et al. (2018) tested that explanation directly and it did not survive.

The math same formula, different axis

x^=σ2+ϵ​x−μ​,y=γx^+β  ·  BN: μ over (N,H,W) per channel  ·  LN: μ over C per exampleThe formula is identical; only the axes under μ and σ2 change. For a convolutional activation of shape (N,C,H,W), batch norm reduces over N, H and W and keeps C separate, learning 2C parameters; layer norm reduces over the feature dimension and keeps N separate. Batch norm additionally maintains running estimates, μrun​←(1−m)μrun​+mμB​ with PyTorch’s m=0.1, and those are what inference uses. RMSNorm removes the centring entirely: y=γx/d1​∑i​xi2​​, one statistic instead of two and no shift parameter.

Which axis each one reduces

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

x = torch.randn(8, 64)                    # (batch, features)
bn, ln = nn.BatchNorm1d(64), nn.LayerNorm(64)

# batch norm reduces over dim 0, layer norm over dim 1. Same arithmetic.
print(bn(x).mean(dim=0)[:3])              # ~0 down each COLUMN
print(ln(x).mean(dim=1)[:3])              # ~0 across each ROW

bn.eval()                                 # now uses running_mean / running_var
print(bn.running_mean[:3], bn.momentum)   # updated in train mode only; 0.1

# and in train mode a batch of one is not even legal:
# ValueError: Expected more than 1 value per channel when training

Where this bites in production

Detection models are the clearest case. Mask R-CNN trains at one or two images per GPU, so batch norm’s statistics come from a batch of two and are worthless; the standard practice became freezing the batch-norm layers outright — Detectron2 ships FrozenBatchNorm2d for exactly this — or swapping in GroupNorm, which Wu and He introduced in 2018 for that reason. Transformers never had the choice: variable sequence lengths and small batches sent them to LayerNorm from the start.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What happens to batch norm at inference time?
It stops using the batch and uses stored running statistics. During training it keeps an exponential average of the batch mean and variance; at inference those fixed numbers replace the batch statistics, because there may be a single example and no batch to compute over. That makes it a genuine train/test discrepancy, and it is why model.eval() exists and why forgetting it is such a common bug.
Why do transformers use LayerNorm rather than BatchNorm?
Because layer norm does not depend on the batch. It normalises across a single example’s own features, so sequence length can vary, the batch can be tiny, and every timestep is handled the same way — none of which is true of batch norm, whose estimates go noisy below a batch of about eight and are worthless at two. That small-batch failure is also why GroupNorm exists for vision.
Validation is far worse than training and the model looks fine. Where do you look first?
Check that you called model.eval(). Without it batch norm normalises using the evaluation batch rather than its running averages, so the number depends on how you shuffled, and dropout is still zeroing units at the same time. It is one line, it fails silently, and it accounts for a large share of “my validation loss is inexplicable” bugs.

Say this back tomorrow

batch norm reduces down the batch  ·  layer norm reduces across the features
  • Batch norm uses running statistics at inference — a real train/test discrepancy
  • Batch norm degrades below a batch of about eight, which is why LayerNorm and GroupNorm exist
  • RMSNorm keeps only the rescaling and is the current LLM default

  • model.eval()
  • small batches
  • GroupNorm
  • RMSNorm

Dropout & Early Stopping

One trains a crowd of smaller networks. The other stops before the crowd memorises.

During training, dropout switches off a random share of the units on every batch. The network can never rely on any one unit being there, so it has to spread the work out, and because a different set is switched off each time you are in effect training a very large crowd of smaller networks that all share the same weights. At prediction time you want the whole network and one fixed answer, so nothing is switched off. To keep the numbers consistent, the switching-off step also scales up whatever survives, by exactly enough to make up for what was removed. Early stopping is the other half: watch the score on held-out data, keep going while it improves, and once it has not improved for a set number of rounds, stop and go back to the best version you saw.

Like a football side that trains with random players missing. Nobody can build the whole plan around one striker, because on any given day he is not on the pitch. Come match day everyone plays. And you end the training session at the point the team looked sharpest, not at the point where everybody is exhausted.

Dropout zeroes each unit independently on every forward pass during training. Because a different mask is sampled each step, you are training an implicit ensemble over 2n subnetworks that share weights, and the single deterministic test-time pass approximates averaging them. The implementation detail that gets asked is inverted dropout: instead of multiplying activations by the keep probability p at test time, you divide the survivors by p during training, so the expected activation is unchanged and inference needs no correction whatsoever. Every framework does it this way. Typical rates are 0.5 on a wide fully connected layer, 0.1 to 0.2 inside a transformer, and effectively zero at the largest pretraining scales. It is a training-time-only layer, which is exactly why the mode switch matters.

Early stopping is regularisation that costs nothing: it bounds how far the weights travel from their initialisation, which is closely related to an L2 penalty, and it needs one held-out set and a counter. Two settings matter. Patience is the number of evaluations without improvement you tolerate before stopping, and it should scale with how noisy the metric is. And you restore the best weights rather than keeping the last ones — stopping without restoring throws away the point of the exercise. The monitored set has to be validation, never test; early stopping on the test set turns it into a tuning set and whatever you quote from it afterwards is no longer held out. As for dropout, it has quietly receded. Large transformers use very little of it and often none during pretraining, because a model that sees most tokens once has little to memorise and the data scale does the regularising. It survives in fine-tuning, in small-data regimes, and in the fully connected heads of vision models.

You reach for it when

  • A wide fully connected head is overfitting a small dataset
  • The same input returns a different prediction on every call
  • Choosing patience for a run that costs an hour per epoch
  • Porting a small-data recipe to a run with far more data

The trap

Leaving dropout on at prediction time and then wondering why the same input scores differently on every call. That is model.train() still being set, and it is the same single missing line that leaves batch norm computing statistics from the evaluation batch. The related mistake is early stopping on the test set. That makes the test set a tuning set, and any number you quote from it afterwards is no longer a held-out estimate of anything.

The math inverted dropout

train: a~=pa⊙m​,mi​∼Bernoulli(p)  ·  test: a~=am is a Bernoulli mask with E[mi​]=p, so E[a⊙m]=pa and dividing by p restores E[a~]=a. The expected activation is unchanged, which is why the test-time pass needs no correction at all. The older form — keep the raw activations at train time and multiply by p at test time — is mathematically equivalent but puts the cost in the wrong place, on every inference call rather than during training. Watch the convention: here p is the keep probability, but PyTorch’s nn.Dropout(p=0.2) takes p as the probability of zeroing an element. Getting that backwards turns a light regulariser into a crippling one.

Inverted dropout, and patience

import copy
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

drop = nn.Dropout(p=0.2)     # in PyTorch p is the DROP rate, not the keep rate
drop.train(); print(drop(torch.ones(1, 10)))   # zeros, survivors at 1.25 = 1 / 0.8
drop.eval();  print(drop(torch.ones(1, 10)))   # all ones - test time does nothing

best, wait, snap = float("inf"), 0, None
for epoch in range(200):
    v = validate()           # VALIDATION. Early stopping on test IS tuning on test.
    if v < best - 1e-4:
        best, wait, snap = v, 0, copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())
    else:
        wait += 1
    if wait >= 10:                        # patience
        model.load_state_dict(snap)       # restore the BEST weights, not the last
        break

Where this bites in production

PaLM (Chowdhery et al., 2022) states it plainly: no dropout during pretraining, dropout of 0.1 for fine-tuning. At that data scale the model sees most tokens once, so there is little to memorise and the regularisation is not earning its place. Contrast Srivastava et al. (2014), where 0.5 on the hidden layers was the difference between usable and unusable at MNIST scale. PyTorch also encodes the confusion: nn.Dropout(p) zeroes with probability p, the opposite of the paper’s convention.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What do you do about dropout at test time?
Nothing at all, and that is the whole point of inverted dropout. The scaling is done during training instead: divide the surviving activations by the keep probability, so the expected activation matches what the next layer would have seen with everything on. Inference then runs the plain deterministic forward pass. The only thing you must do is switch the model into eval mode so the masks stop being sampled.
Why is early stopping a form of regularisation?
Because it limits how far the weights travel from where they started. Fewer steps means a smaller effective parameter norm, which is closely related to what an L2 penalty does, and you get it for the price of a held-out set and a counter. Two details make or break it: patience sized to the noise in your metric, and restoring the best checkpoint rather than keeping the final one.
Why do large transformers use so little dropout?
Because the data scale does the regularising. A model that sees most of its tokens once has very little opportunity to memorise them, so the variance dropout was invented to control is largely gone — PaLM used none in pretraining and 0.1 only for fine-tuning. Dropout is still the right tool on small data, in fine-tuning, and in the fully connected heads of vision models.

Say this back tomorrow

divide by the keep rate while training  ·  do nothing at test  ·  restore the best weights
  • Inverted dropout scales at train time so inference needs no correction
  • Dropout left on at inference makes predictions non-deterministic — that is a missing eval mode
  • Early stopping needs patience and a restore, and must watch validation, never test

Unlocks

  • inverted dropout
  • model.eval()
  • patience
  • restore best weights
  • implicit ensemble

Convolutions, Pooling & the Receptive Field

One small detector, slid everywhere — and a window that widens with every layer.

A dense layer connects every input to every unit, which for a modest photograph means a hundred and fifty thousand weights per unit and no notion that two neighbouring pixels have anything to do with each other. A convolution replaces that with one small detector, a few pixels across, slid over the whole image and applied identically at every position. Two things follow. The parameter count collapses, because you store one detector rather than one weight per position. And the detector finds its pattern wherever it happens to sit, since it was the same detector everywhere. Stack these layers and each one sees a little further than the one below, so the patch of the original image a single unit depends on widens with depth. Early layers respond to edges. Deep ones respond to whole objects.

Like one rubber stamp instead of a wall of them. You carve a single stamp that recognises a corner, then press it across the whole page. There is no need for a separate stamp for every square inch, and a corner in the bottom left is caught by the very same stamp that catches one in the top right.

Two ideas do the work. Parameter sharing: one kernel is applied at every position, so a 3×3 kernel over 64 input channels producing 128 output channels costs (3⋅3⋅64+1)⋅128=73,856 parameters whatever the image size, where a dense layer on a 224×224×3 input needs 150,528 weights for a single unit and learns nothing transferable about position. Translation equivariance: shift the input and the feature map shifts with it, because the same kernel ran everywhere. Pooling adds a weak invariance on top — shift the input slightly and a max-pool output does not change — and those two words are worth keeping straight, because convolution is equivariant and pooling is what makes it invariant. Stride and pooling are the two ways to shrink the spatial dimensions.

The receptive field is what depth actually buys. Stack two 3×3 convolutions at stride 1 and one output unit depends on a 5×5 patch of the input; three of them reach 7×7, with fewer parameters than a single 7×7 kernel and two extra non-linearities along the way. Every stride-2 or pooling layer doubles the rate at which the field grows, which is the other reason to downsample. If the receptive field at your final layer is smaller than the object you are trying to detect, no amount of training will fix it — that is a design bug, and it is a calculation you can do on paper before you train anything. One more piece: a 1×1 convolution has no spatial extent at all. It is a per-pixel linear map across channels, used to mix or reduce channel count cheaply, and it is what opens a ResNet bottleneck and an Inception branch.

You reach for it when

  • Explaining why a convolution beats a dense layer on images
  • Computing an output shape and parameter count on a whiteboard
  • A detector misses objects larger than its final receptive field
  • Cutting channel count between two expensive layers

The trap

Answering “I would use a ResNet” when the question was what a convolution does. Naming architectures is not an explanation. A dense layer on a 224 by 224 colour image needs 150,528 weights for one unit and has no idea that adjacent pixels are related; a shared kernel needs a few hundred and finds its pattern anywhere in the frame. The second trap is swapping the two words: convolution is equivariant, pooling is what buys invariance.

The math the three you must be able to write

O=⌊SI−K+2P​⌋+1  ·  params =(Kh​Kw​Cin​+1)Cout​  ·  rl​=rl−1​+(Kl​−1)i<l∏​Si​Worked: I=224, K=3, P=1, S=2 gives ⌊223/2⌋+1=112. “Same” padding at stride 1 is P=(K−1)/2, which is why odd kernel sizes are the convention. The parameter count for that layer with Cin​=64 and Cout​=128 is (3⋅3⋅64+1)⋅128=73,856, and notice that the image size does not appear anywhere in it — that absence is parameter sharing. The third line is the receptive field: it grows by the kernel size minus one, multiplied by the product of every stride below it, so a stride-2 layer permanently doubles the rate at which the field widens.

Shapes and parameter counts

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

conv = nn.Conv2d(64, 128, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1)
x = torch.randn(8, 64, 224, 224)

print(conv(x).shape)     # (8, 128, 112, 112)  <- floor((224 - 3 + 2) / 2) + 1
print(sum(p.numel() for p in conv.parameters()))    # 73856 = (3*3*64 + 1)*128

# the image size appears nowhere in that count. THAT is parameter sharing.
print(conv(torch.randn(1, 64, 32, 32)).shape)       # (1, 128, 16, 16)

# 1x1: no spatial extent, just a linear map across channels
print(sum(p.numel() for p in nn.Conv2d(256, 64, 1).parameters()))   # 16448

Where this bites in production

VGG-16 is the clearest illustration of what sharing is worth. Its entire convolutional stack holds about 14.7 million parameters; its three fully connected layers hold roughly 124 million — nearly 90% of the model sitting in the part that shares nothing. Everything after it removed them. The other detail worth carrying is that both a ResNet bottleneck and an Inception branch open with a 1×1 convolution purely to cut the channel count before the expensive 3×3 runs.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What does a convolution buy you over a dense layer?
Parameter sharing and translation equivariance. One kernel is applied at every position, so the parameter count does not depend on the image size at all, and a pattern is detected wherever it appears rather than only where it appeared in training. A dense layer on a 224 by 224 colour image needs 150,528 weights per unit and treats neighbouring pixels as unrelated. Keep the words straight: convolution is equivariant, pooling is what adds invariance.
Give the output shape and parameter count: 3×3, stride 2, padding 1, 64 channels in, 128 out, 224 input.
112 by 112 by 128, and 73,856 parameters. The shape is floor of 224 minus 3 plus 2, over 2, plus one, which is 112. The count is kernel height times kernel width times input channels, plus one for the bias, all times output channels: 3 times 3 times 64 plus 1, times 128. The input size does not enter the second calculation, which is the point worth saying out loud.
Why does stacking convolutions help?
Because the receptive field widens with depth. Two stacked 3 by 3 layers give a unit a 5 by 5 view of the input, three give 7 by 7, with fewer parameters than one 7 by 7 kernel and extra non-linearities in between. Every stride-2 or pooling layer doubles the rate of growth. If the final receptive field is smaller than the object you want to detect, training cannot rescue it — check it on paper first.

Say this back tomorrow

one kernel, every position  ·  depth is how the window widens
  • Parameter sharing removes the image size from the parameter count entirely
  • Convolution is translation equivariant; pooling is what buys invariance
  • Receptive field grows with depth and doubles its growth rate after every stride-2 layer

RNNs, LSTMs & Why They Lost

The gates are the famous part. The reason they lost has nothing to do with them.

A recurrent network reads a sequence one item at a time and carries a running summary forward. Read a word, update the summary, read the next word. That summary is the only memory it has. It works over a short span and fails over a long one, because on the way back through the sequence the learning signal gets multiplied by roughly the same quantity at every step. Multiply something smaller than one by itself fifty times and it vanishes. Multiply something larger than one and it explodes. Either way the network cannot connect a word at the start of a paragraph to a word at the end. The gated version fixes this by giving the memory a lane it can travel down almost untouched, with small valves deciding what to erase, what to add, and what to reveal.

Like passing a message down a line of people. Each person hears it, adds a little, whispers it on. By the fortieth person the first sentence is gone. The gated version also hands along a sealed envelope: most people are told to leave it alone, a few are allowed to add a page or tear one out, and the beginning survives the journey.

A vanilla RNN carries a hidden state and updates it as ht​=tanh(Wh​ht−1​+Wx​xt​). Backpropagation through time multiplies the Jacobian ∂ht​/∂ht−1​ once per step, so the gradient reaching k steps back carries a factor that decays or grows geometrically. Vanishing is silent and kills long dependencies; exploding is loud and is fixed by clipping the global norm, typically at 1.0. The LSTM adds a cell state plus three gates, and each one answers a question: the forget gate decides what leaves the cell, the input gate decides what is written into it, the output gate decides how much of it is exposed. The cell updates additively, so a path exists along which the gradient passes almost unchanged — the constant error carousel. A GRU merges forget and input into a single update gate, keeps a reset gate, drops the output gate, and usually matches the LSTM with fewer parameters.

They did not lose on accuracy. They lost on hardware. The recurrence is sequential by definition — step t needs ht−1​ — so a sequence of length 1,000 is 1,000 dependent matrix multiplies and nothing along the sequence can be batched. Self-attention computes every position in one pass, so the sequence axis becomes parallel work and the accelerator stays saturated. Attention pays O(n2) against the RNN’s O(n) and wins anyway, because the constant is parallel. Module 04 picks this up from the attention side.

You reach for it when

  • Explaining why a sequence model forgets the start of a document
  • An interviewer asks what transformers actually fixed
  • Choosing between a GRU and an LSTM on a small dataset
  • Training loss goes to NaN on long sequences

The trap

Listing the three gates without saying what each one is for. Forget decides what leaves the cell, input decides what is written, output decides what is exposed — if you cannot attach a job to a gate, you have memorised a diagram. The second trap is saying LSTMs solve vanishing gradients. They mitigate it: the additive cell path keeps one route open, and very long dependencies still degrade.

The math the product that kills it

ht​=tanh(Wh​ht−1​+Wx​xt​)  ·  ∂ht−k​∂L​∝∏j=1k​∂ht−j​∂ht−j+1​​That product is the whole story. Each factor is bounded by the largest singular value of Wh​ times tanh′, which is at most 1. If the typical factor is 0.5, then twenty steps back the gradient is about one in a million; if it is 1.5, it is three thousand times too large and you clip. In an LSTM the corresponding factor is the forget gate, and a gate sitting near 1 leaves the path open.

The axis that will not parallelise

import torch, torch.nn as nn

lstm = nn.LSTM(64, 256, batch_first=True)
x = torch.randn(32, 1000, 64)            # batch 32, sequence length 1000

out, (h, c) = lstm(x)                    # 1000 dependent steps, strictly in order
loss = out.pow(2).mean()
loss.backward()

# the exploding half is a one-liner. The vanishing half is architectural.
nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(lstm.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)

# batch and feature axes parallelise. The sequence axis cannot, and that single
# fact is why attention won - not accuracy.

Where this bites in production

Google’s GNMT (Wu et al., 2016) stacked eight LSTM layers and had to be split across eight GPUs just to train in reasonable time. The Transformer paper a year later (Vaswani et al., 2017) trained its base model to a better BLEU in twelve hours on eight P100s, and named the inability to parallelise within a training example as the motivation in its opening section. Google Translate moved off recurrence within about two years.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why did transformers replace LSTMs?
Parallelisation, not accuracy. The recurrence is a dependency chain along the sequence: step t cannot start until step t−1 finishes, so a thousand-token sequence is a thousand serial matrix multiplies and the accelerator idles. Self-attention computes all positions in one batched pass, which turns the sequence axis into parallel work. The quadratic cost is worth paying because the constant is parallel.
What problem does each LSTM gate solve?
Each one controls a different edge of the cell state. The forget gate decides what is erased from the cell, which is what stops it saturating with stale content. The input gate decides what new information is written in. The output gate decides how much of the cell is exposed to the rest of the network at this step. The cell itself updates additively, and that is the part that keeps the gradient alive.
Your loss becomes NaN at epoch two on long sequences. What is happening?
Exploding gradients, and it is the easy half. The backward product has a typical factor above one, so the norm grows geometrically until an update overflows. Clip the global gradient norm at around 1.0 and check your initialisation and learning rate. The opposite failure never shows up as NaN — vanishing gradients are silent, and look like a model that simply refuses to learn long-range structure.

Say this back tomorrow

one state, one multiply per step  ·  gates keep a path open  ·  the sequence axis will not parallelise
  • The backward pass multiplies one Jacobian per timestep, so it decays or explodes geometrically
  • Each gate has a job: forget erases, input writes, output exposes — the cell adds
  • They lost to attention on parallelism, not on accuracy

Unlocks

  • BPTT
  • cell state
  • gradient clipping
  • GRU
  • sequential bottleneck

PCA, t-SNE & UMAP

Two of these are pictures, not preprocessing. Only one of them belongs in a pipeline.

The first method finds the directions along which your data spreads out most and keeps a few of them. It is a fixed recipe learned from the training rows, so you can apply exactly the same recipe to a row that arrives tomorrow, and the number you report is how much of the total spread your kept directions actually cover. The other two are drawing tools. They arrange points so that near neighbours stay near, which makes a lovely picture and nothing you can put in a pipeline. One of them cannot handle a new point at all: to add a row you redraw the whole picture. And the picture misleads in two specific ways. A bigger blob is not a bigger group, and a wider gap between two blobs is not a bigger difference.

Think of a seating plan for a wedding. One method finds the long axis of the room and lines everybody up along it, so a late arrival can be seated by the same rule. The other shuffles friends onto tables until nobody sits with a stranger — lovely to look at, but the gaps between tables are just where the furniture happened to fit.

PCA finds an orthogonal basis ordered by variance — the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, or equivalently the right singular vectors of the centred data matrix. What you report is the cumulative explained-variance ratio, and 90, 95 or 99 per cent are the usual cut-offs. It is scale-dependent, so you standardise first, and it is a learned map, so you fit on train and call transform on validation and test — fitting on the full matrix before the split leaks test variance into training. Two limits matter in interviews. PCA is unsupervised, so a high-variance direction can be pure noise and the direction that separates your classes can be the one you discarded; LDA maximises between-class over within-class scatter and is the supervised counterpart. And PCA is linear, so a curved manifold needs kernel PCA or a neighbour-embedding method instead.

t-SNE and UMAP both preserve local neighbourhoods and neither preserves global geometry. Three facts settle most questions. t-SNE has no out-of-sample extension: scikit-learn’s TSNE exposes fit_transform and no transform, because there is no map to apply. UMAP does have transform, so it can sit in a pipeline, though it rarely should. And the dial is the same dial in both — perplexity in t-SNE, n_neighbors in UMAP, defaults 30 and 15 — trading local detail against global shape. Run three settings. If the story changes, the story was the setting.

You reach for it when

  • A stakeholder asks what the clusters in the t-SNE plot mean
  • Compressing 300 correlated features before a linear model
  • A dimensionality-reduction step has to run at serving time
  • Deciding how many components to keep

The trap

Putting a t-SNE plot in a deck and reading the gaps. Cluster sizes and between-cluster distances carry no information — the algorithm normalises local density, so a tight group and a diffuse one come out the same size, and the space between blobs is whatever the optimiser had left over. Pure noise resolves into convincing islands at low perplexity. The second trap is fitting PCA before the split.

The math what you actually report

Σ=n−11​X⊤X,   Σvi​=λi​vi​  ·  explained variance ratio =∑j​λj​λi​​The eigenvectors are the directions and the eigenvalues are the variance along them, so the ratio is the fraction of total spread each component buys. X must be centred, and standardised too unless every column already shares a unit — otherwise the feature measured in pounds drowns the one measured in years. Nothing in this expression looks at y, which is exactly why PCA can delete the direction that separates your classes.

Fit on train, then check for transform

import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PCA(n_components=0.95))
pipe.fit(X_train)                       # train only. Fitting on all of X leaks.
X_te = pipe.transform(X_test)

evr = pipe.named_steps['pca'].explained_variance_ratio_
print(np.cumsum(evr)[:5], X_te.shape[1])   # the number you actually report

print(hasattr(TSNE(), 'transform'))     # False. There is nothing to apply.

Where this bites in production

scikit-learn’s TSNE class has no transform method at all, only fit_transform — that missing method is the entire answer to whether it can serve. The other named source is Wattenberg, Viégas and Johnson’s “How to Use t-SNE Effectively” (Distill, 2016), which shows pure Gaussian noise resolving into crisp clusters at low perplexity, and one dataset producing quite different pictures at perplexity 5, 30 and 100.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Can you put t-SNE in your production pipeline?
No, and the API tells you why. There is no out-of-sample extension: the algorithm optimises the positions of the points it was given, so a new row has no position and the only way to get one is to refit the whole embedding. UMAP does expose a transform, and PCA is a learned linear map you can apply to anything. t-SNE is a diagnostic picture.
Two clusters in your t-SNE plot sit far apart. What does that tell you?
Nothing at all. Between-cluster distances are not preserved, and neither are cluster sizes — the objective normalises local density, so a compact group and a diffuse one render at similar scale. The gaps are an artefact of a non-convex optimisation with a random initialisation. Change the perplexity or the seed and the geometry changes while the data does not.
Your classifier got worse after you added PCA. Why?
Because PCA never looked at the labels. It keeps the directions of largest variance, and variance is not discriminative power — a high-variance axis can be sensor noise while the separating direction sits in a component you dropped. Keep more components, use a supervised reduction such as LDA, or select features against the target instead of compressing blindly.

Say this back tomorrow

PCA is a map you can apply  ·  UMAP has one  ·  t-SNE is a drawing, and its gaps mean nothing
  • Fit PCA on train only, and report cumulative explained variance, not a component count
  • t-SNE cannot transform new data; UMAP can, PCA can
  • PCA is unsupervised and can discard the discriminative direction — LDA is the supervised one

Unlocks

  • explained variance
  • out-of-sample
  • perplexity
  • n_neighbors
  • LDA

Training–Serving Skew

This is not drift. The model was wrong on the day you shipped it.

You trained on features computed by one piece of code and you serve features computed by another. The two were written months apart by different people, and they do not agree. The batch job fills a missing value with the column average; the live service fills it with zero. The warehouse stores timestamps in one time zone and the request carries another. A count the training set took over thirty days is taken over seven at request time. None of this is the world changing. The world is exactly as it was. Your model is being handed different numbers from the ones it was fitted on, and it has been since the very first request. That is why retraining does not help. You have to make the two paths compute the feature the same way.

Like a recipe tested in one kitchen and cooked in another. The test kitchen weighed flour in grams; the restaurant scoops it by the cup. Same recipe on paper, a different cake every service. Nothing has gone off and nothing has changed since opening night — the two kitchens never measured the same way, and fresher flour will not fix it.

Drift and skew are different failures with different fixes, and conflating them is the tell. Drift means the distribution moved after you shipped: the world changed, and retraining on recent data is the answer. Skew means the training path and the serving path compute the same-named feature differently, so the model has been scored on inputs it never saw in training since request one, and retraining faithfully reproduces the mismatch on a newer model. The usual causes are two implementations of one feature — a Spark job and a service — different null and default handling, a unit or time-zone mismatch, a different aggregation window, and a feature that exists in the warehouse but is not available at request time, so it silently becomes a default. The signature is a large offline-to-online gap on day one with no downward trend.

Detection is mechanical rather than statistical. Log the exact feature vector the model scored, then compare each column against the training set — null rate, mean, cardinality, min and max, not the mean alone. The sharper test is a replay: take one training row, push its raw inputs through the serving path, and diff the two vectors field by field. Any field that differs is a bug with an owner and a fix. The structural cure is one feature definition materialised into both stores, which is the argument for a feature store.

You reach for it when

  • Validation looked excellent and production has been flat since launch
  • The same feature is written in SQL for training and in Go for serving
  • A feature exists in the warehouse but not at request time
  • Someone proposes retraining to close a gap that never trended

The trap

Calling it drift and asking for a retrain. Drift has a shape: performance was fine, then decayed. Skew has no shape — it is flat and wrong from the first request, because the model is being fed a feature the training set never contained. Retraining rebuilds the same mismatch on newer data and buys nothing. Unify the two implementations, or at minimum train on the logged serving features.

The math two different failures

skew: ϕtrain​(r)=ϕserve​(r) for the same raw record r  ·  drift: Pt​(X,Y)=P0​(X,Y)The first line is skew: one raw record, two transforms, two different feature vectors, and the difference is present on day one. The second is drift: one transform, applied to a distribution that has moved since you fitted. Only the second is fixed by training on newer data. The first is fixed in code, and no amount of fresh data will touch it.

Replay one row through both paths

import pandas as pd

# 1. log the exact vector the model scored, keyed by request id. Always.
log_features(request_id, feats)

# 2. replay one raw row through BOTH transforms and diff them
offline = batch_pipeline.transform(raw_row)     # the Spark / pandas path
online = serving_pipeline.transform(raw_row)    # the service path

diff = (offline - online).abs()
print(diff[diff > 1e-9])          # any non-empty output is a bug, not drift

# 3. and compare the logged serving columns against training - nulls too
train.describe().T.join(served.describe().T, rsuffix='_served')

Where this bites in production

Google’s “Rules of Machine Learning” gives this its own rule. Rule 29: the way to be sure you train the way you serve is to save the features used at serving time, pipe them to a log, and train on that log. Rule 32: reuse code between the training and serving pipelines wherever you can. TensorFlow Data Validation ships a skew comparator for precisely this diff, which tells you how often it happened.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Validation AUC was 0.87 and production is flat. Where do you look first?
Training–serving skew, before you consider drift. A gap present from the first request is not the world moving, it is the two feature paths disagreeing. Log the serving feature vector and compare it column by column with the training data — null rates and defaults first, then units and time zones, then aggregation windows. Only after that has come back clean should you look at leakage or a bad split.
How do you tell skew from drift with one chart?
Plot the online metric from launch and look at the shape. Drift starts at the offline level and decays, so there is a good period before the bad one. Skew is a flat line that starts below where it should be and never had a good period at all. If you cannot see a launch that worked, stop investigating the data distribution and start diffing the pipelines.
You found a skewed feature. What do you change?
The pipeline, not the model. Make one implementation the single source of truth and have the other call it, or move the definition into a feature store that materialises to both. The stopgap, if you cannot unify today, is to train on the logged serving features so the model at least learns the distribution it will actually be given.

Say this back tomorrow

drift = the world moved  ·  skew = you were wrong on day one  ·  one is a retrain, the other is a code fix
  • Skew is flat and wrong from request one; drift decays from a good start
  • Two implementations of one feature is the usual cause — defaults, units, windows
  • Log serving features and replay a training row through the serving path

Unlocks

  • feature parity
  • serving log
  • replay diff
  • null handling
  • pipeline unification

Data Drift & Concept Drift

Three different failures wear the same word, and only one of them poisons your old data.

Three different things can go wrong after you ship, and people call all of them drift. The first: the kind of traffic changes. You trained mostly on desktop users and now most arrive on phones, but a phone user who behaves a certain way still means what they always meant. The second: the mix of outcomes changes. Fraud used to be one in a thousand and is now one in two hundred, though fraud itself looks the same. The third is the serious one. The relationship changes, so the same customer with exactly the same history is now a different risk, because the world moved underneath the question. The first two you can usually fix by feeding the model recent data. The third means your old data is not merely stale, it is actively wrong.

Like a shop whose customers change. More students walk in than pensioners — the crowd moved, but a student still wants what students have always wanted. Then a rival opens across the road, and the same customer who used to buy from you walks straight past. Nothing about that customer changed. What their behaviour means did.

Name the three precisely. Covariate shift: P(X) moves while P(Y∣X) holds, so retraining on recent data works and importance weighting works too. Label or prior shift: P(Y) moves while P(X∣Y) holds, which for a classifier is often fixed by correcting the prior or moving the threshold rather than refitting at all. Concept drift: P(Y∣X) moves, and P(X) may not move one bit, so every input monitor you own stays green and only labels reveal it — here old data is actively harmful and you may need to relabel and drop history. For detection, PSI is the industry metric, credit-risk in origin, with the convention that under 0.1 is stable, 0.1 to 0.25 warrants investigation and above 0.25 means act. The KS two-sample test is one-dimensional and degrades in high dimensions; MMD is the multivariate kernel option, common in papers and rare in production.

The subtlety almost nobody raises is the window. Whether a distribution has drifted depends entirely on what you compare against: a sliding seven-day window against the previous seven can scream while the cumulative distribution since launch stays flat, and the reverse happens too. Pick the window from the decision you intend to make, then hold it fixed. Classify the shape as well — sudden shifts have a date and usually a nameable cause, gradual ones need a trend test rather than a threshold, and a seasonal cycle is not drift at all. Compare December against last December, not against November.

You reach for it when

  • A monitoring dashboard fires and nobody can say which kind it is
  • Model quality decayed slowly across two quarters
  • Deciding whether a retrain will actually help
  • A December spike that looks exactly like last December’s

The trap

Retraining the moment a drift alert fires. PSI above 0.25 says an input distribution moved; it does not say the model got worse, and a feature the model barely uses can breach it while performance is untouched. Check the performance metric, or a label-free proxy, before spending a retrain and a release. The mirror trap is calling seasonality drift — compare against the same period last year.

The math the industry drift metric

PSI=∑i​(ai​−ei​)ln(ai​/ei​)ei​ and ai​ are the expected and actual fraction of rows in bin i, usually ten bins cut on the training distribution. Unlike KL it is symmetric, and it is unbounded above. The 0.1 and 0.25 cut-offs come from credit scorecards rather than from a theorem. And note what it cannot see: PSI is computed on inputs, so it detects P(X) moving and is completely blind to P(Y∣X) moving.

PSI, and why the window decides

import numpy as np

def psi(expected, actual, bins=10):
    cuts = np.quantile(expected, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1))   # bins from TRAIN
    cuts[0], cuts[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    e = np.histogram(expected, cuts)[0] / len(expected) + 1e-6  # never divide by 0
    a = np.histogram(actual, cuts)[0] / len(actual) + 1e-6
    return float(((a - e) * np.log(a / e)).sum())

print(psi(train.amount, last_7_days.amount))     # sliding window
print(psi(train.amount, since_launch.amount))    # cumulative - often disagrees
# 0.1 investigate, 0.25 act. Both are conventions, not laws.

Where this bites in production

PSI arrived from credit-risk scorecards, where 0.1 and 0.25 have been convention for decades — a rule of thumb, not a result. The expensive public case is Zillow Offers: the algorithmic home-buying arm was closed in November 2021 after its pricing model misread a moving market, with an inventory write-down of over 300 million dollars in a single quarter and about a quarter of the company’s staff cut.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

PSI fired at 0.31 and accuracy has not moved. What do you do?
Nothing to the model yet. PSI measures an input distribution, not model quality, and a feature with low importance can breach the threshold while predictions are unaffected. Check which feature moved and how much the model leans on it, then check the performance metric or a label-free proxy. Retrain when quality moves or when the shift touches a feature the model depends on.
House prices before and after a market shock. Which drift, and does retraining fix it?
Concept drift, and retraining only helps once you have new labels. The mapping from features to price changed, so a house with identical attributes is worth something different. Fresh inputs are useless without fresh outcomes, and the old rows are actively harmful because they teach the previous relationship — drop or down-weight them rather than appending new data to the pile.
Two teams disagree about whether a feature drifted. How is that possible?
They chose different windows. A sliding seven-day comparison and a cumulative-since-launch comparison can return opposite verdicts on identical data, because one tracks the recent regime and the other averages it away. Neither is a mistake. Agree the reference window and the comparison period up front, tie them to the decision the alert triggers, and record the choice next to the threshold.

Say this back tomorrow

covariate = the inputs moved  ·  label = the base rate moved  ·  concept = the right answer moved
  • Only concept drift makes your old labelled data actively harmful
  • PSI 0.1 and 0.25 are credit-scorecard conventions, not thresholds from a theorem
  • Sliding and cumulative windows can give opposite verdicts on identical data

Monitoring When the Labels Arrive Late

You will not know whether the model is right for another six weeks. Design for that.

What you want to know is whether the model is still right. You almost never get to know that today. A loan either defaults or it does not, and you find out in months. A customer either leaves or stays, and you find out in weeks. A card payment turns out to be fraud when the cardholder disputes it, which can be two months later. So a dashboard built around accuracy is blank at exactly the moment you need it. What you watch instead are the things visible immediately: is the data arriving, are the columns the shape they should be, how many values are missing, what does the spread of incoming requests look like, and what does the spread of scores look like. Accuracy arrives later and confirms what those already told you.

Think of a hospital ward at night. Nobody can run bloods until morning, so the nurse checks pulse, breathing and colour every hour. None of those is the diagnosis. All of them move first, and a nurse who waits for the lab result before starting to worry is a nurse who finds out too late to do anything.

Label delay drives the whole design, so write the feedback-loop length down before anything else: seconds for a click, days for a return, weeks for churn, months for a loan default, and for card fraud however long the chargeback window runs. Anything shorter than that gap is monitored with label-free proxies, and accuracy becomes a lagging confirmation rather than an alarm. The layers, in the order they should fire: data quality and schema first — row counts, null rates, types, cardinality, ranges — because a broken upstream job is the most common incident and it is not a model problem at all; then feature distributions against the training reference; then the prediction distribution, which is one-dimensional, cheap and the earliest honest warning; then business proxies such as click-through, approval rate or downstream conversion; and finally precision, recall and calibration once labels land.

Two operational details decide whether any of it survives. Every alert needs a named action, because a threshold with no runbook is muted within a month, and monitoring hundreds of features across dozens of models manufactures false positives by construction — alert on a small set and let the rest be dashboards you look at during an incident. And the score histogram is the single highest-value chart: if the mean predicted probability moves from 0.03 to 0.11 on the same traffic mix, something changed upstream, and you know it weeks before one label lands.

You reach for it when

  • Designing monitoring for a model whose labels take weeks
  • An on-call rota needs alerts that actually mean something
  • Accuracy cannot be computed and someone asks if the model is healthy
  • A stakeholder wants one dashboard for a fraud model

The trap

Presenting a monitoring plan whose first chart is accuracy. If labels take six weeks, that chart is empty for six weeks and then reports a problem that started six weeks ago. The companion trap is an alert with no runbook: a drift threshold nobody knows how to act on gets muted within a month, and after that you are not monitoring anything, you are paying for a dashboard.

The math the label-free check

pˉ​=n1​∑i​p^​i​≈πbase​  ·  watch the gap, not the accuracyOn a calibrated model the mean predicted probability should track the eventual positive rate, so you can compare today’s mean score against a base rate you already know from history — no labels required. This is the idea behind confidence-based performance estimation. It is only as good as the calibration underneath it: on an uncalibrated model the comparison is meaningless, which is one more reason to calibrate before you ship.

The dashboard you can build today

import pandas as pd

today = serving_log[serving_log.date == pd.Timestamp.today().date()]

checks = {
    'rows': len(today),                              # is the upstream job alive?
    'null_rate': today[FEATURES].isna().mean().max(),  # data quality
    'mean_score': today.score.mean(),                # prediction drift
    'p99_score': today.score.quantile(0.99),
    'approve_rate': (today.score > THRESHOLD).mean(),  # business proxy
}
# all five are computable now. Precision needs labels that land in ~45 days.
alert_if(abs(checks['mean_score'] - TRAIN_MEAN_SCORE) > 0.02, runbook='RB-014')

Where this bites in production

Card fraud is the clean case: a cardholder dispute can arrive months after the transaction, so a fraud model’s labels are still landing long after it shipped, and its true precision for last week is unknowable this week. Chip Huyen’s Designing Machine Learning Systems builds its monitoring chapter on exactly this ordering, and the library NannyML exists for the gap — its confidence-based performance estimation infers ROC-AUC from calibrated scores before a single label arrives.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

You cannot compute accuracy for two weeks. What do you monitor?
Everything upstream of the label, in order. Data quality and schema first — row counts, null rates, types, ranges — because a broken pipeline is the most likely incident. Then feature distributions against the training reference, then the prediction distribution, which is cheap and one-dimensional. Then business proxies such as approval or click-through rate. Accuracy arrives in a fortnight and confirms what those already said.
One chart only, for a fraud model. Which?
The score histogram against its training reference. It is one dimension, it needs no labels, and it moves when almost anything upstream breaks — a dead feature, a changed default, a shifted population, a bad deploy. It will not tell you why, and it will not catch concept drift where the inputs hold still. It is the cheapest early warning you can have on day one.
An alert fires weekly and the team ignores it. What went wrong?
It was created without a runbook. An alert is a promise that somebody will do a specific thing, so a threshold with no named action decays into noise and takes the credibility of every other alert with it. Either write the action down, widen the threshold until firing genuinely means something, or demote it to a dashboard you consult during an incident.

monitor what you can see today  ·  accuracy is the confirmation, never the alarm
  • Write the feedback-loop length down first — it decides the whole monitoring design
  • Data quality, then feature drift, then prediction drift, then labels when they land
  • An alert with no runbook gets muted, and then you are monitoring nothing

Feature Stores & Point-in-Time Correctness

Not a convenience layer. A defence against joining the future onto the past.

To train a model you need rows that look the way the world looked while the outcome was still unknown. Say a customer defaulted in March. To learn anything from that row you need what you knew about them in March: their balance then, their missed payments then. What you must not use is what their record says today, because today includes everything that happened afterwards, including the consequences of the default itself. Joining the current value onto an old outcome is time travel. It produces a model that looks brilliant in testing and is worthless in service, because at the moment of a real decision the future has not happened yet. A feature store exists to make that join correct by default, and to make the training path and the serving path read one definition.

Like marking an exam with the answers written in. You want to know what the student knew in the hall that morning. If you grade the paper after they have gone home and looked everything up, the marks are wonderful and they tell you nothing about the exam. The only honest record is the one frozen at the moment they sat down.

The point of a feature store is not reuse, it is point-in-time correctness. A training row is a label with a timestamp, and every feature on that row must be the value that was current as of that timestamp — not the latest value, and not one computed over a window extending past it. So the join is an as-of join on entity plus event time, taking the most recent feature row at or before the label time, with a bounded look-back so a stale value cannot fill in silently. Get it wrong and an aggregate computed over all history leaks the future into every training row: the offline metric climbs and production does not move. The second half is architectural. One definition materialised into an offline store for training and an online store for serving means the two paths cannot diverge, which is the structural fix for training–serving skew.

Three operational pieces follow. A backfill recomputes a new feature across history, and it must run through the same as-of logic or you have manufactured a leak at scale in one job. Feature versioning matters because editing a definition in place silently invalidates every model trained on the old one — add a version rather than change the meaning. And a time-to-live bounds how old an online value may be before it counts as missing, which is what stops a dead upstream job from serving last month’s numbers forever. One honest caveat: for a three-person team with one model, a feature store is premature, and a well-tested shared transform library does the same job.

You reach for it when

  • Building a training set from a warehouse full of mutable tables
  • An offline metric is far better than anything production has ever reached
  • Two teams want the same feature and each computes it separately
  • Backfilling a new feature across two years of history

The trap

Reciting a vendor’s feature list instead of naming the problem. The answer is one sentence: a single definition materialised into an offline and an online store, joined to labels as of each label’s own timestamp. The concrete failure is joining a current aggregate onto a six-month-old label — the model reads the future, the offline score is superb, production is flat. The mirror trap is proposing one for a three-person team.

The math the as-of rule

xi​=ϕ(data≤ti​)  ·  never ϕ(data≤tnow​)ti​ is the timestamp of label i and ϕ is the feature transform. Every feature on a training row must be a function of data available at or before that row’s own label time — per row, not per dataset. A single global cut-off is not enough, because a January label and a June label need different cut-offs. The look-back bound matters as well: allow an arbitrarily old value and you have traded leakage for staleness.

A point-in-time join, in Feast

from feast import FeatureStore
import pandas as pd

store = FeatureStore(repo_path='.')

# one row per LABEL, each carrying its own timestamp. That is the whole trick.
entity_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'customer_id': [101, 102],
    'event_timestamp': pd.to_datetime(['2025-03-14', '2025-06-02']),
    'defaulted': [1, 0],
})

training = store.get_historical_features(   # as-of join, per row, offline store
    entity_df=entity_df,
    features=['cust:balance_30d', 'cust:late_payments'],
).to_df()

serving = store.get_online_features(        # same definitions, online store
    features=['cust:balance_30d', 'cust:late_payments'],
    entity_rows=[{'customer_id': 101}],
).to_dict()

Where this bites in production

Uber built Palette inside Michelangelo in 2017 for exactly this: one feature definition materialised into Hive for training and Cassandra for serving, so the two paths could not drift apart. Feast puts the rule in its API — get_historical_features takes an entity dataframe in which every row carries its own event_timestamp, and a feature view’s ttl bounds how far back the as-of join may reach.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What is a point-in-time join and why does it matter?
An as-of join that gives each label the feature values current at that label’s own timestamp. Without it you attach today’s aggregates to an outcome from six months ago, so the training row contains information that post-dates the event, including its own consequences. The model learns a relationship that cannot exist at decision time, and the offline score is a fiction.
Offline AUC is 0.94 and production sits at chance. Name the two suspects.
A point-in-time leak, or training–serving skew. The leak means your training features contained the future, so the offline number was never real. Skew means the features are honest but the serving path computes them differently. Distinguish them by replaying: rebuild one training row with a strict as-of cut-off, and separately diff the serving vector against the training vector.
When is a feature store premature?
One team, one model, one pipeline. A feature store buys point-in-time correctness, a shared definition across offline and online, and lineage — all of which a single well-tested transform library gives a small team for a fraction of the operational cost. Adopt one when several teams reuse features, or when the same feature is already implemented twice and has begun to disagree.

Say this back tomorrow

join every label to the features as they were, not as they are
  • Point-in-time correctness is why a feature store exists; reuse is the side effect
  • One definition, two stores — the structural fix for training–serving skew
  • Backfills must run through the same as-of logic, or they leak at scale

Offline Metrics vs Online Metrics

The model with the better AUC routinely loses the A/B test.

Before you ship a model you score it on data you already have. That number is cheap, it comes back in minutes, and you can run it a hundred times a day. After you ship it you measure what people actually did. That number is expensive, it takes weeks, and you only get a few of them. The two disagree far more often than anyone expects. The old model chose what your logged data contains, so your test set is a record of its taste, not of the world. Users click the top result partly because it is on top. And the thing you scored offline is rarely the thing the business is paid for. Offline evaluation is a filter that decides what is worth testing. Online evaluation is the decision.

Like a driving test in an empty car park. You can measure steering, mirror checks and parking to the centimetre, and whoever scores highest really is better at those things. Then you put them on a motorway in rain. The car park told you who was worth testing. It did not tell you who can drive.

Four things drive the gap. Position and presentation bias: your logged clicks record what the old ranker put at rank one, so a model that agrees with the incumbent scores well offline by construction. Selection bias: the logs only contain actions the old policy took, so you are scoring a new policy on a distribution it did not generate. Metric mismatch: NDCG is not revenue and log loss is not retention, so the offline number is not the overall evaluation criterion. And the latency budget — the offline winner is often the model that misses it, and a 200ms regression costs more than the ranking gain returns. The principled correction is off-policy evaluation: inverse propensity scoring or a doubly robust estimator over logged propensities.

Off-policy estimation is only as good as your logging. Inverse propensity weighting is unbiased when every action had some non-zero chance of being shown and you recorded that chance. Its variance is brutal when propensities get small, which is why people clip the weights and why doubly robust estimators exist at all. If you never logged propensities, the honest answer in the room is that you cannot reconstruct them retrospectively — you start logging them today and you gate on something else this quarter.

You reach for it when

  • A clear offline win comes back flat in the A/B test
  • Choosing which two of five candidates get a test slot
  • Someone proposes shipping on an offline number alone
  • Setting up click logging before any experiment exists

The trap

Letting the offline metric make the decision. The specific failure is reporting an NDCG gain and asking to ship. The mirror-image trap is killing a model because offline is flat, when the offline set was generated by the incumbent and structurally cannot reward a ranker that disagrees with it. Pick one offline gate and one online decision metric before you start, write both down, and never let the gate become the decision.

The math the off-policy estimate

V^IPS​=n1​∑i=1n​πlog​(ai​∣xi​)πnew​(ai​∣xi​)​ri​Each logged event is reweighted by how much more likely the new policy was to take the action the old one took. Unbiased only if the logging policy gave every action some chance; the variance explodes as the denominator shrinks, which is why weights get clipped.

Estimating a new policy from old logs

import numpy as np

# logged per impression: the action the OLD policy took, its propensity, the reward
p_new = new_policy.prob(x, a)              # prob the new ranker would show this item
w = np.clip(p_new / p_log, 0, 10)          # clip: raw IPS variance is brutal

v_new = (w * reward).mean()                # off-policy estimate of the new policy
v_old = reward.mean()                      # what the old policy actually earned

ess = w.sum() ** 2 / (w ** 2).sum()        # effective sample size
print(v_new, v_old, ess / len(w))          # ess/n below ~0.1 -> do not trust the number

Where this bites in production

The Netflix Prize is the canonical case. The winning ensemble improved RMSE by just over ten percent and took the million dollars in 2009. Netflix said publicly in 2012 that it never shipped the full thing — the engineering cost of running it did not pay for itself, and by then the business had moved from predicting star ratings to deciding what to autoplay. The offline metric was real. It was not the objective.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Offline NDCG is up 4% and online CTR is flat. Give three explanations.
Position bias, distribution mismatch, and metric mismatch. The logged clicks were produced by the old ranker, so agreeing with it scores well offline for free. The new policy is being judged on a distribution it did not generate, which is exactly what off-policy estimation exists to correct. And NDCG is not the criterion the business is judged on. Check the latency budget too — a slower ranker loses clicks that no ranking gain recovers.
What must you have logged to evaluate a new ranker without shipping it?
The propensity of every action the old policy took. Inverse propensity scoring reweights logged rewards by how likely the new policy was to take the same action, and that ratio needs a denominator. You also need overlap: the old policy must have had some chance of showing the items the new one likes. Nobody can reconstruct propensities after the fact.
Your offline gate and your online metric disagree every quarter. What do you change?
The gate, not the decision. The online metric is what the business is measured on, so it does not move. Refit the gate until it correlates — usually that means adding display position as a feature and evaluating on the randomised exploration slice, where the incumbent did not choose the impressions.

Say this back tomorrow

offline decides what is worth testing  ·  online decides what ships
  • Logged data was chosen by the old policy, so it flatters models that agree with it
  • Off-policy estimation needs propensities you had to log before the fact
  • One offline gate, one online decision metric, both written down first

A/B Tests, Novelty & Interference

Day one lies in both directions, and the discipline is not calling it.

You split traffic in two, show one group the new thing, and compare. It works, but three things break it. People click anything that looks new, so a fresh feature gets a bump that has nothing to do with whether it is better, and the bump fades. The opposite also happens: people who liked the old layout resist the new one, so the first few days look worse than the truth. Both settle within a week or two. Then there is the harder one. If the two groups can affect each other — they share a marketplace, they message each other, they bid against each other — the control group is no longer a clean control, and splitting by person does not give you an answer at all.

Think of a new restaurant. The first fortnight is packed because it is new, not because the food is good, and judging it then overrates it. A regular pub that changes its menu has the opposite problem: the regulars grumble for a fortnight whatever you cooked. Either way, the queue on opening night tells you almost nothing about next year.

Novelty and primacy are transient treatment effects that bias in opposite directions, so “it is up on day one” is not evidence of anything. Run a minimum of one full week to absorb day-of-week seasonality, discard the first days, and check whether the effect is stable in week two or still trending. Size it up front: per arm you need roughly 16σ2/δ2 for 80% power at α=0.05, which for a proportion is 16p(1−p)/δ2. Fix the minimum detectable effect before you look, because peeking turns a fixed-horizon test into a sequential one and inflates Type I error badly. And if you are watching twenty metrics, either correct for multiple comparisons or declare one overall evaluation criterion plus named guardrails.

Interference is the assumption you violate without noticing. User-level randomisation assumes one user’s treatment does not change another user’s outcome. In a two-sided marketplace it does: a treated rider takes the driver a control rider would have had, so the measured lift is partly cannibalisation. The fix is to randomise at a unit that contains the spillover — cluster, geo, or time-sliced switchback — and pay for it in power. For ranking changes specifically, interleaving mixes both rankers into one list per query and attributes clicks within the list, which removes between-user variance and needs one to two orders of magnitude fewer impressions.

You reach for it when

  • A launch is up 12% on day one and someone wants to ship
  • Comparing two rankers with very little traffic
  • Designing an experiment for a marketplace or a social feed
  • Deciding how long to run before you are allowed to look

The trap

Calling day one. Novelty inflates and primacy deflates, both fade, so an early read is a measurement of newness. The second trap is peeking: checking daily and stopping the moment it goes significant guarantees a false positive eventually, because you took twenty draws at a 5% error rate. The third is randomising by user in a marketplace, where the control arm is contaminated by the treatment arm by construction.

The math per arm, 80% power

n≈δ216σ2​  ·  for a proportion, n≈δ216p(1−p)​The 16 is 2(zα/2​+zβ​)2=2(1.96+0.84)2≈15.7 at α=0.05 two-sided. Halving the effect you want to detect quadruples the traffic you need, which is why the minimum detectable effect is a business decision and not a statistical one.

Size it before you run it

from statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_effectsize

p0, mde = 0.042, 0.002        # baseline CTR, and the absolute lift worth shipping
h = proportion_effectsize(p0 + mde, p0)

n = NormalIndPower().solve_power(h, power=0.80, alpha=0.05, ratio=1.0)
print(round(n))               # per arm. Halve mde and this goes up 4x, not 2x

# then: whole weeks only, discard days 1-3, and do NOT stop the first day p < 0.05

Where this bites in production

Uber does not randomise dispatch or pricing experiments by rider, because a treated rider takes a driver a control rider would otherwise have had. It randomises time slices within a city — switchback experiments — and accepts far lower power for an unbiased number. From the other side, Kohavi’s team at Bing reported that only about a third of tested ideas improved the metric they were built to improve, and roughly a third made it worse.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Treatment is up 12% on day one. When do you call it?
You do not call it. Run at least one full week so day-of-week seasonality cancels, then discard the first few days and check whether the effect is flat in week two or still decaying. A 12% day-one lift that settles at 1% was novelty. A 12% lift that holds for a fortnight is a result.
Why can you not randomise by user for a marketplace pricing change?
Because the arms are not independent. A treated rider consumes supply the control rider would have had, so treatment changes control’s outcome and the measured difference is inflated by cannibalisation. Randomise at a unit that contains the spillover — city, region, or a time-sliced switchback — and accept far fewer effective samples.
You must compare two rankers and you have very little traffic. What do you run?
An interleaving experiment. Mix both rankers’ results into a single list per query and attribute each click to whichever ranker contributed the item. Every user sees both, so between-user variance drops out and you need orders of magnitude fewer impressions. It only answers ranking comparisons — it cannot measure an interface change or overall engagement.

Say this back tomorrow

day one measures newness  ·  week two measures the change
  • Novelty inflates and primacy deflates, and both fade — early reads are worthless
  • Fix the minimum detectable effect and the horizon before you look, or peeking eats your alpha
  • If units interfere, randomise clusters or geos; for rankers, interleave

Time-Series Validation & Backtesting

A random split on temporal data is the most common leak in the industry.

When your data has a time order, the only honest question is whether the model would have worked had you trained it last month and used it this month. So you train on the past, test on the future, and slide that window forward. Shuffling the rows and taking a random fifth for testing quietly hands the model tomorrow’s answers, and it will look wonderful right up until the day you ship it. There is a subtler version that almost nobody mentions. If the thing you are predicting is measured over the following thirty days, then a training row near the boundary already contains part of the test period. You have to throw away the rows that straddle the line, and leave a gap after it.

Like testing a weather forecast. You do not judge it by hiding a random Tuesday from the year and asking it to fill in the blank — it can see Monday and Wednesday. You judge it by standing on the first of the month, forecasting the week ahead, and waiting. Then you step forward and do it again. That is the only version anyone would pay for.

Walk-forward validation: fit on everything up to a cut, score the next block, move the cut, repeat. An expanding window keeps all history and is right when the process is stationary; a sliding window drops old data and is right when it is not, and comparing the two tells you which regime you are in. TimeSeriesSplit gives you the expanding version, and it is not sufficient on its own. If the label is computed over a forward horizon — a thirty-day default flag, a seven-day churn window — then training rows whose label windows overlap the test block contain test information. Purging drops those rows; an embargo adds a further gap after the test block so serial correlation does not carry across. Almost nobody raises this unprompted.

Two more things worth saying. Test stationarity before you model — ADF and KPSS have opposite null hypotheses, so run both — because two independent trending series will regress beautifully on each other, and that is spurious regression, not signal. And count your backtests. Re-run the same backtest two hundred times and keep the best Sharpe and you have selected on noise; the honest corrections are a period you never look at until the end, or deflating the statistic by the number of trials you actually ran.

You reach for it when

  • Any dataset with a timestamp and a forward-looking label
  • A backtest that looks far too good to be true
  • Choosing between an expanding and a sliding window
  • Someone reports the best of many backtest runs

The trap

Shuffling. A random k-fold on temporal data puts next week in training and this week in test, and the resulting score means nothing. The subtler trap is stopping at TimeSeriesSplit and calling it safe: when the label looks forward, rows near the boundary carry the test period into training and you need purging plus an embargo. The third is reporting the best of two hundred backtests as though it were one.

The math purge and embargo

purge i when [ti​,;ti​+H]∩[T0​,;T1​]=∅  ·  then train resumes at T1​+hH is the label horizon — how far forward you look to compute the answer. Any training row whose label window touches the test window [T0​,T1​] has already seen the test period. The embargo h buys a further margin against serial correlation leaking across the boundary.

Walk forward, then purge

from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit
import numpy as np

HORIZON = np.timedelta64(30, 'D')        # the label looks 30 days forward

# gap= is the embargo, in rows; it landed in scikit-learn 0.24 for exactly this
for tr, te in TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, gap=30).split(X):
    t0 = ts[te].min()
    keep = ts[tr] + HORIZON < t0         # purge rows whose label window crosses t0
    model.fit(X[tr][keep], y[tr][keep])
    score(model, X[te], y[te])

Where this bites in production

scikit-learn added a gap parameter to TimeSeriesSplit in 0.24, in December 2020, for exactly this reason — before that, everyone on the default was training right up to the test boundary. The other named source is López de Prado’s purged k-fold with embargo, which exists because in finance the label is nearly always a forward return, and he shows that running enough backtest variants will hand you a Sharpe of two out of pure noise.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Your TimeSeriesSplit is clean. Can you still leak?
Yes, through the label horizon. If the label is computed over the next thirty days, a training row dated three days before the test block already contains twenty-seven days of the test period. Purge the training rows whose label windows overlap the test window, then add an embargo after it so serial correlation in the features does not carry across either.
Expanding window or sliding window?
Expanding if the process is stationary, sliding if it is not. Expanding keeps all history and gives more data per fold; sliding drops regimes that no longer describe the world. Run both. If the sliding version scores better, old data is actively harmful and you have found concept drift, which is a modelling finding rather than a validation choice.
You ran two hundred backtests and the best has a Sharpe of 2.1. What is it worth?
Almost nothing on its own. The maximum of two hundred noisy statistics is large by construction — that is selection, not skill. Either hold out a period you have never touched and run the single winner on it once, or deflate the statistic for the number of trials and report the deflated figure.

Say this back tomorrow

train on the past, test on the future, and cut the rows that straddle the line
  • Random k-fold on temporal data is the most common leak in the industry
  • TimeSeriesSplit alone is not enough when the label looks forward — purge and embargo
  • The best of two hundred backtests is a selection effect, not a result
