Recommenders & Degenerate Feedback Loops

The model recommends what it already believes, and the catalogue collapses.

The oldest idea in recommendation is that people who agreed before will agree again, so you find the users who look like you and show what they liked. The modern version squeezes every person and every item into a short list of numbers, so that a person and an item which belong together end up pointing the same way. Two problems follow you forever. A brand new user or a brand new item has no history, so there is nothing to match on. And people rarely tell you they dislike something — they just do not click, which could mean anything. Then there is the one that only appears after you ship. Users can only click what you showed them, and what they click trains the next model. So the model teaches itself that it was right.

Like a bookshop that only restocks what sold last week. The front table sells well because it is the front table, so next week it gets more of the same. The shelves at the back sell less, so they get thinner, and eventually the shop holds forty copies of three books. Sales per square foot look excellent right up until nobody comes in.

Collaborative filtering factorises the user-item interaction matrix into low-rank user and item embeddings, and a dot product predicts affinity. With implicit feedback there are no negatives — an absent click is not a dislike — so you either weight all unobserved pairs with low confidence, as in ALS, or sample negatives and accept the noise. In production this is a funnel: retrieval pulls a few thousand candidates by approximate nearest neighbours over embeddings in under 50ms, a heavier ranker scores those inside a 100 to 200ms budget, and a re-ranker applies diversity, freshness and business rules. Cold start is handled with content features, popularity priors, onboarding elicitation and explicit exploration. The failure that only appears after launch is the degenerate feedback loop.

You detect it with diversity metrics, not accuracy metrics — aggregate catalogue coverage, long-tail impression share, and accuracy bucketed by item popularity, which will show the head improving while the tail rots. The two named fixes are randomised exploration, where a slice of impressions is allocated without regard to the score so the logs contain counterfactuals, and positional features, where display position is fed to the model during training and zeroed at serving, so the model learns how much of the click was the slot rather than the item.

You reach for it when

  • Engagement is rising while catalogue coverage falls
  • A good new item never gets any impressions at all
  • Designing a feed, a home page, or a search ranker
  • Someone proposes training purely on logged clicks

The trap

Answering the recommender prompt with matrix factorisation and stopping. Interviewers are listening for three things most candidates never say: the retrieval-then-ranking funnel, that implicit feedback has no negatives so a non-click is an unknown, and the degenerate feedback loop. The specific wrong move is trying to measure the loop with accuracy — accuracy goes up while the catalogue collapses, because the model really is better on the narrower distribution it created.

The math implicit-feedback ALS

minP,Q​;∑u,i​cui​(rui​−pu⊤​qi​)2+λ(∥P∥2+∥Q∥2)The sum runs over all user-item pairs, not just observed ones, and cui​ is a confidence weight — high where you saw an interaction, low but non-zero everywhere else. That is the Hu, Koren and Volinsky formulation, and it is how “no negatives exist” actually gets handled.

The two fixes, in code

# 1. positional feature: teach the model what the slot did, then take it away
train['position'] = impression_position          # 0 = top slot, 39 = bottom of page
model.fit(train[FEATS + ['position']], clicked)

serve['position'] = 0                            # score every candidate as if top slot
scores = model.predict(serve[FEATS + ['position']])

# 2. exploration: a slice of impressions the ranker did not choose
if random.random() < 0.02:
    scores = rng.permutation(scores)             # unbiased labels for the next model

Where this bites in production

YouTube’s 2019 ranking paper describes this fix directly: a shallow side tower takes display position and device as input, is trained jointly with the main model, and is fed a position of zero at serving so the main tower is left with the item’s own merit. TikTok does the other one — every new video gets a small pool of essentially random impressions, so it has a chance to earn its way out of cold start.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Engagement is up 6% and catalogue coverage is down 20%. What is happening?
A degenerate feedback loop. The ranker concentrates impressions on items it already scores highly, those impressions produce the clicks that become the next training set, and popularity compounds. Accuracy will not show it, because the model genuinely is better at the narrower distribution it created. Watch aggregate diversity, long-tail share, and accuracy bucketed by popularity.
How do you handle cold start for a brand new item?
Content features plus a deliberate exploration budget. Embed the item from its own attributes — text, category, creator — so it is placeable before it has any interactions, and back that with a popularity prior. Then spend impressions on it regardless of predicted score, epsilon-greedy or Thompson sampling, because an item with no impressions can never earn any.
Why is an absent click not a negative label?
Because the user may never have seen the item. Implicit feedback gives you positives and unknowns, not positives and negatives — a non-click mixes genuine disinterest with items never shown, or shown at position forty. Either weight the unobserved pairs with low confidence, as ALS does, or sample negatives and accept the label noise.

Say this back tomorrow

the model chooses what users see  ·  what users see becomes what the model learns
  • Retrieval, then ranking, then re-rank — never answer with a single model
  • Implicit feedback has no negatives; a non-click is an unknown
  • The two named fixes are randomised exploration and positional features

Unlocks

  • matrix factorisation
  • implicit feedback
  • cold start
  • feedback loop
  • position bias

SHAP, Permutation Importance & Their Pitfalls

All of them explain the model. None of them explains the world.

There are three common ways to ask a model which inputs mattered. The first asks the trees how often each input was used to make a split, which is fast and free but flatters any input with many distinct values, and it is measured on the data the model was trained on. The second scrambles one input, sees how much worse the model gets, and reports the damage. The third splits every individual prediction into contributions that add up to that prediction. All three tell you what the model is doing. None of them tells you what causes what. If you go and change the thing at the top of the chart, the world is under no obligation to respond the way the chart implies.

Like working out who won the match by taking each player off the pitch. Remove the striker and the score collapses, so the striker mattered. But remove one of two interchangeable full-backs and nothing changes, because the other one covers, and you conclude that neither matters. That is precisely what correlated features do to permutation importance.

Tree gain, or MDI, sums the impurity reduction each feature bought at its splits. It is computed on training data and it is biased toward high-cardinality and continuous features, because a column with many distinct values gets many more chances to fit noise. Permutation importance shuffles one column on a held-out set and measures the loss increase — model-agnostic and honest about the split — but under correlation it evaluates points that cannot exist, so it extrapolates off-manifold and splits credit arbitrarily between correlated columns. Partial dependence has the same defect. SHAP gives per-prediction additive attributions with the Shapley axioms and an exact fast path for trees, but interventional and conditional expectations give different answers under correlation, and neither is a causal effect.

Two more that get asked. A flat partial dependence plot does not mean an unimportant feature: averaging over the other columns can cancel an effect that is strongly positive in one subgroup and negative in another, which is why you look at the individual conditional expectation curves before concluding anything. And when a feature is startlingly important, check leakage before anything else. The canonical case is the number of collection calls predicting loan default — a consequence of the default rather than a cause, so it is both a leak and the reason the model can never tell the business what to do.

You reach for it when

  • A stakeholder asks which features drive the prediction
  • One feature has implausibly high importance
  • Explaining a declined loan or a flagged transaction
  • Someone asks what to change to move the prediction

The trap

Reading a SHAP plot as a causal story. “Lower this feature and the outcome improves” is a claim about the world, and SHAP only attributes the model’s output. The second trap is quoting tree gain at all: it is training-set impurity, biased toward high-cardinality and continuous columns. The third is calling a feature useless because its partial dependence is flat — the effect can live entirely inside an interaction the averaging cancels.

The math local accuracy

ϕ0​+∑j=1M​ϕj​=f(x)  ·  ϕj​=∑S⊆F∖{j}​∣F∣!∣S∣!(∣F∣−∣S∣−1)!​[fS∪{j}​(x)−fS​(x)]The attributions sum exactly to the prediction, and that property is what makes SHAP feel trustworthy. Read the axioms carefully, though: efficiency, symmetry, dummy and additivity together say the split of f(x) is fair. Not one of them says anything about what happens if you intervene on x.

Permutation importance, done honestly

from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

# never quote model.feature_importances_ for a decision: it is MDI, on train data
r = permutation_importance(model, X_val, y_val, n_repeats=20,
                           scoring='neg_log_loss', random_state=0)

for i in r.importances_mean.argsort()[::-1][:5]:
    print(f'{cols[i]:<20} {r.importances_mean[i]:+.4f} +/- {r.importances_std[i]:.4f}')

# correlated columns split the credit and both look useless.
# cluster on Spearman rho first, then permute each cluster as a block.

Where this bites in production

scikit-learn ships a worked example titled “Permutation Importance vs Random Forest Feature Importance” that adds a column of pure random numbers to the Titanic data and shows MDI ranking it near the top, purely because it is continuous and almost unique per row. The default feature_importances_ attribute on every tree ensemble is that same MDI number, computed on the training set, and it is what most people paste into a slide.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Your top feature has suspiciously high importance. What do you check?
Leakage first, cardinality second. Ask whether the value could only be known after the label event — a consequence of the outcome rather than a cause — because that is the most common explanation and it invalidates the whole model. If it is clean, check whether the number came from tree gain, which inflates high-cardinality and continuous columns on training data.
Two features correlate at 0.95. What does permutation importance report?
Roughly zero for both. Permuting one leaves the other intact, the model barely degrades, and each looks unimportant even though the pair matters a great deal. You are also generating rows that cannot exist, so the model is being scored off-manifold. Cluster the correlated columns and permute the whole cluster together.
A feature’s partial dependence plot is flat. Drop it?
No, not on that evidence. Partial dependence averages over the other features, so an effect that is positive for one subgroup and negative for another cancels to a flat line. Plot the individual conditional expectation curves instead — if they fan out, the effect is real and lives inside an interaction.

Say this back tomorrow

these explain the model, not the world  ·  suspiciously important means check for a leak
  • Tree gain is training-set impurity, biased toward high-cardinality columns
  • Permutation and PDP evaluate impossible rows once features correlate
  • A flat PDP can hide an interaction, and SHAP is never causal

  • SHAP
  • PDP and ICE
  • off-manifold

Designing an ML System

The failure is not a wrong answer. It is naming a model in the first minute.

These questions are open on purpose, and the person asking wants to hear an order, not a list. Start with what the business is trying to change and how they would know it worked. Turn that into something a model can predict. Work out where the answers come from and how late they arrive, because that decides almost everything downstream. Then the data, then the simplest thing that could possibly work, and only then a real model. Say how you will judge it before you build it, including on the groups where it will fail. Say how fast it has to answer. Say what you will watch after it ships and what makes you retrain. Then say how it breaks.

Think of a builder pricing an extension. Nobody opens by naming a brand of brick. They ask what you want the room for, what the budget is, where the drains run, what the council will allow, and what happens if it rains in March. The brick is the last decision and the easiest one. Candidates who open with the model have named the brick.

Nine steps, and I say them in order. One, clarify the objective: the business metric, the users, the scale in queries per second, the latency budget. Two, translate that into an ML objective and name where the two diverge. Three, labels — where they come from, natural or hand-annotated, and how delayed. Four, data and features, with point-in-time correctness. Five, a baseline: a rule, the current system, or zero-rule, before any model. Six, the model, justifying each step up in complexity. Seven, the offline evaluation plan, sliced rather than aggregate. Eight, serving — batch or online, the funnel, and how the latency budget is spent. Nine, monitoring, the retraining trigger, and the failure modes. Which nine matters less than never skipping the first.

Fraud, in one pass. Objective: cut chargeback losses without driving away good customers, so the guardrail is the false-decline rate. ML objective: probability this transaction is fraudulent, end to end under 150ms. Labels are chargebacks — weeks late, and censored, because a blocked transaction never generates one. Features are velocity aggregates over sliding windows, precomputed in a streaming store because that is where the latency goes. Baseline is the existing rules engine. Evaluation is precision at fixed recall, sliced by card type and geography, plus expected cost. And the real constraint is the review queue: if analysts clear 500 cases a day, the threshold is whatever produces 500 cases.

You reach for it when

  • Design a recommendation system for a feed
  • Design real-time fraud detection under a 150ms budget
  • Design churn prediction for a SaaS product
  • This model degraded in production — detect and diagnose it

The trap

Naming an architecture in the first minute. Every source lists jumping to a solution as the top failure, and it costs you the whole rubric because steps one to five then never happen. The second trap is a design with no baseline — if you cannot say what a rules engine or a popularity ranker would score, you cannot justify the model you chose. The third is stopping at deployment and never saying what triggers a retrain.

The math the budget is a constraint, not a wish

Tfeature​+Tretrieval​+Trank​+Tnetwork​≤150 msSay this out loud early and allocate it. Feature lookup from a streaming store is typically the largest term, which is why velocity aggregates get precomputed rather than calculated at request time, and why the model you can afford is decided before you choose it.

The threshold is a capacity decision

import numpy as np

p = model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]

# the operating point is set by what the review team can process, never by 0.5
CAPACITY = 500                                  # cases the analysts clear per day
thr = np.quantile(p, 1 - CAPACITY / len(p))     # send exactly the top 500

flag = p >= thr
print(f'recall {y_val[flag].sum() / y_val.sum():.2f} at {flag.sum()} reviews/day')
# move CAPACITY, not the model, when the business wants more coverage

Where this bites in production

KORE1’s 2026 loop runs a full 45-minute round on exactly this, with the numbers stated up front — a 150ms budget for fraud scoring, or a SaaS churn brief with 40,000 customers and six quarters of history. Interviewers score the ordering, not the architecture. Stripe frames Radar the same way from the other side: the expensive error is the false decline, because a blocked good customer costs more than the fraud you stopped.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Where do you start on “design a churn model”?
With the label definition, not the model. Churn over what horizon, measured how, and observed from which window — get that wrong and the observation window overlaps the prediction window and you leak. Then ask what intervention follows a high score, because a churn model with no retention offer attached is a report rather than a system.
Fraud detection, 150ms end to end. What actually constrains the design?
Feature freshness and the review queue. Velocity aggregates over sliding windows are what make the model work and what eats the budget, so you precompute them into a streaming store and read them as a lookup. Downstream, analyst capacity sets the threshold: if the team clears 500 cases a day, the operating point is whatever produces 500 cases.
Precision dropped from 91% to 76% overnight. What do you check first?
A data bug, before anything else. An overnight cliff is almost always a schema change, an upstream pipeline failure, or a feature that went all-null — drift does not move that fast. Then training-serving skew, then covariate versus concept shift, then whether the base rate moved and the threshold is now wrong. Interviewers score the ordering.

Say this back tomorrow

objective → labels → baseline → model → eval → serve → monitor, and never skip the first
  • Jumping to an architecture is the single most-named failure in this round
  • Label definition and label delay decide almost everything downstream
  • Say the baseline, the slices, the latency budget and the retraining trigger

Unlocks

  • business objective
  • label delay
  • baseline first
  • latency budget
  • retraining trigger
